Intentions are not available in detail, which is covered under 5.1.

The outcome domain (pain intensity) was measured with one instrument, the daily diary 11-point NRS, and the 24-week time point is the one named in the methods. Both prespecified thresholds (>=50% and >=30%) are reported, with the favourable 30% result and the null 50% result both given. The extra thresholds in the supplement (70%, 30% worse) are labelled post hoc and are also reported. There is no sign that a result was chosen on its findings.

The ClinicalTrials.gov record was first submitted 2010-11-30 with a start date of 2010-10, so enrolment had already begun and the entry cannot show what was fixed beforehand. It registers only 'Evaluate pain relief at 24 weeks' (other outcome 2) and average diary pain intensity as primary; it does not specify 50%/30% responder thresholds. The main report lists the 50% and 30% responder analysis as a secondary outcome in its methods, but no protocol or SAP was captured and nothing dates the plan before unblinded data. Web Extra file 6 labels the 70% and '30% worse' rows as post hoc.

Table 1 shows broadly similar baseline characteristics across the M1, DLPFC and sham arms. Mean age was somewhat lower in sham (52.9 vs about 56.6), which is compatible with chance in a trial of this size. Group sizes (49/52/48) match the intended ratio. Three patients withdrew after the first randomization and before arm assignment, and they are not part of the 149.

Randomization was centralized at the Clinical Research Unit of the coordinating centre, independent of the enrolling sites. Each patient was identified by a randomization ID entered on the eCRF. The active/sham result was stored on a personalized USB flash drive blinded to investigators, so the allocation was concealed until assignment.

The report states that a computer-based algorithm generated random permuted blocks stratified by study centre, with a first 1:1 randomization to M1 or DLPFC and re-randomization to active or sham at 0.67:0.33. This is a random component.

The analysis population was all randomized patients who received at least one rTMS session (149 of 152, called a modified ITT). The 3 excluded patients withdrew before assignment to an arm, so the exclusion is not related to assignment. Patients were analysed in the groups to which they were randomized. Loss of outcome data at Week 25 is assessed in the missing-data Domain.

An active/placebo figure-of-eight coil with two non-differentiable sides, matching sound, and synchronized scalp electrical stimulation in all arms were used to blind participants. A Week 25 blinding questionnaire showed that guesses of active treatment (58% M1 vs 44% sham) were mostly attributed to efficacy or non-efficacy rather than device cues. Supplementary Table 4 shows no significant difference in guesses between arms (P=0.42 for M1 vs sham). Guesses driven by perceived efficacy do not by themselves show that participants knew their assignment.

Allocation was concealed on a personalized USB drive that was blinded to the investigators. The operator connected the drive to the stimulator and the device selected the active or sham coil side, which was non-differentiable. Active-scalp sensation was mimicked in all arms, and the report states that the procedure fully ensured double blinding.

Only 93 of 149 modified-ITT participants (62%) had Week 25 data; the Week 25 responder proportions are for patient completers. Missing data (~38%) far exceed the number of responders, so outcomes of those missing could matter.
Early dropouts were not imputed and were censored at last visit; no missing-data sensitivity analysis or method addressing informative missingness was found for the Week 25 responder outcome.

Dropout proportions and reasons differed between arms (lack of efficacy mostly in sham/DLPFC, adverse events in DLPFC), and lack of efficacy is directly tied to pain relief; the completer analysis likely overstates the M1 vs sham difference.
Late dropouts were for lack of efficacy (M1 2%, DLPFC 17.3%, sham 25%) and analgesic changes led to discontinuation, so missingness plausibly depended on the pain relief outcome.

The assessor is the participant. Participants were blinded by an active/placebo coil with indistinguishable sound and synchronized scalp electrical stimulation in all arms. The Week 25 blinding questionnaire showed guesses largely efficacy-driven (58% M1 vs 44% sham thought active; not significantly different per Supplementary Table 4), so blinding is not shown to be broken.
Same scale, schedule and 25-week visit structure for all arms; identical session numbers in active and sham arms, so no differential opportunities for ascertainment.
Patient-reported 0-100% pain relief scale (BPI) is a standard, sensitive instrument for analgesic effects, collected at scheduled visits; no sign it is inappropriate.

The >=50% cut-point is one of the two registered responder thresholds (30% and 50%), and a simple proportion with NNT leaves little analytic flexibility. No sign of multiple analyses with a favourable one picked, although the analysis is exploratory without multiplicity adjustment.

The same responder cut-off (>=50%) was reported for both the pain relief scale (NNT 3.1) and the 0-10 NRS (NNT 7.7), the less favourable one included, which argues against picking the most favourable scale. Week 25 is the registered end-of-treatment time point.

The registry record (first submitted 2013-11-07, before the 2014-03 start) lists only a generic secondary outcome 'Proportion of responders to rTMS' (>=30% and >=50% improvement in pain vs pre-treatment, 25 weeks). It does not name the 0-100% pain relief scale, so no dated source specifies this measurement. No protocol or SAP was captured, and the report says only that statisticians were blinded.

Randomized group sizes were 33, 32 and 33 against a 1:1:1 allocation. Table 1 shows two nominally different baseline variables: sex (P = 0.034) and CYP2B6 genotype (P = 0.059). Both are compatible with chance in a small three-arm trial. The authors attribute the imbalance to chance. Other characteristics, such as age, weight, CD4 count, viral load, cavities and smear status, are similar. Sex and genotype could influence PK findings, but they are not obvious determinants of Grade 3 or 4 adverse events. Nothing suggests subversion of randomization.

Sealed, serially numbered, opaque envelopes, each holding the allocated regimen, were sent to the site. Eligible participants were randomized by the clinical investigator at enrolment. The sequence was generated by the statistician, who was independent of enrolment. Mixed block sizes of 3 to 6 limit prediction of the last allocation in a block. This meets the minimal envelope criteria. The report does not say that envelopes were tamper-proof or opened only after irreversible assignment, so the answer is Probably yes rather than Yes.

The randomization list was generated by the trial statistician with nQuery Advisor software, using a fixed randomization method with mixed block sizes of 3 to 6 and a 1:1:1 ratio. Computer generation by a statistician implies a random component. Varying block sizes also make the sequence harder to predict.
Safety population is all enrolled participants with at least one dose; all 98 randomized took at least one dose, so effectively all randomized participants were analysed in their assigned arm.

No non-protocol interventions or trial-context-driven failures of implementation are reported. Toxicity-related switches, discontinuations and the planned Week 8 switch to standard doses are protocol-consistent; intake was directly observed and ATT adherence was reported as high. Protocol is unavailable, so some uncertainty remains.
Open-label trial with different rifampicin/efavirenz doses and directly observed intake; participants knew their regimen.

Open-label; sealed envelopes contained the allocated regimen and were opened by the clinical investigator at enrolment; doses were supplied by site and a domiciliary treatment monitor, so personnel knew assignments.

Table 5 reports AEs for the safety population (N = 33, 32, 33), which covers all 98 randomized participants; safety data were collected from the first dose, so every participant contributes AE data up to their last follow-up. Figure 1 shows only a few early exits (about 3 deaths, 2 lost to follow-up, 1 voluntary withdrawal, 1 MDR-TB, 3 toxicity switches/discontinuations), and participants who died or switched for toxicity had their events recorded. Participants lost before Week 28 could have had unrecorded later events, but the number is small relative to the AE counts and similar across arms.
The trial was open-label and the registry lists masking as none; no outcome-assessor blinding is reported. The clinicians recording and grading AEs delivered care and knew the regimen.

All arms followed the same visit schedule with the same laboratory monitoring and the same DAIDS grading; no arm had extra visits or tests. Passive collection between visits is not described, so some uncertainty remains.

Grade 3/4 events are severe and largely defined by DAIDS laboratory or clinical thresholds; comparators are all active regimens, the assessors are clinicians with no stated strong belief about harm, and the fixed visit schedule limits discretion. Influence is possible but not clearly likely.

Grade 3/4 TEAEs are investigator-reported; laboratory-defined terms follow thresholds, but clinical events (e.g. septic shock, dyspnoea, vomiting) and attribution involve some judgement, so knowledge of the regimen could influence assessment.

AEs were graded with the DAIDS v2.0 table and MedDRA terms, with scheduled symptom assessment, examination and blood counts, ALT, AST and bilirubin. This is a defined system for identifying and grading events, so the method looks suitable for Grade 3/4 events.

Safety outcomes were described as counts and proportions per arm, with ad hoc chi-squared or Fisher tests. No alternative adjusted or composite analyses are mentioned, and all graded terms are tabulated, so there is no sign that one analysis was picked from several.

Grade 3/4 adverse events were graded one way (DAIDS v2.0) over a single window, and Table 5 reports all graded terms by arm, plus the SAE, transaminase and death counts in the text. Nothing suggests that other eligible measurements were collected and left out.

The ClinicalTrials.gov record was first submitted 2013-11-12, before the 2013-12 start, and lists secondary outcome 5 'Grade 3 and 4 adverse events' over 0-28 weeks. The report presents Grade 3/4 TEAEs (DAIDS v2.0) per arm over the same period and describes them as proportions. No protocol or SAP was available, so this rests on the dated registry plan alone; the registry gives no analysis detail.

Table 1 shows near-identical baseline characteristics across arms (age 55-56, HbA1c 8.1% in all arms, BMI 33-34, diabetes duration 9 years). Arm sizes (279/280/276/141) match the 2:2:2:1 ratio. The text states baseline characteristics were balanced. The only visible differences (e.g. number of OAMs at screening, DBP 81 vs 77) are modest and compatible with chance. Baseline data cover all randomized/treated patients.

Allocation used an interactive voice response system, which is a central telephone-based randomization service of the kind the guidance accepts as concealed. The report does not say who ran the system or that it was independent of enrolling staff, so the answer is Probably yes, not Yes. Blinded dosing (placebo-controlled) adds no contrary signal.

The report states patients were randomized 2:2:2:1 'according to a computer-generated random sequence using an interactive voice response system', stratified by country. A computer-generated random sequence is a random component.

Safety analyses used all randomized patients who received at least one dose. Every dulaglutide and placebo participant received a dose (flow: 279/280/141 started; 280/279/141 at risk in the AE table), so no eligible participant in the compared arms was excluded. Only 2 participants in the unused exenatide arm did not take the drug. Participants were analysed in their randomized groups.

The registry record lists quadruple masking (participant, care provider, investigator, outcomes assessor) and the comparator was a once-weekly SC placebo, with placebo patients switched 'in a blinded fashion' at 26 weeks. Dulaglutide and placebo are given by the same route and schedule, so participants were probably unaware of assignment.

The registry lists care providers and investigators as masked, and allocation was by a computer-generated sequence through an interactive voice response system, which suggests concealed allocation. Personnel were probably unaware of assignment.

The AE tables use all randomized participants who received a dose as denominators (280/279/141), so no participant is formally excluded. By 26 weeks, however, 19/279 (6.8%) on 1.5 mg, 17/280 (6.1%) on 0.75 mg and 17/141 (12.1%) on placebo had not completed. About 16/17/10 of these left for lost to follow-up or withdrawal by subject, and nothing read says whether serious events were still captured after withdrawal. The event of interest is rare (1 cholelithiasis event in total), so the observed events do not outnumber the participants whose follow-up may be incomplete, and I cannot say that 'nearly all' participants contributed full data.

No sensitivity analysis or bias-correcting method for missing safety data was found. The AE counts are crude participants-affected over participants-at-risk; the registry mentions LOCF only for efficacy measures, which does not correct bias.

Reasons for non-completion are of a general type and are not specific to cholelithiasis or GI events: lost to follow-up, withdrawal by subject, protocol violation, noncompliance and in placebo lack of efficacy. Reasons are similar in dulaglutide arms. The higher placebo non-completion (12.1% vs about 6.5%) is largely explained by lack of efficacy and hyperglycaemia, which does not relate to the occurrence of a serious GI event. Adverse-event discontinuations were followed for safety. I find no reason that makes dependence of missingness on cholelithiasis likely, although it remains possible.

Reasons for non-completion include lost to follow-up (7/10/5), withdrawal by subject (9/7/5), adverse events, deaths and physician decision. Withdrawal or loss to follow-up could be linked to participants' health, including having a biliary or GI event, so I cannot exclude that missingness could depend on the true outcome.

The registry records quadruple masking, and dulaglutide was compared against a placebo injection given on the same weekly schedule, so participants and investigators who judge and report serious AEs were blinded for the placebo-controlled 26-week period. Nothing reports unblinding. Pancreatic events were additionally adjudicated by an independent committee. The exenatide arm was an open-label-type BID regimen but it is not part of this comparison.

Serious AEs were collected by the same systematic assessment and MedDRA coding in all arms, with the same scheduled visits and central laboratory monitoring. Dulaglutide and placebo were both once-weekly injections, so the contact schedule was comparable between the arms being compared here. Patients who stopped drug for an AE stayed in for safety follow-up in all arms. No source describes passive collection or extra visits in one arm.

Serious AEs were collected through a systematic-assessment AE module coded with MedDRA 15.0 (CT.gov), with protocol-specified safety assessments (AEs, vitals, ECG, serial hepatobiliary and pancreatic enzyme labs at a central laboratory). A defined system for identifying and coding events was in place, so the method is unlikely to be insensitive for serious GI events such as cholelithiasis.

The reported value is a raw count of participants affected over participants at risk per arm. Counts of serious AEs allow essentially one analysis, and the article describes only a chi-square/Fisher test for AE percentages. No evidence of several analyses with selective reporting.

The result is a simple count of participants with a serious AE of one MedDRA preferred term over a single window (baseline to 26 weeks), taken from a registry table that lists every serious AE term by arm, including zero-event terms (e.g. cholecystitis acute, GERD). The table is not a subset chosen from a larger set of measurements of the same outcome, so there is no evident opportunity for results-based selection among measurements. The 52-week period is reported separately by design.

No protocol or SAP is among the Sources, and the registry capture lists no linked documents. The registry record was first submitted 2010-02-05 with start date 2010-02, so the month of enrolment start and the submission coincide and the record cannot show that it preceded enrolment or unblinded data. The current record also cannot show earlier versions. The record registers only an overall TEAE-count outcome, not serious cholelithiasis (or the other serious GI terms) as a specified measurement; those appear only in the results Reported Adverse Events module. No source dated before outcome data specifies this measurement or its analysis.

The report states 'Baseline characteristics were similar between treatment groups (table 1)'. Table 1 shows close balance in sex, BMI, weight, diabetes duration, HbA1c (8.04 / 8.04 / 8.05%), fasting glucose, blood pressure and metformin use (94% / 96% / 96%). Group sizes (142 / 142 / 140) match the 1:1:1 ratio. Age differences (mean 56.2 / 58.6 / 57.1; aged >=65 16% / 31% / 22%) are modest and not beyond chance for a trial of this size. No baseline imbalance suggesting a randomisation problem. No GI-haemorrhage-specific risk factor (e.g. NSAID or anticoagulant use) is tabulated.

Allocation was done through a central IWRS: 'Randomisation was done by site personnel who accessed the sponsor's interactive web-response system. The system assigned cartons of double-blind study drug for each patient', with site staff confirming the correct carton by entering a confirmation number from the label. The protocol adds that active and placebo pens are identical-looking, packed in cartons dispensed via IWRS, and that only a minimum number of sponsor staff see the randomisation table. Central web-based allocation with identical masked packs conceals the sequence until participants are irrevocably assigned.

The protocol states 'Assignment to treatment groups will be determined by a computer-generated random sequence using an interactive web-response system (IWRS)' with block randomisation at country level and stratification (HbA1c, SGLT2 inhibitor dose, metformin use). The main report says 'The system assigned cartons of double-blind study drug for each patient using a computer-generated random sequence.' This is a random component in the sequence generation.

The safety analysis population is the ITT population, 'defined as all randomly assigned patients who received at least one injected dose of study drug', and the registry AE table reports 'All participants who received at least one dose of study drug' (denominators 142 / 141 / 140). One randomised patient (0.75 mg group) who 'did not receive any doses of study drug' and completed the study was excluded. In RoB 2 terms this is an exclusion based on the intervention received, not on missing outcome data, so the analysis is not a strict analysis by randomised group. All other randomised participants were analysed in their assigned groups.

AWARD-10 was 'double-blind' with 'Patients and investigators ... masked to dulaglutide and placebo assignment'; the protocol defines double-blind as neither the patient nor investigator or sponsor staff involved in treatment or evaluation being aware of treatment. Placebo and dulaglutide were delivered as identical-looking single-dose pens in numbered cartons allocated via IWRS. Dulaglutide-associated GI effects (nausea 15% vs 4%) could partly reveal assignment, but they are common, non-specific and also occurred with placebo, so there is no strong reason to think blinding failed.

Investigators were masked ('Patients and investigators were masked to dulaglutide and placebo assignment'). The protocol states that neither patients nor investigator or sponsor staff involved in treatment or clinical evaluation are aware of treatment, and allocation was concealed through IWRS with identical pens, so carers and people delivering the intervention were probably unaware. Only a minimum number of sponsor personnel see the randomisation table; the sponsor performed masked trial-level safety reviews.

Only one of 424 randomised participants (0.2%) was excluded, a patient who never received study drug and therefore could not have had a drug-emergent serious GI haemorrhage; exclusion was not related to prognosis in a double-blind trial. Although the outcome is rare (1 event in total) the single exclusion had no plausible way to change the event counts of 0 / 1 / 0, so the potential for substantial impact is small.

CONSORT shows 424 randomized (142/142/140) and early study discontinuation in 7/5/3 patients (15, 3.5%), with 135/137/137 completing; the registry AE table uses safety denominators 142/141/140 (all participants with at least one dose), so one undosed 0.75 mg patient has no AE data. AE data for the other discontinuers exist only up to the time they left, so follow-up for GI haemorrhage was incomplete in about 3.5% of participants. For a rare dichotomous event (1 observed event), the guidance says the observed events must greatly exceed the number with missing data for bias to be necessarily small; here 15 participants with incomplete follow-up exceed the single observed event, so 'nearly all' cannot be confirmed.

The paper's sensitivity analyses (MMRM, LOCF, rescue data) address HbA1c, not adverse events. No analysis or sensitivity analysis for GI haemorrhage addressing participants lost to follow-up was found; AEs are reported as simple counts among dosed participants.

Proportions with early discontinuation were small and modestly different (7/5/3, i.e. 4.9%, 3.5%, 2.1%). Reasons were mixed and none is reported as GI haemorrhage; the single observed event was captured. Nothing indicates that missingness was likely driven by the occurrence of GI haemorrhage, although the higher 1.5 mg discontinuation with AEs and deaths leaves some concern.

Early study discontinuations included adverse events (2, 1.5 mg arm), deaths (2, 1.5 mg arm), lost to follow-up and withdrawals. Discontinuation for adverse events or death can plausibly be related to health status and so to occurrence of a serious AE such as GI haemorrhage, so missingness could depend on the true value of the outcome.

The trial was double-blind with identical pens, and the protocol and SAP specify masking of patients, investigators and outcome assessors, with unblinding limited to defined circumstances. The investigators who judged and reported SAEs were therefore blinded to assignment; the funder's safety reviews were masked.

AEs/SAEs were collected under the same protocol-specified reporting process, visit schedule and MedDRA coding in all three arms, from baseline to end of study; all arms had the same weekly injection and visit schedule, and no extra contacts differ by arm. Dulaglutide's GI side effects (nausea, diarrhoea) could prompt more clinical contact, but a serious bleed would be investigated and reported regardless of arm, so diagnostic detection differences are unlikely to be material.

GI haemorrhage was captured as a serious adverse event: the protocol defines SAEs (death, hospitalization, life-threatening, disability, medically significant), requires site reporting to the sponsor within 24 hours, and the registry codes events by MedDRA 20.0 with SYSTEMATIC_ASSESSMENT. A systematic, defined AE-reporting system for a serious, clinically conspicuous event is appropriate for detecting GI haemorrhage; an SAE-level bleed is unlikely to be missed.

The result is a simple arm-wise count of participants with the event in the dosed population, which is the protocol's planned summary (counts and proportions per treatment group). Only one analysis of this count is possible in the reported form, and no alternative analyses were reported or suggested.

The result is a participant count of a single MedDRA preferred term over the whole study period, from a table that lists all serious AE terms with events, not a chosen subset. There is one way to ascertain the event and one time window, so no opportunity to choose among measurements. The main article's statement on pancreatic cancer, C-cell hyperplasia, medullary thyroid carcinoma and cholelithiasis concerns different terms.

The protocol (section 9.5.2) prespecifies that all AEs and SAEs will be coded with MedDRA and reported by preferred term and system organ class, with counts and proportions per treatment group. The GI haemorrhage result is one preferred-term row in the registry's systematically generated SAE table (MedDRA 20.0), so it follows that prespecified AE reporting rather than a bespoke analysis. The registry record was first submitted 2015-11-03, at the start of enrolment (start 2015-11), long before results. GI haemorrhage is not itself a named prespecified outcome, and the protocol and SAP dates relative to unblinding are not established.

Table 1 shows baseline characteristics for all randomized patients (144 vs 147, consistent with the 1:1 ratio) as broadly balanced. No imbalance beyond chance that would suggest a randomization problem is apparent.

Allocation used a central interactive web response system, and the study drug was supplied in identical cartons with unmarked injection devices, with allocation masked from patients, investigators and sponsor staff. The SAP (p27) says treatment assignments are blinded to patients and investigators and that only a minimum number of sponsor personnel see the randomization table. Central IWRS allocation meets the minimal criterion. The reports do not explicitly state that the IWRS was run independently of enrolment staff, so this is Probably yes rather than Yes.

The report states 'Randomization was implemented using a computer-generated random sequence and an interactive web response system', stratified by HbA1c and OAD use. A computer-generated random sequence has a random component.

Safety analyses were by assigned arm in all randomized patients who received at least one dose (SAP: ITT; safety data not censored). The registry AE denominators are 144 and 147, which equal the 291 randomized, so no randomized participant appears excluded from the safety analysis. The 'at least one dose' definition could in principle exclude participants but none were excluded here.

Allocation was masked from patients; placebo once weekly was given in 'identical cartons containing unmarked injection devices'. The SAP (p27) states assignments are blinded to patients and investigators until study end and that unblinded patients must be discontinued. Nothing reported suggests blinding failed. Dulaglutide has known GI effects, which could in principle hint at assignment, but placebo-arm GI AEs were also common and no unblinding is reported.

Allocation was masked from investigators and sponsor staff involved in treatment or clinical evaluation; identical cartons with unmarked devices were used and allocation was central (IWRS), with emergency unblinding only via IWRS and recorded.

Gastritis is a treatment-emergent AE recorded and summarized for the whole safety population. The registry reports 144 dulaglutide and 147 placebo participants (all 291 randomized) for adverse events: Gastritis 2/144 vs 1/147. The main article states safety was analysed in all randomized patients who received at least one dose. AEs were summarized descriptively with no exclusion for missing post-baseline measures, and 94.8% completed the study, so outcome data were effectively available for all or nearly all randomized participants. A few early study discontinuations (4 reported) could have truncated AE ascertainment, but AE data up to discontinuation were captured.

Allocation was masked from patients, investigators and sponsor staff involved in treatment or clinical evaluation, using identical cartons with unmarked injection devices and matching placebo. The AE assessors (participants reporting and investigators recording and coding) were therefore blinded, and the sources report no breaking of the blind.

AEs were collected over the same baseline-to-32-week window in both arms, with the same coding system and the same visit schedule for a once-weekly injection versus matching placebo; the registry reports a single AE reporting description for all randomized participants. Nothing suggests the active drug creates extra contacts or prompts differential testing. A higher GI TEAE incidence on dulaglutide is a plausible true drug effect, not evidence of different ascertainment.

Gastritis was captured as a systematically assessed, MedDRA 24.1-coded adverse event (registry: 'SYSTEMATIC_ASSESSMENT MedDRA 24.1'), with a pre-specified safety analysis in the SAP. Routine AE collection with standard coding is not unlikely to detect plausible effects, and no poor-validity instrument is involved.

The SAP plans a single analysis for AEs: counts and proportions of patients with events per arm in the ITT population, compared with Fisher's exact tests. The registry and paper report exactly these counts for all randomized participants who received at least one dose, with no adjusted or alternative models, so there is no evidence of choosing among multiple analyses.

The SAP specifies that all AEs and TEAEs are listed and summarized by MedDRA preferred term and SOC with counts and proportions per arm, and the registry reports all serious AEs and all non-serious AEs above a 1% threshold in both arms. Gastritis is reported as one MedDRA preferred-term count over the single safety window. There is one way to count participants with a gastritis AE, so the result was not plausibly picked from several measurements or time points.

The SAP revision history states 'SAP Version 2.0 was proved prior to first unblinding' (the protocol was approved 06-March-2020 and v1.0 before first patient visit). The SAP states that it 'describes all priori statistical analyses for efficacy and safety' and plans summaries of TEAEs, SAEs and discontinuations due to AEs, with counts and proportions per arm compared by Fisher's exact test, in the ITT population. Sponsor and trial-level unblinding was planned only after database lock. The registry AE table (all randomized, MedDRA-coded, 1% threshold for non-serious events) and the paper follow this plan. The cover page carries a 29-Jun-2022 approval date, after primary completion on 2022-04-28, but the revision history dates v2.0 before first unblinding. The registry record was submitted 2020-10-16, before enrolment began on 2020-12-07, but registers only efficacy outcomes, not AEs.

Table 1 baseline characteristics for all 276 randomized participants (138 per arm) are similar, and baseline pain (5.6 vs 5.8) and disability (9.6 vs 10) are balanced; any differences are compatible with chance.

Allocation used sequentially numbered, sealed, opaque envelopes opened after baseline assessment, with the sequence generated by a person independent of the trial. Tamper-proofing and irreversible-assignment safeguards are not fully described, and envelopes are somewhat manipulable, so Probably yes rather than Yes. Variable small block sizes limit predictability.
The report describes a computer-generated blocked allocation sequence with varying block sizes, generated by a person independent of the trial, which is a random component.

Analysis was by randomized group in a linear mixed model of all participants with outcome data (modified ITT excluding only those with missing outcomes, which is assessed under missing data). No per-protocol or as-treated exclusion was used for this result.

Intervention delivery was audited for fidelity with no concerns, attendance was high and similar across arms, and no non-protocol co-intervention or contamination attributable to the trial context was reported.

Participants were masked using a time-matched sham/attention control, and credibility and expectancy at 2 weeks did not differ between groups (29.3 vs 27.4, P=.10). Blinding cannot be guaranteed, so Probably no.
Treating clinicians delivering the intervention and control could not be masked to what they delivered; masking was of participants and outcome assessors only.

Pain at 52 wk was available for 257 of 276 randomized participants (93%): 128/138 intervention and 129/138 control; 19 missing (10 vs 9; lost to follow-up or withdrew), balanced between arms. The 95% guide for continuous outcomes is just missed, but the missing 7% is too few to alter the estimate materially: to move the -0.5 difference by even 0.5 points, the missing participants' arm difference would need to be implausibly large on a 0-10 scale. Part of the shortfall was administrative (trial closed early for lack of funding), unrelated to the outcome value. The mixed model also used each participant's earlier pain measurements.

The outcome is participant-reported, so the participant is the assessor. Participants were masked to the intervention through a sham procedure and attention control. Credibility and treatment-expectation scores at 2 wk were similar between arms (29.3 vs 27.4, P=.10), which supports that masking was maintained. No report of broken blinding was found. Residual doubt remains because the intervention is behavioural and complete masking cannot be guaranteed.

Both arms completed the same NRS questionnaire at the same scheduled time points. Both received the same number of sessions (median 12 each) and the same contact structure, because the control was an attention control with sham procedures. Intervention does not create extra detection opportunities for a self-reported scale.

Pain intensity was the pre-specified primary outcome, measured as mean pain over the previous week on a standard 0-10 numerical rating scale, a widely used and validated self-report instrument sensitive to the effects seen here (18-wk difference -1.0, 52-wk -0.5).

One prespecified analysis (a linear mixed model with group-by-time interaction) produced all time-point estimates, with a single planned missing-data approach (likelihood-based under MAR). No alternative adjusted or unadjusted, change-score or final-value analyses of pain are described as run and withheld. The CACE analysis was a prespecified additional analysis and is reported alongside, which counts against selection.

The pain domain was measured with a single instrument (past-week average pain, 11-point NRS) at baseline, 18, 26 and 52 weeks. Table 2 reports all three follow-up time points (-1.0, -0.7, -0.5) plus the overall effect, so the 52-week result was not picked from an unreported set. The 18-week primary designation was fixed in the protocol and SAP.

Protocol version 5 (27 Nov 2015) was submitted to ethics before the first participant was randomised. It specified pain intensity (past-week 11-point NRS), measurement at baseline and 18, 26 and 52 weeks, intention-to-treat analysis by a blinded statistician, and linear mixed models with random intercepts and contrasts at each follow-up time point. The 52-week estimate in Table 2 is one such contrast from that model. The SAP was drafted on 2 Mar 2020, after follow-up ended, so it cannot itself date the plan before unblinded data. However, it matches the earlier protocol (same mixed model with time-by-group interactions; effects at each time point), so the reported result does not depend on a post-hoc plan. The one protocol change (June 2016: sample size and RMDQ moved from primary to secondary) predates outcome data and does not concern this pain result.

Table 1 shows similar groups on age, sex, severity (SAPS II), diagnosis, blood gases and oxygen supply, all p>=0.1; group sizes 26 vs 27 after exclusions are compatible with 1:1 allocation; no excess of significant differences. Table 1 covers analysed participants only (4 excluded), a minor limitation.

Envelopes were opaque, sealed and numbered 'to ensure concealment and sequential use', meeting the minimal envelope criteria in outline. Residual doubt: the same investigators generated the table, prepared the envelopes and enrolled patients, and the report does not say envelopes were opened only after irreversible assignment or whether tamper-proof measures were used. Two-site trial with consecutive enrolment and balanced arms makes subversion unlikely, so Probably yes rather than No.
Methods state the investigators generated a random-number table on a computer and used it to prepare envelopes for random allocation.

Four of 57 randomized patients (2 per group) were excluded from analysis for 'lack of exhaustive data'. It is not clear whether this means missing outcome data or missing other data. For ICU mortality, which is probably available for all randomized patients, this looks like exclusion of eligible randomized participants, which is not a full ITT analysis.

The intervention was a single 3-min preoxygenation immediately before standardized rapid-sequence intubation, leaving little opportunity for trial-context-driven switching or co-interventions. The report describes no non-protocol changes arising from the trial context. The authors note that investigators were sometimes part of the primary clinician teams, but they report no deviations arising from this.

Face-mask NIV versus a bag-valve mask cannot be masked, and the authors state the study could not be blinded. Patients were awake and hypoxemic when preoxygenated, so they were probably aware of the assigned mask.
The clinicians delivering preoxygenation operated an ICU ventilator with a face mask or a bag-valve mask and so knew the assignment. The authors confirm the study was unblinded.

The exclusions affected 4 of 57 (7%) and were balanced, 2 per group. The stated reason concerns data completeness rather than prognosis or assigned intervention. The impact on ICU mortality is probably modest relative to the observed 50% versus 30% difference, though the trial is small and the reason is vague.

Table 4 reports ICU mortality for 26 control and 27 NIV patients, but 4 of 57 randomized patients (7%, 2 per group) were left out of the analysis for 'lack of exhaustive data'. Whether their ICU vital status was known is not reported. About 21 deaths were observed against 4 patients with unaccounted outcomes, and the between-arm difference is only 5 deaths. The four missing patients could therefore have changed the estimate importantly, so data are not clearly available for nearly all randomized participants.
The report gives no sensitivity analysis or bias-correcting method for the 4 excluded patients. The analysis is a complete-case analysis of 53 patients.

Exclusions were identical between groups (2 per group), so there is no differential missingness. The reported reason is the same for both groups. A difference of one or two participants is not itself evidence of outcome-dependent missingness, and nothing in the circumstances makes outcome dependence likely.

In critically ill hypoxemic ICU patients, incomplete data could be linked to early death or to rapid clinical deterioration, so missingness could depend on the outcome. The reason given is vague and not shown to be unrelated to the outcome.
The authors state the study could not be blinded and investigators were sometimes part of the clinical teams. Nothing indicates that the people recording ICU death were blinded.

Death in the ICU was ascertained in the same way in both groups, through routine inpatient follow-up of all patients in the same units. The 3-min preoxygenation intervention creates no extra contacts or detection opportunities for mortality.
ICU death is an observer-reported event involving no judgement, so knowing the assignment could not influence its recording.
ICU mortality (death during the ICU stay) is a routinely recorded, unambiguous event, and recording it in the ICU is an appropriate method.

The result is a simple count per arm with a single p value (chi-square or Fisher as stated for the study); no adjusted or alternative analyses are indicated, and the text reports it as not different between groups regardless of direction.
ICU mortality is an all-cause death count during the ICU stay, so there is essentially one way to measure the outcome domain; the table reports it for both arms in full.

No protocol, SAP or registry record dated before outcome data was captured. The article names only the primary (SpO2 drop during ETI) and secondary (PaO2) endpoints; ICU mortality appears only as an outcome in Table 4, so no pre-specified source is known to specify this measurement or its analysis.

Table 1 and Table 2 show similar groups (age, SAPS II, SOFA, organ failures, PaO2/FiO2, prior NIV 46% vs 45%). The Knaus functional-limitation distribution differs somewhat (no limitation 47% vs 31%) but is a single modest difference compatible with chance, and group sizes (99 vs 102) fit 1:1. The Fig 1 flow chart shows 207 enrolled, with duplicate inclusions and one consent loss explaining the exclusions.

Assignment was by an interactive voice response system at a central randomisation centre, remote from enrolling sites, which meets the guidance criterion for central allocation; an SOP was also used to prevent knowledge of the list.

The report says patients were randomised 1:1 via a central interactive voice response system, stratified by centre and prior ventilation, in a multicentre trial run with an academic clinical research unit. The sequence-generation method (e.g. computer random numbers) is not stated, but central IVR allocation with stratification makes a random sequence reasonable to assume. No protocol is available (registry lists no documents).

The analysis is stated as intention-to-treat, all randomised patients analysed as randomised. Table 4 denominators (99 and 102) equal the analysed numbers in Fig 1. The six excluded patients were duplicate enrolments (included twice) and one lack-of-consent withdrawal, which are not exclusions of eligible participants influenced by assignment.

Both preoxygenation methods were standardised (3 min, 100% FiO2, rapid sequence induction by a senior physician). No non-protocol co-interventions or trial-context-driven deviations are reported. Any preoxygenation failures would be consequences of the intervention itself rather than arising from the trial context. Deviation reporting is limited and no protocol is available.
The trial is explicitly open-label; NIV versus face-mask preoxygenation cannot be concealed from the patient, so participants were aware of their assigned intervention during the trial.
Open-label design with a visibly different device (NIV vs bag-valve-mask) delivered by clinicians, so personnel delivering the intervention were aware of assignment.

Table 4 reports death for NIV n=99 and face mask n=102, which equal the 201 patients analysed in Fig 1 (all randomised after removal of duplicate enrolments and one consent withdrawal). Death in the ICU is an event that is routinely recorded, and the report describes no loss to follow-up for mortality. The 69 observed deaths would greatly outnumber any plausibly unascertained participants. The report does not explicitly state that vital status was ascertained for every patient, so the answer is probably yes rather than yes.
The trial is open-label and the data were recorded in case report forms by the treating teams, so those recording the outcome were aware of the assigned intervention.

Both arms were managed in the same ICUs under the same protocol. Mortality was recorded with the same definition (death in the ICU within 28 days) in both arms, and there is no reason to expect different detection opportunities. Passive collection and extra contacts do not apply to a death event.
All-cause death in the ICU is an observer-reported outcome that involves no judgement. Knowledge of the assigned intervention is unlikely to influence its assessment.
Death in the ICU within 28 days is a pre-specified secondary endpoint (endpoint 6) and a simple, valid, routinely recorded event. It is sensitive to plausible effects of the intervention.

The Methods describe one analysis for binary variables (multivariate logistic regression including group, centre and strata) and the ITT population. The death result is reported once (31.3% vs 37.3%, P=0.76) and the text states no centre or strata interaction effects. There is no sign of several analyses with only one reported, though without a SAP this is inferred.

All-cause death in the ICU within 28 days has one way of being measured, and it is reported once at the planned follow-up in Table 4 and the text. No other time point or measure of mortality is described in the Methods, so there is little opportunity to select among measurements.

The ClinicalTrials.gov record NCT00472160 was first submitted 2007-05-10, before enrolment began (article: July 2007 to January 2010), so it is a dated plan. It lists 'Mortality' (time frame 'in reanimation', i.e. in ICU) as a registered secondary outcome. The article lists ICU death within 28 days as endpoint 6 in its Methods and analyses it with the single method it describes for binary variables (logistic regression with group, centre and strata). No protocol or SAP is available, and the registry gives no 28-day window or analysis detail, so correspondence is inferred. The null result is not the basis for this answer.

Group sizes were 78 vs 79. Of about 25 baseline comparisons in Table 2, only age (P=.02) and haemoglobin (P=.01) were nominally significant, and diabetes was P=.07. The age difference is 1 year in medians. This is compatible with chance and none approaches P<0.001.

Patients were randomized using a web-based interactive response system, a central remote allocation method independent of enrolment staff. Variable block size limits predictability of the last allocations in a block.
The original AVATAR paper states the assignment was computer-generated and stratified by centre using a permuted-block sequence with variable block size, which is a random component.
All analyses were intention-to-treat as randomized, and all 157 patients were included. One early-surgery patient lost to follow-up was censored and still analysed.

Crossover from conservative care to surgery (35/79) was driven by protocol-defined indications (symptom onset, AS progression, LVEF decline), as Table 3 and the protocol show, so it is consistent with the protocol rather than trial-context driven. Surgical delays beyond 8 weeks arose from the COVID-19 public-health emergency and were documented as an anticipated minor deviation in the SAP amendment. Four early-surgery patients did not receive surgery as assigned, for reasons like infection or declining, which could occur outside a trial.
The registry lists masking as NONE, and the comparison is surgical valve replacement versus watchful waiting, which cannot be hidden from participants.
Open-label surgery versus conservative care means clinicians and surgeons delivering care knew the assignment. Allocation was concealed until assignment, but blinding afterwards was impossible.

All 157 randomized patients were analysed and median follow-up was 63 months. Only one patient (early-surgery arm) was lost to follow-up and censored at last contact, so 1/157 (0.6%) has incomplete outcome data. This is far fewer than the observed deaths, so any outcome for that patient could not materially change the HR of 0.44.

The trial was open-label (registry masking: none), and the report states that DSMB members were not blinded to allocation when reviewing events. Site investigators recording deaths were also aware of the allocation.

Both arms followed the same protocol schedule, and COVID-related phone follow-up applied to patients regardless of arm. Death is hard to miss, so any difference in contact opportunities (e.g. surgery visits) is unlikely to change ascertainment of death.

All-cause death is an observer-reported outcome that involves no judgement, so knowledge of the intervention is unlikely to influence its assessment, even though the assessors were aware of the allocation.

All-cause death is a pre-specified, objective event ascertained through scheduled follow-up (6-monthly in year 1, then yearly), phone contact when in-person visits were not possible, and review of medical records for any registered event. Nothing suggests an insensitive method or an instrument with poor validity.

Time-to-event secondary outcomes were analysed with the same Kaplan-Meier, log-rank and Cox model (treatment only) used for the primary outcome, and the same method was used in the 2022 paper. No covariate-adjusted or alternative models are described, and the long-term and 3-year analyses are both reported.

All-cause death is a single, unambiguous event, so there is essentially one way to measure the outcome domain. The registered time frames were 36 months and 5 years. The 2024 report states that all-cause death was analysed over the full follow-up and also restricted to 3 years, so no eligible time point appears to have been omitted in favour of a more favourable one.

The registry entry (first submitted 30 Apr 2015, before enrolment began in June 2015) names all-cause death only as a component of composite outcomes. It does not list time to all-cause death as a separate outcome. The Circulation 2022 and EHJ 2024 reports describe 'time to death' as a prespecified secondary end point analysed with Kaplan-Meier and Cox models, citing a published protocol. That protocol is not among the captured Sources, and the report statements are not date-stamped before unblinded data. The only SAP-type document is an amendment dated 4 Jan 2021 about COVID surgical delays. No dated source therefore specifies this measurement and analysis.

Group sizes (22 vs 9) match the intended 2:1 ratio. Table 1 shows differences in sex, BMI, blood pressure, eGFR and baseline UPCR, but with 31 randomized patients these are compatible with chance, no extreme P values or excess of significant differences are reported, and the report describes groups as comparable. Baseline UPCR was lower in the cemdisiran arm (1.55 vs 1.97), and the analysis adjusted for baseline log UPCR. Residual uncertainty remains because of the very small sample.

Treatment assignments were maintained by an Interactive Response System (central, remote allocation), the stratification factor was recorded in it, and drug was identically packaged with site personnel and patients blinded. The fixed block size of three is a theoretical predictability risk, but assignments were centrally held and the trial was double-blind, so the last allocation in a block could not be inferred. Who ran the system and how assignments were released is not detailed.

Main report states patients were randomly assigned 2:1 using permuted blocks of three, stratified by baseline urine protein; the supplement states permuted block randomization with assignments maintained in an Interactive Response System. Permuted-block randomization has a random order within blocks.

Efficacy was analysed in the mITT set, with patients grouped by randomized assignment. The set requires any study drug and a baseline plus at least one post-baseline 24-hour UPCR. Figure 2A shows 22 cemdisiran and 9 placebo patients at baseline, equal to the 31 randomized, so apparently nobody was excluded. The MMRM uses all available data to week 32. A 'received any study drug' criterion would be an inappropriate exclusion if it removed anyone, but all randomized patients appear to be included.

Double-blind placebo-controlled design: all site personnel and patients were blinded to study drug up to week 36, and cemdisiran and placebo were packaged identically. Nothing reported suggests unblinding through intervention-specific side effects.

All site personnel were blinded, drug packaging was identical, assignments were held by a central Interactive Response System, and syringes were masked by a site pharmacist before a healthcare professional administered the dose. Only the independent DMC had access to unblinded data.

Of 31 randomized patients (22 cemdisiran, 9 placebo), Figure 2A shows week-32 24-hour UPCR data for 29 (cemdisiran 21/22, placebo 8/9; 93.5%). The two without week-32 data are the two patients who died (one per arm). The MMRM includes all available post-baseline data, and all 31 contribute to the mITT. Availability is just under the usual 95% guide for continuous outcomes and the placebo arm is small, so 'probably yes' rather than 'yes'.

The outcome is an automated laboratory value from a central laboratory. Per the supplement, all site personnel and patients were blinded to treatment through week 36 using a randomization system, identical packaging and pharmacist-masked syringes, so neither participants nor staff handling samples knew assignment. The laboratory is not described as unblinded.

Both arms had the same schedule, the same central-laboratory 24-hour urine method, the same validity criteria and the same visits; dosing was q4w in both arms with placebo matched. Nothing in the reports suggests extra contacts or passive detection in one arm.

The prespecified primary end point is 24-hour UPCR, an established, objective measure of proteinuria in IgA nephropathy, analysed by a central laboratory. Baseline and week-32 values are the average of two valid 24-hour collections with defined validity criteria (22-26 h, no missed voids). Nothing suggests insensitivity to plausible effects or poor validity.

The supplement and SAP prespecify the MMRM (treatment, visit, treatment-by-visit, log baseline, random patient effect) as the primary analysis in the mITT set, with a stratified rank ANCOVA as sensitivity analysis. The article reports the MMRM as primary, and the registry results use the same MMRM. The registry reports the same -37.367% estimate. Alternative analyses were prespecified as sensitivity analyses rather than competitors; the article's primary report matches the prespecified one.

The prespecified primary outcome is a single measurement, week-32 percent change in 24-hour UPCR. The registry and the article use the same measurement and time point, and the secondary measurements (spot UPCR, 24-hour urine protein, remission, >50% reduction, hematuria) are all registered and all reported. The MMRM also yields the week-16 values in Figure 2A, so no measurement was dropped. Nothing suggests this result was picked from alternatives.

The registry record was first submitted on 2019-02-13, before the start date of 2019-09-30, and lists as its primary outcome 'Percent Change From Baseline in UPCR as Measured in 24-hour Urine at Week 32'. This matches the reported measurement and time point. The SAP specifies the 24-hour UPCR MMRM on log baseline-adjusted data (supplement/SAP section 5.1), and states the study stays blinded until the last patient completes Week 36, with only the DMC seeing informal unblinded looks. The report analyses the outcome as its Methods describe (MMRM, mITT). Caveats: the current SAP is Amendment 2 dated 31 March 2022, which is after primary completion (17 March 2022) and the exact unblinding date is not given, and the registry text is the current version, not the 2019 one. Because registration predates enrolment and names this measurement and time point, and the SAP describes unblinding only after all patients finish week 36, 'probably yes' is justified.

Randomized numbers were 64 vs 64, as intended for 1:1. Table 1 (analysed 61 vs 61) shows similar disease stage, comorbidity, neoadjuvant chemotherapy scheduling (85.2% vs 83.6%) and smoking, with modest differences in age (61 vs 64 years), male sex (57% vs 69%) and BMI (25.5 vs 27.1). No P values are given, and these differences are compatible with chance in a trial of this size. They do not clearly suggest a randomization problem.

Allocation designations were sequentially numbered and placed in opaque, sealed envelopes opened by the investigator at the time of randomization, with variable block sizes (4 and 6) limiting prediction of the last allocation in a block. This matches the guidance's envelope method, but the report does not state tamper-proof sealing or that envelopes were opened only after irreversible assignment, and the opening was done by an investigator rather than an independent unit; the registry adds nothing on concealment. A judgement of probably yes rather than yes follows.

Methods state allocation 1:1 was determined by a computer-generated randomization schedule stratified by neoadjuvant treatment using random permuted blocks of 4 and 6, created with the sealedenvelope.com online tool. This is a random component with varied block sizes.

Of 128 randomized, 6 (3 per arm) were excluded after randomization: 3 for screening errors (did not meet inclusion criteria, so ineligibility could not have been influenced by assignment) and 3 who withdrew consent (a missing-outcome issue for Domain 3). A further 4 (2 per arm) did not undergo surgery (1 died of sudden cardiac arrest before surgery, 3 unfit), so the postoperative 90-day outcome is undefined for them (also a Domain 3 matter). The remaining 59 per arm were analysed as randomized. This is close to a modified ITT confined to ineligible or outcome-unavailable participants rather than a per-protocol analysis by adherence.

The report describes intervention delivery and adherence monitoring (diary, routine telephone calls) and reports no adverse events related to prehabilitation. It identifies a risk of contamination in the control group and the lack of an objective adherence measure as limitations, but it does not report that control participants sought prehabilitation or that staff gave non-protocol co-interventions. Only some controls were recommended nutritional supplements for 10-14 days, which the report describes as part of the control group's care. Such potential contamination is speculative rather than evidenced, so deviations arising from the trial context are probably absent.

The Methods call the trial open-label and state that neither participants nor personnel were blinded owing to the nature of the intervention (home-based exercise, nutrition and psychological programme versus standard care). The Discussion repeats that blinding of participants was not possible.

The report states personnel were not blinded to group allocation, and envelopes were opened by the investigator at randomization. The statement that care staff 'were not actively informed about the allocation' does not establish that they were unaware, and the prehabilitation group was contacted by study staff. Carers and deliverers are therefore treated as aware.

128 were randomized (64 per arm). Outcome data (90-day complications) were analysed for 59 per arm (118/128, 92%). The 10 not analysed were 3 ineligible by screening error (1 prehabilitation, 2... per report 2 prehabilitation and 1 control), 3 who withdrew consent (1 prehabilitation, 2 control) and 4 who did not undergo surgery (1 died of sudden cardiac arrest before surgery and 1 unfit in prehabilitation; 2 unfit in control). Ineligible participants are not counted as missing outcome data. The remaining at most 7 (about 5.6% of 125 eligible) are few and evenly split (3 versus 4), whereas 49 patients had events (14 versus 35), so even extreme outcomes in the missing patients would hardly change the estimate. The report states there were no missing data for the primary outcome among those analysed.

Participants and personnel were not blinded, but the report states that the medical staff providing care were not actively informed about allocation and that data collection and analyses were performed in a blinded manner with respect to allocation. The registry lists masking as single (outcomes assessor). Complications are mostly clinical events recorded and graded from the clinical course, so the assessors were most likely blinded, with residual uncertainty because patients themselves know their allocation and could reveal it.

The same outcome definition (any complication, Clavien-Dindo graded) and the same 90-day window after surgery applied to both groups. Complications occur after surgery in hospital and are ascertained identically from the clinical course in both arms. Extra prehabilitation contacts (supervised sessions, phone calls) occurred before surgery and are not described as additional postoperative outcome surveillance.

The outcome was pre-specified as the number of patients with at least one complication within 90 days after surgery, graded with the Clavien-Dindo classification, a standard validated system for postoperative complications. It is sensitive to plausible effects (complications were detected in 24% and 59%).

The result is a simple binary comparison (risk ratio with a chi-squared or Fisher test) of 14/59 versus 35/59. The report also gives sensitivity analyses (comprehensive complication index, mean number of complications) and subgroup analyses that point the same way, which argues against selection. No sign that adjusted or alternative analyses were run and withheld.

The outcome domain, any postoperative complication within 90 days, has essentially one way of being measured, as a count of patients with at least one Clavien-Dindo graded complication at the single registered 90-day time frame. The reported result matches the registered primary outcome and its time frame, and the severity breakdown, complication types and mean complication count are reported alongside it. No evidence of other eligible measurements being omitted.

The registry entry was first submitted on 2020-01-06 and enrolment started on 2020-02-06, so the entry predates enrolment. It names the primary outcome (postoperative morbidity rate by Clavien-Dindo) with time frame 90 days postoperatively, and the report analyses exactly this outcome (patients with at least one complication within 90 days, Clavien-Dindo graded) as its Methods describe. The report also says the protocol was published previously. Under the guidance a registry entry submitted before enrolment that names the measurement and time point is a dated plan, so Probably yes applies although no analysis detail is given.

Randomized group sizes were 16 and 19. Table 2 reports baseline for 26 completers (14 LGI, 12 control) across about 25 variables; only waist:hip ratio differed at P<0.05 (0.87 vs 0.82, P=0.021), which is compatible with chance and well above the P<0.001 benchmark. Baseline body mass, BMI, body fat, leptin, ghrelin and causes of infertility were similar. Baseline data cover completers only, so imbalance in all 35 randomized cannot be fully checked.

Nothing in the methods, results, or registry describes how assignments were made or protected (no central service, envelopes, or numbered containers). The trial is open-label and patients were recruited in chronological order from a waiting list, but that does not show enrolling staff knew the next assignment. The context does not support Probably yes or Probably no.

The report says only that the trial 'followed a randomized block design' and that patients were 'randomly assigned'. It never says how the sequence was generated or that order within blocks was random. Per RoB 2 guidance, a bare 'randomized' statement or blocked allocation without a stated random order is No information, and this is a small single-centre trial with no clinical-trials-unit context that would justify Probably yes. Recruitment from a waiting list in chronological order concerns enrolment, not the allocation sequence, so there is no sign of a non-random rule.

Figure 1 shows that only completers were analysed: 14 of 16 LGI and 12 of 19 control women, with independent t tests on those groups. Exclusions included women who 'could not comply with the intervention' (1 LGI, 3 control). For IVF outcomes, a further 5 LGI women were excluded (3 spontaneous pregnancies, 2 cycle cancellations), so oocyte counts cover about 9 LGI and 12 control women. No ITT analysis of all randomized participants is reported; excluding non-adherent women and those who conceived spontaneously after randomization is not an analysis by randomized group, although some of this is missing outcome data (Domain 3).

The report describes the diet delivery and adherence (Table 4): LGI women ate fewer calories (1332 kcal) and less fibre than targeted, and controls kept usual diets with no change in composition. These are ordinary non-adherence that could occur outside a trial; no report of controls seeking the intervention or of personnel undermining the protocol. Dropouts are handled in Domain 3.
The report describes an open-label design in which participants were not blinded; a hypocaloric low-GI diet versus continued usual diet cannot be concealed from participants.
The dietitians delivering the diet and the investigators were not blinded; the report states participants and dietitians were not masked, and the registry lists masking as NONE.

For oocytes retrieved only about 21 of 35 randomized women (roughly 40% excluded: 7 of 16 LGI, 7 of 19 control) contributed, and exclusions were unequal in reasons (3 LGI women excluded because they conceived spontaneously, plausibly an effect of the intervention). With an effect of 7.75 vs 4.18 on small groups (P = 0.039), such exclusions could readily change the result.

Figure 1 shows 35 randomized (16 LGI, 19 control). Nine dropped out (2 LGI, 7 control). Among the 14 LGI completers, 5 more were excluded from IVF outcomes (3 spontaneous pregnancy, 2 cycle cancellation), leaving about 9 LGI women; all 12 control completers contributed. So oocyte data are available for roughly 21 of 35 (60%): about 56% of LGI and 63% of control women. This is far below 'nearly all' for a continuous outcome.

The statistical analysis section describes only independent t tests on women with data. There is no imputation, sensitivity analysis, or reported assumption about the excluded women's oocyte counts, so nothing shows the result is robust to the missing data.

Missingness for IVF outcomes differs by arm in both proportion and reason: 5 of 14 LGI completers were excluded from IVF outcomes (spontaneous pregnancy and medical cycle cancellation) versus 0 of 12 controls, while dropouts were 2 of 16 LGI versus 7 of 19 control with differing reasons (3 control women could not comply, 2 had other health problems). Spontaneous pregnancy occurs only because of a possible intervention effect, and cycle cancellation for medical reasons likely reflects poor response. Differing reasons and proportions make outcome-dependent missingness likely, and no analysis accounted for this.

Reasons for missing data include IVF cycle cancellation for medical reasons (plausibly poor ovarian response, directly tied to oocyte yield), spontaneous pregnancy (no retrieval), health problems and inability to comply with the diet. These could plausibly relate to the oocyte count.

The study is described as open-label and the registry lists masking as NONE. No blinding of IVF clinicians or laboratory staff who count oocytes is reported, so assessors are assumed to have been aware of assignment.

Both arms underwent the same IVF stimulation protocol (cetrorelix, alfacorigonadotropin trigger, aspiration 34-36 h later) with the same ultrasonographic monitoring, so measurement of oocyte yield was comparable across groups.

The oocyte count is an observer-recorded count of retrieved oocytes at aspiration, with little room for judgement and no participant-reported component. Knowledge of the diet allocation is unlikely to change the number counted.

The outcome is the number of oocytes retrieved at ultrasound-monitored follicle aspiration in a standard antagonist IVF cycle, a routine and appropriate count for assessing ovarian response to stimulation. Nothing suggests the method is insensitive or invalid.

The methods describe an independent t test for all reproductive outcomes, and only one analysis of oocytes is reported. No analysis plan is available, and other analyses (for example adjusting for baseline BMI, or non-parametric tests for a small-count outcome) were possible, so absence of selection cannot be confirmed.

The result is the single count of oocytes retrieved at follicle aspiration in one IVF cycle, which leaves little room to choose among scales, definitions or time points. The registry lists the same outcome with the same window, and the article reports it as registered.

The only pre-specified source is the ClinicalTrials.gov record NCT02416960, first submitted 2015-04-07 although the trial ran 2012-01 to 2013-12, so it was registered after enrolment and follow-up ended and cannot show what was fixed before outcome data were available. No protocol or SAP is among the Sources. The record does list number of oocytes retrieved as a secondary outcome, but its date means it cannot count as a plan finalized before unblinded data.

Group sizes were 10 and 8 (compatible with chance for a 1:1 intention in a small sample). Age was similar (33.8 vs 33.6 years) and body weight at the start of the cycle 'did not differ significantly' between groups; IVF indications were broadly similar. No baseline table exists, so assessment is limited, but nothing suggests a problem with randomization. The low-sodium group's lower weight (about 57 vs 63 kg) was non-significant and, with n of 8 vs 9, compatible with chance; the 1.0 kg loss is post-randomization diet effect.

The report does not describe how allocations were made or protected (no envelopes, central service or similar). Allocation was to open diets given by dieticians, and the report is silent on whether enrolling staff could foresee assignments. Circumstances (small pilot, 10 vs 8) give no basis for a probable answer in either direction.

The only statement on sequence generation is that patients were 'randomly divided' into two groups (abstract: 'randomly divided into groups'). No method (random numbers, coin, etc.) is described, and no protocol or registry is available. This is a small single-centre pilot study, not a trial by an experienced trials unit, so there is no reasonable basis for 'probably yes' or 'probably no'.

Results are reported by randomized group for the patients with data. One normal-sodium patient's results were not included because her IVF cycle was cancelled for inadequate ovarian response, presumably before day 0 so that day-of-retrieval weight and BP were not obtained, which is a missing-outcome issue handled in Domain 3 rather than an exclusion of a measurable participant. No per-protocol or as-treated analysis is described.

No deviations from the assigned diets or non-protocol co-interventions are reported. Compliance was checked by urinary sodium:creatinine ratio on days -4, 0 and +9, and the ratio was significantly lower in the low-sodium group at each time (Table I), supporting that diets were followed. Stimulation duration and HMG dose were similar between groups. Nothing suggests trial-context-driven deviations.
The intervention is a dietary sodium restriction (10-20 vs 100-150 mmol Na/day) with dieticians' instructions; participants must know what they are eating, and no placebo or masking is described.
Dieticians gave diet-specific instructions to each group, so the people delivering the intervention knew the assignment; no blinding is described.

18 women were randomized (10 normal, 8 low sodium). One normal-sodium patient had her IVF cycle cancelled for inadequate response and her results were not included, so day-of-retrieval weight and BP exist for 17 of 18 (9/10 vs 8/8). That is 5.6% overall but 10% of the normal-sodium arm, with none missing in the other arm, in a very small trial with large SDs (about 11 kg). This is not clearly 'nearly all' for a pilot of this size, so probably no.
The report contains no sensitivity analysis, imputation or other method addressing the one excluded patient; the results are simply 'not included'.

The only documented reason for missingness is cancellation of the cycle for inadequate ovarian response. This is a documented reason about the IVF response, not about body weight or blood pressure. Weight and BP at retrieval are physiological measures driven mainly by the sodium diet, and no plausible route is reported by which ovarian response would determine them. One patient with one reason does not suggest outcome-dependent loss.

The report does not say who took the measurements or whether they were blinded. Participants and dieticians could not be blinded to a sodium-restricted diet, so assessors may well have known the assignment.

The same devices, protocol and schedule (start of cycle, days -4, 0, +3, +6, +9, +12) applied to both groups. Visits were part of the IVF cycle for everyone, so the diet did not create extra measurement opportunities.

Weight on an electronic scale and BP on an automatic device (mean of three) are observer-recorded values with no clinical judgement, so knowledge of assignment is unlikely to change them. Participant behaviour (for example, relaxing before BP) is not an assessment judgement.

Body weight was measured on a calibrated electronic SECA scale to 0.1 kg, and BP with an automatic BOSO device as the mean of three readings after 5 min seated rest. These are standard, valid, sensitive methods for detecting the expected differences (a ~1 kg weight change, BP differences of several mm Hg).

The reported results are group means (SD) at one time point with a simple significance comparison between two small groups. The report shows no sign of several adjusted or alternative analyses (no change-score versus final-value or covariate-set variants), so selection among analyses is unlikely.
