Not stated explicitly whether AEs were sought after withdrawal.

Patients and clinicians were not masked to allocation. Only laboratory assessments were done blind; clinical AEs, their grading and causality attribution (Table 4 'considered probably related or related') were recorded by the unmasked study clinicians. Only the IDMC and statisticians saw aggregated data.

All five arms followed the same clinic and laboratory schedule and the same CTCAE 4.03 grading, and no arm had additional visits or passive-only collection. Higher-dose rifampicin might prompt closer hepatic monitoring but nothing in the Sources indicates different monitoring or thresholds by arm. Unblinded assessment is dealt with in 4.3-4.5, not here.

The outcome counts severe (grade 3-5) events, which are unlikely to be influenced by knowledge of the intervention, and the comparator is an active standard regimen rather than no treatment. Counts are similar across arms (11-14%), IDMC reviewed safety data, and no QTcF >480 ms occurred. The documented influence was limited to two grade 2 transaminase interruptions in RIF35HZE, which are not grade 3-5 events. A possible expectation of more hepatotoxicity at 35 mg/kg leaves some concern.

Clinicians' recording and grading of AEs involves judgement (grade assignment, causality, decisions to interrupt treatment), so awareness could influence the assessment, although the blind laboratory results anchor part of the grade 3-5 events. The authors themselves note unblinded clinicians may have influenced treatment-stopping decisions.

AEs were 'registered according to the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events 4.03', a standard grading system, and safety was a pre-specified secondary endpoint (registered as Frequency of Adverse Events). Grade 3-5 events are severe and readily detected, so the method is sensitive to plausible effects.

The result is a simple count and percentage of patients per arm in the safety population, with no model, adjustment or comparative test applied. There is little scope for choosing among adjusted/unadjusted or covariate-set analyses, and the safety analysis is described once in the methods. Table 4 and Table S3 are consistent (S3 grade 3-5 counts sum to 13, 9, 7, 7, 9). The same descriptive method is used for all arms.

The safety outcome is reported as a whole-arm set: any AE, grade 3-5 AE, grade 3-5 AE related to treatment, serious AE and deaths in Table 4, plus a full SOC-by-grade breakdown in Table S3. Nothing indicates that further eligible AE measurements were computed and withheld, and the CTCAE 4.03 grading and patient-count method are applied uniformly across arms. The reported grade 3-5 count is one of several summaries presented together, which argues against selection.

The registry record was first submitted 2012-12-17, before the 2013-04 start, and lists the secondary outcome 'Frequency of Adverse Events': 'All Adverse Events (AE), and AEs considered to be drug-related will coded using standard AE dictionaries.' The report's methods state 'the proportion of adverse events and the proportion of adverse events assessed by the investigators as probably related or related to treatment was presented by group', which is what Table 4 and Table S3 do. Grade 3-5 patient counts are a severity cut of the registered AE frequency measure. The current registry record cannot show earlier versions, and no protocol or SAP is among the Sources, so this is an inference from the dated registry entry. Only the IDMC and trial statisticians saw aggregated data during the trial.

Group sizes (90 vs 94) are close to 1:1. Table 1 shows similar demographics, medications and clinical characteristics, and the text reports baseline distributions as very similar. Among the biomarkers at baseline only VWF differed (P=0.01 unadjusted, 0.07 adjusted), a single difference among many comparisons that is compatible with chance.

The report says the trial was double-blind and multicentre with central laboratory analysis, but does not describe how assignments were made or delivered (central/remote allocation, numbered identical containers, sealed envelopes). Blinding after assignment is not allocation concealment, and the circumstances give no firm basis for a probable answer.

Methods state patients were randomly allocated using a 'randomized permuted block allocation rule' in a randomized double-blind multicentre trial. This implies a random component, but the generation mechanism (computer, block size, order within blocks) is not described, so Probably yes rather than Yes.

Analyses 'were based on intention to treat' with the exception of eight warfarin-takers (5 aspirin, 3 clopidogrel) excluded because warfarin interferes with some assays. Only one of these eight completed the study, so nearly all would lack a 6-month value anyway, and the exclusion is small (about 4%) and balanced. Table 2 analyses n=85 and n=91, more than the 72 and 79 completers in Fig. 1, so participants who stopped treatment but attended appear to be analysed by randomized group. Not a naive per-protocol analysis.

The trial is described as randomized, double-blind, comparing two oral antiplatelet tablets at fixed 75 mg daily doses; compliance was measured by tablet returns. Nothing suggests the blinding failed or that either drug has a distinctive, recognisable effect. Who exactly was blinded is not spelled out, so Probably no.

Described as double-blind in both methods and abstract, so carers and people delivering the intervention were presumably masked. Concealment of the sequence is unreported rather than shown to have failed, so there is no positive reason to believe carers knew the assignments.

184 were randomized and only 151 (82%) completed the 6 months by attending the last visit; Fig. 1 shows aspirin 3 died and 15 discontinued, clopidogrel 5 died and 10 discontinued, so roughly 16-20% lack end-of-study follow-up. Table 2 reports n=85 and n=91 but does not say how many have a 6-month value, so some of those may be baseline-only. Well below the ~95% that would be 'nearly all' for a continuous outcome.

The analysis section describes t-tests and general linear models on complete data with no imputation, weighting or sensitivity analysis for missing data. Adjustment for covariates and thrombolytics/statins is for confounding, not for missingness.

The report says similar numbers died or were discontinued in each group (aspirin 18/90, clopidogrel 15/94 per Fig. 1), a difference of a few participants. Reasons are mixed and not shown to differ by arm, and the trial gives no circumstances making outcome-dependent dropout widely likely. This is a could-be (3.3) rather than a likely dependence, so Some concerns rather than High.

Withdrawals were largely for adverse events (14), death (8), angiography or PTCA (2) and unspecified reasons (4). Illness or drug intolerance could plausibly relate to inflammatory and thrombotic marker levels after MI, so missingness could depend on the true value.
The trial is called double-blind with central laboratory analysis, but the passages do not say whether laboratory staff were masked to allocation. The assessor is an automated laboratory assay.

Blood samples were taken at baseline and at 1, 3 and 6 months for all participants in both arms with central laboratory analysis, so methods, thresholds and timing were the same. Both arms had the same visit schedule and the same tablet-count compliance checks.

The outcomes are plasma concentrations from automated laboratory assays, an observer-reported measure not involving judgement. Knowledge of assignment is unlikely to influence them, even if laboratory staff were unmasked.

Clauss fibrinogen and the other markers are standard laboratory assays run centrally on blood samples. The trial was powered on Clauss fibrinogen, so the method was chosen to detect plausible effects. Nothing suggests poor validity.

Table 2 reports both unadjusted and covariate-adjusted comparisons and also change from baseline, and the text states that adjustment for thrombolytics and statins made no difference. Several analyses are reported and agree, which is evidence against selection. The one oddity is the warfarin exclusion, but it was explained by assay interference rather than the results.

The report gives results for all measured biomarkers (both fibrinogen assays, D-dimer, VWF, FVIII, t-PA, CRP) at baseline and final, and states results at 1, 3 and 6 months. The null result for all variables at 6 months is reported in full rather than a favourable subset. No sign that a favourable measurement was picked.

The article describes a sample-size calculation based on Clauss fibrinogen and the analysis methods, which suggests a design stage plan. No protocol, SAP or registry record is among the Sources, so nothing dated before unblinded data shows that this measurement and analysis were fixed beforehand. The adjustment set is described only in the Table 2 footnote.

Table 1 shows closely similar groups across demographics, CV history, HbA1c, BP, lipids, eGFR and albuminuria; the report states baseline characteristics were balanced. Small differences (any atherosclerotic disease 71.2% vs 73.5%) are compatible with chance. Unequal group sizes reflect the intended allocation (CANVAS 2:1, CANVAS-R 1:1).

Randomization was central via an interactive web-based response system; protocol states the code is held within IVRS/IWRS and study drugs are identical in appearance and packaging; participants and all trial staff unaware of assignments.
Report states randomization used a computer-generated schedule with randomly permuted blocks prepared by the sponsor.

The primary analysis was intention-to-treat on the full integrated data set of all 10,142 randomized participants with all available follow-up, using Cox regression stratified by trial and CVD history, all canagliflozin groups combined versus placebo. No post-randomization exclusions from this analysis are described. Premature regimen discontinuation (29.2% vs 29.9%) and greater use of other glucose-lowering agents in placebo do not alter the ITT population and bear on the effect of adhering, not assignment.

Both trials were double-blind, placebo-controlled; participants and all trial staff were unaware of assignments until trial completion, and the protocol states study drug and placebo were identical in appearance and packaging, with the code held in the IWRS. Canagliflozin has recognisable adverse effects (e.g. genital infections, volume depletion) that could partially unmask some participants, so 'probably no' rather than 'no'; no evidence of blinding failure is reported.

Randomization was central via IWRS with allocation concealed, the code was not given to investigators and was broken only in emergencies, study drugs were identical, and all trial staff were stated to be unaware of assignments until trial completion.

All 10,142 randomized participants were in the ITT analysis; 96.0% completed the trial and vital status was confirmed for 99.6% (only 42 unknown). Follow-up length was similar between groups and the premature-discontinuation rates (29.2% vs 29.9%) were similar and discontinuers continued to be followed. The 42 participants with unknown vital status are far fewer than the several hundred primary-composite events (trial closed after >=688 events), so their outcomes could make no important difference to the estimate. A multiple-imputation sensitivity analysis gave HR 0.85 (0.75 to 0.97), consistent with the primary result. Per-arm censoring counts were not read, hence 'probably'.

Participants and all trial staff were unaware of treatment assignments until trial completion, and events were classified by adjudication committees; the protocol states study drug was identical and the code was held in the IWRS. Assessors (adjudicators) are therefore unaware; no report of blinding being broken was found.

Both arms followed the same visit schedule and the same central adjudication definitions; the trial was double-blind with matching placebo, so there is no reason for extra contacts or detection opportunities in one arm. Follow-up length was similar in both groups.

The prespecified primary composite (CV death, nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke) was ascertained and adjudicated by clinical-event committees under the program's prespecified procedures; this is a standard, sensitive method for these events.

The SAP specifies one main analysis for the primary hypothesis (ITT, stratified Cox, all canagliflozin groups vs placebo) and lists the supportive analyses (proportional-hazards check, multiple imputation, on-treatment, components, subgroups). The report gives the main analysis (HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.75 to 0.97) and the multiple-imputation result (HR 0.85, 0.75 to 0.97), which agree. The report's Result is the SAP main analysis, so it was not chosen from alternatives. Sensitivity analyses that agree argue against selection.

The outcome is a single prespecified composite (CV death, nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke; time to first event, adjudicated) with one defined analysis time window (full follow-up), as set out in the SAP key-analysis table and the report. Neither the SAP nor the report shows alternative eligible definitions or time points for this composite from which one could have been chosen. The report's Result matches the SAP primary hypothesis.

The integrated CANVAS/CANVAS-R SAP, approved 20 September 2016, already named the primary hypothesis (MACE, ITT, CANVAS + CANVAS-R, non-inferiority HR 1.3 margin followed by superiority) and a multiple-imputation sensitivity analysis. This predates joint close-out (February 2017), when the final data were available. The SAP states that MACE and mortality data after 19 November 2012 remained blinded to the sponsor and investigators. The final SAP (20 March 2017) lists amendments that only add an On-Study set, supportive analyses and subgroups, and keeps ITT MACE as the main analysis. The report follows this plan (full integrated data set, ITT, stratified Cox, multiple imputation supportive). Earlier interim CANVAS data (to Nov 2012) were unmasked for regulators, but those were an earlier, partial data cut and the 2016 plan postdates them. The 20 March 2017 SAP date is after close-out, but it did not change the main analysis for this Result. I could not date the unblinding of the final data, hence probably rather than definitely yes.
The report states the groups were well matched on age, sex, race and cardiovascular risk factors (Table 4), and group sizes were near equal (9599 vs 9586 followed up).

Allocation was controlled by an independent statistical centre, and code access was restricted to that centre, the monitoring chair and two independent drug-preparation companies. Identical blister packs were dispensed sequentially in cartons of four with sealed code labels, and only 21 code breaks occurred (11 vs 10). Blocks of four are small, but the double-dummy packs are indistinguishable, so staff could not predict the end of a block. The packs were not described as irreversibly assigned, hence 'probably'.
An Independent Statistical Centre provided computer-generated balanced blocks of four with random allocation, stratified by centre and disease subgroup. This is a random component.

The primary analysis was an intention-to-treat analysis of all 19,185 randomised patients. The 42 lost to follow-up were included and censored at last contact. Early drug discontinuation (21.3% vs 21.1%) did not change group assignment in the analysis.

Patients received indistinguishable double-dummy blister packs (clopidogrel plus aspirin placebo vs aspirin plus clopidogrel placebo), and only 21 code breaks occurred (11 vs 10). Blinding was maintained. Both drugs have side effects, and the report gives no sign that any were identifiable to participants.

Packs were identical, supplied in a predetermined sequence, and codes were held by the independent statistical centre and drug companies. Only 21 code breaks were made, balanced between groups. Platelet aggregation testing, which could have revealed allocation, was forbidden.

The analysis was intention-to-treat on all 19,185 randomised patients. Only 42 (0.22%) were lost to follow-up (22 clopidogrel, 20 aspirin) and were censored at last contact, representing 49 patient-years (0.13%). This is negligible against 1,960 first primary events (939 vs 1,021). Outcome data were therefore available for essentially all randomised participants. Not 'yes' because the report does not explicitly state that vital status was obtained for every participant, and censoring of the 42 means their later status is unknown.

Participants and investigators were blinded with indistinguishable double-dummy packs and sealed code labels. Only 21 code breaks occurred (11 vs 10), and the authors state that blinding was well maintained. Allocation was held by the independent statistical centre. Events were reviewed independently by two Central Validation Committee members working from dossiers, with communication only through a secretariat, and no unblinding of the committee is described. The report does not state explicitly that the committee was masked to treatment, so 'probably no' rather than 'no'.

Both groups used the same double-dummy blinded regimen, the same visit schedule and the same event definitions, and all events went through the same central validation process. Neither drug involves extra contacts or testing that would create differential detection opportunities. Platelet aggregation testing was forbidden, which avoids drug-specific testing prompts. Not 'no' because event collection relied on investigator reporting and no explicit statement addresses detection comparability.

Outcomes were prespecified clinical events (ischaemic stroke, MI, vascular death) with explicit criteria for fatal events, and every reported non-fatal event and cause-of-death classification was validated by a Central Validation Committee. These are standard, sensitive clinical event definitions; nothing suggests the method was insensitive or poorly valid.

The report states that the primary analysis was to be the unadjusted ITT comparison, with on-treatment and Cox-adjusted analyses as additional planned analyses. The reported primary result is the ITT analysis of all randomised patients, reported in full in the text and Table 6. There is no sign that several analyses were run and only a favourable one reported; the planned alternatives are described in the methods. Not 'no' because the plan was not available in a dated document.

The outcome is a time-to-first-event composite of ischaemic stroke, MI or vascular death, analysed over the whole follow-up. The report states five prespecified outcome clusters and the primary one is the reported Result. There is no alternative scale or time point from which to choose. All five clusters are named in the methods, and the primary cluster is reported in full.

No protocol, SAP or registry record is among the Sources, so no dated plan can be compared with the report. This is an inference from the report itself. It describes five prespecified outcome clusters and states the primary analysis was to be the unadjusted ITT comparison of the stroke/MI/vascular-death cluster. It also describes a monitoring design fixed before the end of the trial: three interim efficacy analyses on this cluster, a Peto-Haybittle rule, and 0.048 alpha preserved for the end-of-study analysis. Interim results were seen only by the independent centre and disclosed to the Steering Committee only if a stopping rule was met, so investigators did not see unblinded outcome data. Only a blinded review of overall event rates changed the recruitment timetable. The reported Table 6 result is this prespecified primary analysis. The one analysis described as 'not specified in the protocol' concerns the myocardial infarction subgroup, not this Result. Not 'yes' because no dated plan document was inspected.

Table 2 reports baseline characteristics for all 121 randomized knees (61 vs 60, close to the 1:1 ratio). Age, sex, posterior tibial slope, sports participation and meniscal tears all have P between .31 and .96, with no significant differences, compatible with chance.

The report describes the randomization as 'unblinded' but gives no information on how assignments were generated, held or revealed (central, envelopes, etc.). Block randomization with unknown block size and an unspecified allocation mechanism neither supports a Probably yes nor a Probably no. 'Unblinded' is read as no blinding after assignment, not as evidence that enrollers knew the next allocation.

The only description is 'Unblinded block randomization at inclusion of the 121 knees' (p2 lines 76-77). It does not say that a random component (random number generator, table, etc.) was used or that order within blocks was random, so per section 4.3.1.1 blocked allocation without a stated random order warrants No information. It is a single-center trial of an academic team, with no basis to assume a non-random sequence; no protocol or registry was captured.

Table 4 presents the IKDC by randomized group (BTB n=42 of 61; BTB-LET n=38 of 60). Participants are missing because of loss to follow-up (41) or one total knee replacement at 18 years whose knee could not be scored for the ACL outcome; these are missing outcome data, assessed in Domain 3, not exclusions based on intervention received. No per-protocol or as-treated analysis is described. The grouping is by allocation as reported, though the report does not use the term intention-to-treat.

The report describes the delivered surgical techniques in detail for both groups (p3 lines 1-18) and mentions no crossovers, failures to implement the assigned procedure or non-protocol co-interventions. The intervention is a single operation delivered at baseline, so post-randomization crossover or contamination is implausible. Later events (meniscectomy, graft failure, revision) are reported as outcomes. Postoperative rehabilitation and co-interventions are not described, so some uncertainty remains.

Randomization is described as 'unblinded' (p2 lines 76-77) and the comparison is isolated BTB ACL reconstruction versus the same plus a lateral extra-articular tenodesis with a gracilis graft requiring an extra incision to the Gerdy tubercle (p3 lines 6-18). Participants cannot be unaware of such a procedure difference, and no blinding or sham is described.
Surgeons performing the BTB versus BTB-LET procedures necessarily knew which operation each patient received; the randomization is stated to be unblinded.

121 knees were randomized (61 BTB, 60 BTB-LET) but IKDC data exist for 80 (42 and 38), about 66%, with 41 patients (34%) lost to follow-up. This is far below the roughly 95% availability usually needed for a continuous outcome.

No sensitivity analysis, imputation or weighting for the missing IKDC data is reported. Table 3 compares baseline characteristics of available and lost patients, which says nothing about the missing outcome values. The authors acknowledge that the loss could bias results.

Missing proportions are similar between arms (BTB 19/61, 31%; BTB-LET 22/60, 37%), no reasons are reported that differ by arm or link missingness to outcome, and baseline characteristics did not differ between available and lost patients. Dependence on the true value is possible but not shown to be likely.

Over 19 years, loss to follow-up or declining to return could plausibly relate to knee status (for example, patients with failure or symptoms might be more or less likely to respond), and no documented reasons unrelated to the outcome are given.

The subjective IKDC is participant-reported, so the participant is the assessor. Randomization was described as unblinded, and the two surgeries differ (an added lateral tenodesis with an extended lateral incision), so participants most likely knew or could deduce their arm. The independent examiner who recorded the scores is a facilitator, not the assessor, and no blinding of either party is reported.
The same questionnaire was recorded by an independent examiner at one common last follow-up for both arms; no passive detection or extra contacts differing by arm are described.

Both arms received an active ACL reconstruction (the comparator is another active surgery, not no treatment), the outcome was recorded about 19 years after surgery by an examiner independent of the original surgeon, and no strong belief in a benefit of the tenodesis is reported. Influence is possible but not shown to be likely.
A participant-reported outcome can be influenced by knowledge of the intervention received.

Subjective IKDC is a standard patient-reported knee score, was the stated primary outcome, and the power analysis used a 10-point minimum clinically important difference. Nothing suggests it is insensitive or invalid for this purpose.

The Statistics section describes a simple between-group comparison of continuous data (t test or Mann-Whitney depending on normality). There is no sign of adjusted, change-score or alternative analyses having been run and only one reported.

Subjective IKDC is declared the primary outcome and is reported for the last follow-up alongside the other measurements the Methods list (Lysholm, forgotten knee) in Table 4. The Methods list no further IKDC time points or scales that are unreported, so no sign that one measurement was chosen from several.

The Methods name subjective IKDC as the primary outcome and describe a power analysis and tests, but no protocol, statistical analysis plan or registry record was captured, and nothing dates the plan before outcome data were available. The report itself notes earlier follow-ups were never published.

Table 1 shows group sizes of 9 and 9 among completers and no significant baseline differences (all P values .147 or higher); the larger differences (chondral damage, medial meniscal tear) are compatible with chance in groups this small. The table covers only the 18 completers, not all 20 randomized, so imbalance cannot be fully assessed.

Sealed envelopes were used and opened just after arthroscopic diagnosis (after consent and intraoperative instability screening), which is consistent with concealment until assignment. However, the report says surgeons themselves introduced the sequence, enrolled and assigned participants, and does not say the envelopes were opaque, sequentially numbered, tamper-proof or opened in order; 'selecting' an envelope suggests they may not have been sequential. The safeguards that would support either a probable yes or a probable no are not reported, and no source describes them.

The report states patients were randomly assigned and that randomization was done by selecting and opening a sealed envelope containing the assigned procedure. Envelope-based assignment implies a pre-prepared list with a random component, although how the list was generated is not described.

Comparisons are by assigned group (Mann-Whitney U on SSD) among patients who completed testing; this is a modified-ITT-like analysis with exclusions only for missing outcome data (withdrawals/reinjuries), which belongs to Domain 3.

The procedures were performed intraoperatively after allocation, and the postoperative physical therapy protocol was standardized; no deviation from assigned intervention attributable to the trial context is reported. Only two withdrawals and two graft reinjuries are described, which are not such deviations.

Patients consented before surgery to be randomized to iACLR or ACLR+LET, and the lateral tenodesis creates an additional lateral incision/procedure, so participants were probably aware of their assignment; no blinding of participants is described.
The surgeon opened a sealed envelope during surgery and performed the assigned procedure, so the people delivering the intervention were aware of assignment.

Nine patients per group completed 6-month testing and 2 patients withdrew at 6 months, implying about 20 randomized and roughly 10% missing at the 6-month time point of this Result (more at 12 months: 16 completed, 2 more graft reinjuries). For a continuous outcome in a very small trial, about 10% missing is more than 'nearly all' (about 95%), so the missing participants could plausibly change the estimate.
The analysis is a complete-case Mann-Whitney comparison with no imputation, weighting or sensitivity analysis for the withdrawn participants.

With 9 completers in each group, missingness at 6 months is balanced or differs by at most one or two participants, which is not itself evidence of dependence. No reasons for withdrawal are reported that suggest dependence on the outcome, and no circumstances make dependence widely likely.
Reasons for the 2 withdrawals are not reported, so withdrawal could relate to knee function or instability (health status) and hence to kinematics.
The report does not say whether the people running the registration and analysis were blinded to group, so awareness cannot be established.
The same laboratory protocol (treadmill downhill running, biplane radiography, same registration, SSD against the contralateral knee) was applied at the same 6 and 12 month times in both groups.

The outcome is an objective kinematic measurement from a model-based tracking algorithm whose coordinate systems are determined automatically, with little room for observer judgement, so knowledge of assignment is unlikely to influence it.

Dynamic biplane radiography with CT-based model registration is a validated technique with reported accuracy better than 0.7 mm and 0.9 degrees, suitable for detecting millimetre-scale ATT differences.
The article describes a Mann-Whitney U test of SSD values with no alternative analyses evident, but no pre-specified plan is available to rule out other analyses of the same measurements.

The kinematic domain could be measured in many eligible ways (ATT and tibial rotation, gait-cycle instants 0-40%, 6 and 12 months). The article reports all instants for both variables at both time points, with non-significant results stated, which argues against selection. Without analysis intentions we cannot confirm the reported set matches the intended set, so there is no clear basis for No or Yes.

No protocol or SAP is available. The registry record was first submitted 2016-09-16, after the 2016-01 start, and registers only a vague 'Change of joint kinematics' outcome with a 3-6 month time frame. It does not specify gait-cycle instants, ATT versus rotation, the 12-month time point, or the Mann-Whitney SSD analysis, so the analysis cannot be shown to have been finalized before unblinded data.

Group sizes are consistent with 1:1 allocation (97 vs 95). Some baseline differences exist (intracranial haemorrhage, lower GCS, septic and cardiogenic shock, vasopressor use). The authors attribute the neurological difference to chance and report it as not statistically significant. The differences point in both directions and no extreme P value is reported, so they are compatible with chance and do not suggest a problem with the randomisation process.

Allocation was assigned through a web-based randomisation service, and the report and protocol both state that concealment was maintained until randomisation was completed. Variable block sizes make assignments harder to predict. Concealment from the enrolling ED clinicians in an emergency setting is not described in detail. The blinding of ICU clinicians is not used as support.

Participants were randomised 1:1, stratified by site, with variable blocks of 4 and 6 through a web-based randomisation service generated by an independent statistician. This describes a computer-generated sequence. The order of allocations within blocks is not explicitly called random, so the answer is probably yes rather than yes.

The analysis used the intention-to-treat population, stratified or adjusted for site. All 97 intervention patients and 93 of 95 control patients were included. The two control patients excluded after randomisation were one with a DNR order established after randomisation and one intubated in the operating room. These reasons are unlikely to have been influenced by assignment, so the analysis is close to ITT.

The trial reports intervention delivery, a per-protocol population and as-treated numbers. Few patients changed technique (for example one intervention patient moved to another oxygenation technique), and clinicians could change approach after the first attempt, as is clinically routine in an emergency. Nothing suggests recruitment or engagement activities, or clinicians undermining the protocol because of their beliefs about the allocation. The outcome is in-hospital death, which is unlikely to be driven by such behaviour.
The trial was open-label. The report states that blinding of the ED team and patient was not possible because of the intervention (high-flow nasal cannula versus a non-rebreather mask).
ED clinicians delivering the pre-oxygenation and apnoeic oxygenation could not be blinded. Only the admitting ICU clinicians, who did not deliver the intervention, were blinded.

The CONSORT flowchart shows 97 and 95 randomised, no losses to follow-up or withdrawals, and 97 and 93 analysed by ITT. The only post-randomisation exclusions are 2 control patients (a DNR order established after randomisation, and intubation in the operating room). Mortality on discharge is an in-hospital event that is routinely captured from hospital records, and the trial reports no loss to follow-up. The percentages in Table 3 imply denominators of about 93 and 88, slightly below the n=97 and n=93 header, which suggests status was not counted for perhaps 4 to 5 patients per arm. The reason is unexplained, but the number is small relative to the 24 and 21 events and there is no sign of a pattern linked to the outcome.

The trial was open-label; the ED team and patients were not blinded. Only clinicians in the admitting ICUs were blinded. The paper does not say who recorded in-hospital death, so assessors are assumed to have been aware, at least for ED deaths and probably for the study data collection.

Both arms were followed through the same hospitals to discharge and mortality is reported separately for ED deaths and later in-hospital deaths. The interventions (preoxygenation device) involve no extra visits or follow-up contacts that would create more opportunities to detect death in one arm. Ascertainment was the same in both arms.
All-cause mortality is an observer-reported outcome that involves no judgement, so knowledge of the intervention received is unlikely to influence its assessment even when assessors are aware.

The Result is death from any cause up to hospital discharge, listed as a secondary endpoint in the protocol. Vital status at discharge is a routinely recorded, valid and unambiguous measure and is sensitive to plausible effects. Nothing suggests an unsuitable method.

The methods describe one analysis for dichotomous outcomes (site-stratified Mantel-Haenszel common RR) and Table 3 reports it with event counts for both arms, so the crude comparison can be derived. The protocol allowed Fisher's exact and adjusted regression, but nothing suggests several mortality analyses were run and one chosen. The reported result is null, so it was not obviously picked for favourable findings.

The outcome domain is all-cause death. The protocol names a single measurement, in-hospital mortality in ICU and on discharge, and the report presents both (ICU and on discharge) in Table 3. There is only one sensible way to measure all-cause death during the hospital stay, so no result-driven choice among measurements is evident.

Protocol v1.0, dated 14 May 2017 (about a year before enrolment began in May 2018), lists 'In-hospital mortality in ICU and on discharge' as a secondary endpoint, with follow-up from electronic records, and plans an ITT analysis. The reported result is that endpoint at discharge, analysed by ITT. The protocol's categorical-data method (Fisher's exact test, with regression adjustment if arms differ) was not followed exactly: the report used a site-stratified/adjusted Mantel-Haenszel RR. This looks like a design-driven change (stratified randomisation across two sites, whereas the protocol described one hospital) rather than a result-driven one, and the protocol itself allowed adjusted analysis. The registry (filed before enrolment) does not list mortality, so it adds nothing. No SAP is available.

Group sizes (104 vs 98) are consistent with 1:1 allocation. Table II shows only a few differences at P<.05 (multiple gestation, early-onset bacteremia, diabetes) among many baseline variables, compatible with chance; registry baseline (age, sex, race, region, gestation) is balanced. The authors adjusted for these in a sensitivity model.

Allocation used sealed envelopes assigned sequentially, with 'sealed envelopes read by someone not connected with the study (usually hospital pharmacist)'; the assignment was made from a randomization code kept by the site pharmacist, independent of the enrolling PI/coordinator. Opacity, tamper-proofing and opening only after irreversible assignment are not described, and blocks of two with an unblinded team allow some predictability within a block, but the pharmacist-held code, stratification by centre and gestational age and the absence of any indication that recruiters knew upcoming allocations make concealment probably adequate.

The CONSORT checklist supplement states the sequence was 'obtained from a random number generator for each site' and generated by a pharmacist at the central study site (UCSF); randomization was stratified by gestational age and centre in blocks of two (1:1). A random component is documented.

'All analyses were based on the infants' group randomization assignments.' All 202 randomized infants (CT 98, ERT 104) were analysed in Table IV and in the registry results (104 and 98 analysed for the primary outcome; none lost).

Matching placebo tablets with identical bottles labelled by unique numbers. Site personnel had no access to the randomization scheme, and allocation was by IxRS with concealed sequence, so carers and deliverers were most likely unaware of assignment.

Events were collected by the same protocol-specified process and adjudicated by the same committee against the same prespecified criteria in both groups. The outcome is a prespecified composite with explicit definitions (unplanned HF hospitalization or urgent visit with IV therapy, or CV death), adjudicated against prespecified criteria by a clinical-events committee. The SAP prespecifies one primary analysis (ITT, full analysis set, treatment-policy estimand, time to first event) and the paper reports exactly that, with a stratified Cox model. No alternative adjusted/unadjusted or composite-definition analyses are described as having been run and withheld.

The registered and SAP-specified primary outcome is a single composite with one time-to-first-event measure over follow-up (time frame up to 27.8 months). SAP edition 1.0 is dated 31 January 2017 and specifies the primary variable (time to first event in the primary composite, ITT, full analysis set, events up to PACD, adjudicated). The baseline table covers all randomized infants.

The authors state analysis was by intention-to-treat and Table III reports all 72 randomized infants (35 and 37).

Table 1 shows 8582 vs 8578 participants and closely similar baseline characteristics (age, sex, region, HbA1c, eGFR, ASCVD 40.5% vs 40.8%, heart failure 9.9% vs 10.2%, medications). Differences are compatible with chance, no excess of significant differences, and no excessive similarity.

Allocation was by central IVRS/IWRS, which allocated the kit/randomization numbers from a scheme prepared centrally by AstraZeneca. Protocol states randomization via IVRS/IWRS in balanced blocks stratified by CV risk category and hematuria, from a randomization scheme prepared by AstraZeneca's global randomization administrator; the report says patients were randomly assigned 1:1. The SAP defines the full analysis set as all randomized patients analysed by randomized assignment irrespective of adherence or discontinuation, and the protocol requires follow-up of all randomized patients for vital status and CV events whether or not they took study drug. Randomization was double-blind to dapagliflozin 10 mg or matching placebo; the protocol describes identical single-dummy tablets in IVRS-labelled bottles with no site or TIMI access to the allocation scheme. Participants were therefore very likely unaware of assignment. Glucosuria or other drug-specific effects could have partly unblinded some, but no source reports this.

Investigators and care personnel were blinded with identical-appearing tablets, and allocation was concealed through a central IVRS/IWRS scheme prepared by the sponsor and not accessible to sites. Unblinding by personnel was therefore unlikely.

The CONSORT diagram shows all 17,160 analysed participants were included in the primary efficacy analysis. The appendix states that the TIMI clinical events committee, which adjudicated all primary outcome components including MACE, had members unaware of treatment assignment. The trial was double-blind, with identical tablets.

MACE (CV death, MI, ischemic stroke) is a pre-specified, standard clinical outcome whose components were adjudicated by the TIMI clinical events committee. Nothing suggests an insensitive or invalid method.

The outcome is one pre-specified composite (CV death, MI, ischemic stroke) analysed as time to first event over the whole follow-up, with events adjudicated by the CEC. The SAP, registry and article give one definition and one time frame, so there were no alternative scales, definitions or time points from which a favourable one could be chosen.

Double-blind with matching placebo; treatment codes held in IxRS and unblinded only in medical emergencies, with allocation concealed at randomization.

Same event definitions and adjudication process applied to both arms in a double-blind, matching-placebo trial with identical visit schedules; no extra contacts or detection opportunities by arm.
Prespecified, objectively defined clinical events (unplanned HF hospitalization, urgent HF visit, CV death) adjudicated against prespecified criteria; the method is sensitive and appropriate.

Double-blind placebo-controlled design with matching placebo tablets (registry masking: participant, care provider, investigator, outcomes assessor). Blinded design with an independent random list holder and matching placebos; clinicians administering treatment were blinded. "Patients, investigators, and data analysts were masked to treatment assignment" with matching placebo tablets and matching placebo injections for each arm; the paper reports no unblinding. Allocation used a computerized randomization programme (1:1) with Pocock minimization on several prognostic factors; minimization carries a random element and counts as random.

A 16-week weight-reduction programme with a liquid diet versus no intervention cannot be hidden; the report states blinding was not possible for patients or physicians.

Physicians, dieticians and clinic staff delivering the diet programme knew the assignment; the report explicitly says the study was not blinded for patients or physicians. Only embryologists and statisticians were unaware.

Twelve of 317 (3.8%) were excluded, most likely without a live birth (not starting IVF and no spontaneous pregnancy). Adding them back as non-events gives about 28.1% (45/160) versus 26.8% (42/157), difference about 1.4 points versus 2.2, a small change on an already null result with a wide CI (-8.6 to 12.9). The imbalance (8 vs 4) is modest, so a substantial impact is unlikely, though a small residual concern remains.

Live birth is a registry-based pregnancy outcome followed to delivery (follow-up completed February 2017). The report states no patients were lost to follow-up, and the flow chart accounts for all 317 randomized. The 12 women excluded from the FAS (8 vs 4) were excluded by analysis-set definition for not starting stimulation, not because the outcome was unobserved; that is a Domain 2 issue (2.6). Even treating them as missing, 12/317 (3.8%) against 87 observed events is small, and adding them as non-events changes the risk difference from 2.2 to about 1.4 points.

Patients and physicians were not blinded, and only embryologists and statisticians were unaware of allocation. Who recorded live birth is not specified, so the clinicians and participants who report or record deliveries are assumed to be aware of allocation.

The same outcome definition applied to both arms, and Table II reports live birth including spontaneous pregnancies for both. All women underwent the same IVF and pregnancy follow-up regardless of arm, so live birth ascertainment was comparable. Extra contacts in the intervention arm (diet programme) occurred before IVF and are unlikely to create more opportunities to detect a delivery.

Live birth is an objective event (a child born alive) that involves no judgement by the observer, comparable to all-cause mortality. Knowledge of the assigned intervention is unlikely to change whether a live birth is recorded.
Live birth (at least one child born alive) was the pre-specified primary outcome and is a standard, objectively verifiable IVF outcome. Nothing suggests the method was insensitive or invalid.

The Methods describe the main analysis as an unadjusted comparison on the FAS with Fisher's exact test, plus complementary adjusted and per-protocol analyses and subgroup analyses, and all of these are reported (the per-protocol live birth 44 (29.9%) vs 41 (27.7%), P 0.77 in Supplementary Table S1). Reporting the primary analysis alongside concordant sensitivity analyses is evidence against selection, and the reported result is a null that agrees across analyses.

Live birth is one pre-specified, binary primary outcome with a single definition (at least one child born alive), also registered per participating woman. There is essentially one way to measure it, and the report gives the same definition in Table II. The registered time frame matches follow-up to delivery. No sign of a selected alternative definition or time point.

The registry record (NCT01566929) lists live birth per participating woman as primary outcome, but it was first submitted 2012-03-23, about 17 months after the October 2010 start, so it cannot show what was fixed before outcome data accrued. No protocol or SAP is among the Sources: the registry capture lists no linked documents. No source dated before outcome data could be seen therefore specifies this analysis (FAS, unadjusted Fisher exact test).

Group sizes were 30 and 30 as intended. Table 1 (all randomized infants) shows similar gestation and PDA risk-score components. The reported differences are birthweight (830 vs 970 g, P=.02), fetal growth restriction (23% vs 3%), surfactant at delivery (83% vs 100%) and antenatal steroids (97% vs 80%), with the intervention arm lighter and the control arm having less antenatal steroid exposure. In a 60-infant trial with about 17 baseline variables, a few such differences are compatible with chance, and none reaches the extreme P values that would suggest subversion. Birthweight and gestation had no association with the outcome in the adjusted model, though that model is only exploratory.

The sequence was held by pharmacy only (restricted, encrypted, password-protected), and an unblinded trial pharmacist prepared the drug or placebo after randomization and issued the syringe to the investigator team. The ibuprofen and saline preparations are indistinguishable. So enrolling staff did not hold the sequence and allocation was delivered by an independent pharmacy. Full detail (for example sequential numbering and whether eligibility was confirmed before the pharmacy was contacted) is not reported, so 'probably yes' is chosen rather than 'yes'.

Methods state that a computer-generated central randomization scheme assigned infants 1:1, stratified by gestational age bracket, with the sequence file produced by a statistician not otherwise involved in the study. Computer generation is a random component.

All 60 randomized infants (30 per arm) were analysed in their allocated arms for the composite outcome (16/30 vs 18/30), despite early treatment discontinuation and open-label treatment. The report states outcome data were available for all and the analysis included all infants.

Ibuprofen and saline placebo were colourless, odourless and indistinguishable, and the report states trial participants and their families remained blind throughout. Participants are extremely preterm infants, so awareness is mainly via families, and no drug-specific effect that would reveal allocation is described.

Allocation was concealed centrally via a pharmacy-held, encrypted sequence. Only the designated trial pharmacist was unblinded and prepared an indistinguishable syringe; health care providers, echocardiographers, outcome assessors and analysts remained blinded.

The report states 'None of the infants were lost to follow up' and 'Outcome data were available for all recruited infants and analysis was conducted to include all infants'. Table 2 gives the composite as 16/30 vs 18/30, i.e. all 60 randomized infants; deaths count as events for the composite, so no outcome is unobserved.

The Methods state that participants and families, health care providers, data abstractors, echocardiographers, primary outcome assessors and data analysts remained blind throughout the study. Only the trial pharmacist was unblinded. Primary outcome assessors are therefore reported as unaware of allocation.

The same pre-specified definition and time point (36 weeks corrected GA, or death before discharge) applied to all infants, who were followed to discharge in the same NICU. The intervention was a short course of an IV drug with no extra contacts that would add detection opportunities for oxygen need or death.

The primary outcome was pre-specified as death or chronic lung disease before discharge, with CLD defined as oxygen need at 36 weeks corrected gestational age, a standard neonatal definition with a cited reference. Death is unambiguous. Nothing suggests the method is insensitive or invalid.

The Statistical Analyses section states that a chi-squared (or Fisher) test was used for the primary dichotomous outcome, and Table 2 reports it for all 60 randomized infants. The adjusted logistic regression is described as examining the association of day-8 PDA patency with the outcome, not as an alternative estimate of the treatment effect. No sign of multiple eligible treatment-effect analyses with only one reported.

The Methods name one primary outcome (CLD, oxygen at 36 weeks corrected GA, and/or death before discharge) with a single definition and a single time point (before discharge). Table 2 reports exactly this composite and its two components. No alternative definitions or time points for this outcome are described or reported, so selection among measurements appears unlikely. Inference is from the report alone.

The only captured Source is the published article. It defines the primary outcome and the chi-squared/Fisher analysis in the Methods, but no protocol, SAP or dated registry record is available (registry lookup found none), and the article does not say when the analysis plan was finalized relative to unblinded data. Pre-specification therefore cannot be confirmed.

Groups were equal in size (3034 each). Table 1 shows 4 of 35 comparisons nominally significant (age P=0.005, eGFR P=0.006, HbA1c P=0.02, prior stroke P=0.01), compatible with chance; absolute differences are small (age 0.7 yr, stroke 6.2% vs 4.7%) and no P<0.001. A sensitivity analysis adjusting for these imbalances gave similar results.

Allocation was by a centralized IVRS/IWRS treatment allocation system contacted by the investigator after screening assessments, with treatment kits numbered centrally and identical volume-matched placebo; the allocation was controlled by a central system independent of enrolling staff.

The report says patients were randomly assigned via a centralized assignment system, and the protocol states a Study Biostatistician provided the randomization scheme to a centralized allocation system that generated the patient randomization list (1:1). The protocol does not explicitly say the list was computer-generated random, but a large sponsor-run trial with a central system and statistician-provided scheme makes a random component very likely.

The primary analysis was ITT with a Cox model including study group and region, all 6068 randomized patients (3034 per arm); the SAP defines ITT as all randomized analyzed as allocated regardless of discontinuation.

Double-blind with volume-matched placebo and an indistinguishable investigational product (protocol 8.4); the placebo run-in used the same pen and volumes. Lixisenatide causes more GI adverse events (nausea/vomiting discontinuation 3.0%/1.1% vs 0.4%/0.2%), which could unblind a minority, but this affects few participants and nothing indicates broad failure of blinding.

Investigators had no access to the randomization code except in emergencies via IVRS/IWRS; kits were numbered and indistinguishable; allocation was centrally concealed (Domain 1). Outcome adjudicators were blinded. Injected volume differs by titration step but is unblinded only in step, not by arm.

All 6068 randomized patients (3034 per arm) were in the ITT analysis. Among non-decedents 96.3% (lixisenatide) and 96.1% (placebo) completed the study, and vital status was unknown at study end for only 29 (1.0%) and 42 (1.4%) patients. The protocol required every randomized patient to be followed to death or the common end-of-study visit even after stopping study drug, and required best-effort re-contact (family, physician, registries) for patients who did not return, to establish vital status and endpoint status. Patients without a first event are censored at the last date with information. Even if every patient with unknown vital status (71 in total) or non-completion is treated as missing, the 805 observed primary events greatly outnumber them and the proportions are low and similar across arms, so the missing data could not plausibly have made an important difference to the HR of 1.02. The exact number censored early for the composite is not reported, hence 'probably' rather than 'yes'.

Potential cardiovascular events were classified by an independent Cardiovascular events Adjudication Committee whose members were unaware of study-group assignments (main report; protocol: classification 'in a blinded fashion'). The study was also double-blind with indistinguishable volume-matched placebo, so investigators reporting events were also not told assignment. Hospitalization for unstable angina, which is partly a provider decision, was itself subject to blinded adjudication against prespecified definitions and the investigators were blinded.

Events were collected by the same protocol-specified procedures in both arms (scheduled visits, follow-up of all randomized patients until death or end of study, same CAC adjudication process) under double-blind placebo-controlled conditions, with no extra contacts in one arm. Events were adjudicated by the same committee using the same definitions. GI adverse effects were more frequent on lixisenatide, but the endpoint is not passively detected through symptom-triggered testing in a way that plausibly differs by arm.

The primary composite (CV death, nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke, hospitalization for unstable angina) is a prespecified, standard cardiovascular outcomes endpoint with predefined definitions validated by a Cardiovascular events Adjudication Committee. Nothing suggests the method is insensitive to plausible effects or poorly valid.

The reported hazard ratio comes from the single prespecified ITT Cox model (study group and region). The additional analyses (excluding events >30 days after discontinuation, and a post hoc adjustment for baseline imbalances) were labelled as sensitivity analyses and gave results consistent with the primary analysis, so there is no sign of selection among analyses.

The primary outcome is a single adjudicated time-to-first-event composite with one registered time frame (randomization to end of study). No alternative measurements, scales or time points for this composite were reported, so there was no apparent opportunity to select among eligible measurements.

The registry entry (first submitted 2010-06-17, at study start in 2010-06) registers this exact primary outcome (time to first CV death, nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke or hospitalization for unstable angina) and time frame (randomization to end of study). The report analyses it as ITT with a Cox model by study group and region, matching the SAP. The SAP amendment (Nov 2014) predates study end and unblinding.

The report says baseline characteristics were well balanced. Table S2 shows group sizes (2333 placebo; 2345 and 2342 empagliflozin) consistent with the 1:1:1 ratio. Age, sex, race, region, weight, BMI and cardiovascular history are very similar across arms, with differences compatible with chance. I read only the first part of Table S2 (rows up to CABG).

Assignment was by an interactive voice/web response system. The protocol describes it as third-party phone/web-based randomisation at Visit 3, with the randomisation code access controlled and documented, and numbered medication kits assigned and dispensed after allocation. This is central, remote allocation independent of enrolling staff.

The main report states randomization used a computer-generated random sequence, and the protocol (Section 4.1.2) confirms assignment by a computer-generated random sequence, stratified by HbA1c, BMI, eGFR and region. A random component was used.

The primary analysis was a modified ITT in patients who received at least one dose (7020 of 7028 randomized; 4687 + 2333). Per RoB 2 guidance 5.3.1, this exclusion is based on intervention received, not missing outcome data, so it is formally not a full ITT. Participants were otherwise analysed by randomized group with all events until trial end.

Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial; the protocol supplies matching placebo tablets in numbered kits, with allocation hidden via IVRS/IWRS. No report of blinding failure was seen. Specific side effects (genital infection) could hint at assignment, but nothing indicates participants were aware.

Double-blind design with identical-appearing placebo kits and concealed central allocation; emergency code break limited to the investigator for safety. Carers and investigators were therefore probably unaware of assignment.

Only about 8 of 7028 randomized patients (0.1%) were excluded, versus 772 primary-outcome events. These exclusions could be influenced by assignment only minimally (never took a dose), so a substantial impact on the HR of 0.86 is unlikely.

Of 7028 randomized, 7020 were treated and analysed; 97.0% completed the study and final vital status was known for 99.2% (about 0.8%, roughly 56 patients, unknown). Together with the 8 untreated patients, at most roughly 65 randomized patients could lack outcome follow-up, versus 772 observed primary-outcome events, so their outcomes could not plausibly change the HR materially. The protocol required follow-up of patients who discontinued study drug, so treatment discontinuation (25.4%) did not cause missing outcome data.
The independent Clinical Event Committee adjudicates centrally and in a blinded fashion; the trial was double-blind with matching placebo.
Same visit schedule, double-blind placebo design, and the same central adjudication process applied to both arms; no indication of differing detection opportunities.
Pre-specified MACE components (CV death, nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke) were ascertained and centrally adjudicated against pre-specified criteria using clinical documentation; an appropriate method.

The protocol pre-specifies a single primary Cox model for the pooled empagliflozin vs placebo comparison. The reported HR 0.86 (95.02% CI 0.74-0.99), the same figure as in the registry, matches it. Alternative analyses, such as the per-dose comparisons and the OS analysis, are reported as secondary or sensitivity analyses, not as replacements for the primary.

The outcome is time to first adjudicated 3-point MACE over whole follow-up, with a single registered definition and time frame matching the reported one. There is no alternative scale or time point to select from.

The registry entry, first submitted 2010-05-26 before the July 2010 start, names the 3-point MACE composite as primary. The protocol (revision 4, 2013) specifies the primary analysis: Cox model, pooled empagliflozin vs placebo, in the treated set. The published analysis (modified ITT, pooled arms, Cox HR) follows this. The trial team stayed blinded, since only the independent DMC saw unblinded data. The protocol and TSAP dates relative to unblinding are not fully established, so the answer is Probably yes rather than Yes.

Table 1 for all 5988 randomized patients shows near-identical groups (2997 vs 2991; age, sex, region, NYHA class, LVEF, NT-proBNP, diabetes, eGFR) and the text says baseline characteristics were similar; differences are compatible with chance.
Randomization and kit allocation were done centrally through an Interactive Response Technology system, independent of enrolling site staff, with matching placebo dispensed in double-blind fashion.
The protocol states assignment is determined by a computer generated random sequence via IRT; the report describes a permuted block design stratified by region, diabetes status and eGFR, 1:1.

Primary analysis was intention-to-treat in all 5988 randomized patients (2997 vs 2991), analysed by assigned group regardless of adherence, with follow-up of all randomized patients intended even after treatment discontinuation.
Double-blind, placebo-controlled trial with matching placebo; no report of blinding failure. Some drug-specific effects (genital infections) occur but are not described as unblinding.
Double-blind with central IRT allocation and matching placebo; relevant parties blinded per the protocol, and allocation was concealed.

Analysis covered all 5988 randomized patients. Only 36 (17 vs 19; 0.6% per arm) had unknown vital status at trial end, and 5 of these already had an adjudicated HHF event; against 926 observed primary events, so few missing that their outcomes could not materially change the estimate. Treatment discontinuation (23%) did not imply loss of follow-up, since patients were followed for vital status after stopping drug.
The independent Clinical Event Committee adjudicates events centrally and in a blinded fashion, and the trial was double-blind.
Double-blind, placebo-controlled design with identical follow-up schedule and a common central adjudication process for both arms; no sign of different ascertainment between groups.
The outcome is CV death or hospitalization for HF, prespecified and centrally adjudicated against prespecified criteria; this is an appropriate, valid way to measure it.

The primary analysis was the prespecified Cox time-to-first-event analysis in all randomized patients, matching the SAP dated before enrolment with no planned changes. The registry result reports the same endpoint on the randomized set. No evidence of alternative analyses reported selectively.

The primary outcome is a single prespecified composite (adjudicated CV death or HHF, time to first event over the planned treatment phase). The registered primary outcome matches the reported one in definition and time frame, so there is no sign of choice among alternative measurements or time points.

The registry entry was first submitted 2017-02-16, before the start date (2017-03-02) and first randomization (27 Mar 2017), and names this exact primary outcome (time to first adjudicated CV death or adjudicated HHF). The final signed SAP is dated 21 Feb 2017, also before enrolment, with 'Changes in the planned analysis: N/A'. The report analyses the outcome as time to first event in the randomized set, consistent with the plan.
Baseline characteristics were reported as similar; Table 1 shows near-identical group sizes (1863 vs 1867) and balanced prognostic factors, compatible with chance.
Assignment was central and remote via Interactive Response Technology with controlled, documented access to the randomisation code, so enrolling staff could not foresee allocations.
Protocol states assignment is determined by a computer generated random sequence; the article describes IRS randomization with permuted blocks, stratified.

The primary analysis followed the intention-to-treat principle and included all randomized patients with all data up to the end of the planned treatment period; the SAP states patients are analysed as randomised, even if the wrong drug was received.

The trial is reported as randomized, double-blind and placebo-controlled; the protocol describes blinded treatment assignment through central IRT with matching placebo. Participants were therefore very likely unaware of assignment. No report of unblinding through drug-specific side effects was found in the inspected passages.

Double-blind design with matching placebo, concealed central allocation and controlled, documented access to the randomisation code, so carers and investigators were very likely unaware of assignment during the trial.

The analysis included all 3730 randomized patients. Only 42 patients (22 empagliflozin, 20 placebo; about 1.1%) were lost to follow-up, including 21 with unknown vital status, and the two arms were nearly equal. The 823 observed primary events far outnumber the 42 with possibly missing data, so their outcomes could not have made an important difference. Sensitivity analyses addressing the 42 patients' missing follow-up and competing risk gave results similar to the main analysis. Premature treatment discontinuation (16.3% vs 18.0%) does not cause missing outcomes because follow-up continued regardless of adherence.
A clinical-events committee adjudicated fatal and nonfatal events in a blinded manner according to prespecified definitions. The outcome assessors were therefore blinded to intervention assignment.

This was a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial with a prespecified composite outcome. Events were adjudicated by a central committee using prespecified definitions in both arms, so ascertainment was likely comparable across groups. Nothing suggests extra visits or detection opportunities in one arm.

The outcome is a prespecified composite of adjudicated cardiovascular death or heart-failure hospitalization, analysed as time to first event. These are standard, well-defined clinical events, and the method of ascertainment is not unsuitable for detecting plausible intervention effects.

The protocol prespecified a Cox model with covariates of age, gender, region, diabetes history, LVEF and baseline eGFR on the ITT set. The publication reports exactly this model and population with the same covariates. Sensitivity analyses, which agree, are reported in addition and do not indicate selection.

The primary outcome is a single time-to-first-event composite of adjudicated CV death or HHF over the whole treatment period. The protocol, registry and publication define it identically, so there are no alternative scales or time points to select from. Both the protocol and the registry give one measurement for this outcome.

The original trial protocol, dated 10 Nov 2016, predates the first enrolment (start 6 Mar 2017) and hence any unblinded outcome data. It prespecifies this exact outcome (time to first adjudicated CV death or HHF) as the primary endpoint, the hierarchical testing, the Cox model with a named covariate set, and the ITT population. The registry record was first submitted on 16 Feb 2017, before the start, and names the same primary outcome. The published methods follow the plan. The June 2020 SAP revision postdates follow-up, but the earlier dated protocol already fixed this measurement and analysis.

Table 1 shows chance-compatible differences in a small trial (n=38-41 per arm): placebo had more women (63.2% vs 31.6-42.1%), higher median baseline eGFR (68.5 vs 56.0-64.0; ANOVA P=0.18), longer time since biopsy and somewhat more proteinuria. The report states characteristics were 'generally similar among the four groups' and attributes the differences to chance; the eGFR slope model adjusts for baseline eGFR and the randomization strata. Nothing suggests a problem with the randomization process.

All eligible participants were 'centrally assigned to randomized study intervention using an Interactive Voice/Web Response System (IVRS/IWRS)', with unique randomization numbers that cannot be reassigned; sponsor, personnel and patients were unaware of assignments. Central allocation conceals the sequence until assignment.

Patients were 'randomly assigned in a 1:1:1:1 ratio' via an interactive voice/web response system, stratified by region and UPCR; the protocol (6.3) describes central IVRS/IWRS assignment. The generation method is not stated, but for a sponsor-run multicentre trial with central IVRS/IWRS a random sequence is probable.

The analysis is described as modified ITT (all randomized patients with at least one complete dose), but Table 2 group sizes (38/41/38/38) sum to 155, equal to all randomized patients, and Table 1 states its analysis included all randomized patients. 146 of 155 completed all 12 doses with mean adherence 95.1%, so analysis was by assigned group with no apparent post-randomization exclusions of eligible participants.

Double-blind placebo-controlled trial: 'The sponsor (Visterra), trial personnel, and patients were all unaware of the trial-group assignments.' Placebo was normal saline infused identically (protocol 6.3). Local lab testing of Ig levels that could unblind was prohibited. No evidence blinding failed.

Investigator and all site study staff were blinded; only an unblinded pharmacist prepared doses, and allocation was concealed centrally via IVRS/IWRS. The pharmacist does not deliver care or administer the infusion, so carers/deliverers were probably unaware.

All 155 randomized patients (38/41/38/38) are in the mITT population and Table 2; Fig. S1 shows 146/155 (94.2%) completed the study (35/39/37/35) with only 9 discontinuations (3/2/1/3). The linear mixed-effects model with random intercept and slope uses every available eGFR measurement, including from patients who left early. The exact number with an eGFR value at month 12 is not reported, but about 94% completion with a continuous outcome is close to the ~95% guide, so outcome data were probably available for nearly all participants.

The trial was double-blind: "The sponsor (Visterra), trial personnel, and patients were all unaware of the trial-group assignments." The outcome is an automated central-laboratory creatinine value, and the protocol states that results that could unblind the study will not be reported to sites or other blinded personnel. The laboratory assessor and participants were therefore probably unaware of assignment.

Serum creatinine was collected at the same scheduled visits in all four arms (baseline, days 8/18/30, monthly), analysed by the same central laboratory and formula, with identical monthly infusion visit schedules across arms and a placebo comparator. Collection was protocol-scheduled, not passive, so differential detection opportunities are unlikely.

eGFR was derived from serum creatinine by the CKD-EPI formula in a central laboratory ("The tests detailed in Table 7 will be performed by the central laboratory"; "eGFR will be calculated from Serum creatinine by the CKD-EPI formula"). This is a standard, validated, objective measure sensitive to plausible changes in kidney function and a prespecified secondary endpoint.

The SAP lists two eGFR slope analyses: the per-subject linear slope with ANCOVA (4.4.1.4, also in SAP v1.0) and the LME annualized slope (4.4.2). The article reports only the LME annualized slope, with no mention of the ANCOVA slope or justification for the choice. The reported analysis follows the SAP v5.0 description, and there is no evidence that it was chosen on the basis of results, so selection is neither shown nor excluded.

eGFR was calculated centrally by one method (CKD-EPI from serum creatinine) at scheduled visits, and the LME uses all post-baseline visit values over 12 months rather than one selected time point or scale. No evidence that several eligible measurements were analysed and one chosen.

The only analysis plan clearly dated before outcome data (SAP Final Version 1.0, 09 July 2021, embedded in the protocol) specifies the eGFR slope as a per-subject linear-regression slope compared by ANCOVA, not the linear mixed-effects annualized slope that was reported. The LME annualized slope (SAP 4.4.2, 'Sensitivity Efficacy Analyses') appears only in SAP v5.0 dated 27 Jun 2023, which is after primary completion (2023-05-19), and no source dates its finalization before unblinding. The registry lists only 'Change From Baseline in eGFR at Months 9, 12, and 16', not a slope.

Table 1 shows similar age, BMI, body composition and antral follicle count, and the authors report no statistically significant baseline differences. Some categorical differences (male factor 76% vs 50%, amenorrhea 0 vs 20%, infertility duration 68 vs 53 months) are not significant and are compatible with chance in a 41-participant trial. Group sizes (21 vs 20) fit 1:1. A typo in the control weight SD (1.5) is a reporting error, not an imbalance.

The report says a physician (A.P.) checked eligibility and that participants were then allocated using a computer-generated list. It does not say who held the list or how assignments were hidden from the person enrolling until assignment. Blinding of the fertility team afterwards is not concealment. The registry record (masking: single, investigator) and the provenance capture (no protocol or SAP linked) add nothing about allocation procedures.
Participants were randomly allocated to groups using a computer-generated list, which is a random component.

The assessed per-embryo-transfer result excludes 4 randomized women (2 per arm) with no transfer (non-viable embryos, or cryopreservation to avoid OHSS), a post-randomization exclusion not justified by ineligibility. The all-randomized per-cycle analysis (21 vs 20) is also reported, but it is not the approved Result.

The paper does not report whether control participants sought lifestyle changes or whether IVF treatment differed by arm because of the trial context. Treatment was apparently standard IVF/ICSI in both arms.
A 12-week diet and exercise programme versus no prior intervention cannot be masked from participants; the paper states only that the fertility specialists were blinded.
Staff delivering the lifestyle programme must know who is in it. The IVF team was reported as blinded, but allocation concealment is not described (Domain 1), so that blinding may not have held.

Four of 41 randomized women (about 10%) were excluded, balanced across arms (2 each). Including all randomized women gives a similar estimate (OR 2.47 vs 2.85, both with CIs spanning 1), so substantial impact is unlikely.

Table 3 reports clinical pregnancy over all randomized women (12/21 vs 7/20), and the four women without embryo transfer (2 per arm) have a known outcome of no pregnancy after that cycle. The reported per-ET result drops them from its denominator by choice, not because data are missing. No loss to follow-up for this early outcome is described.

Pregnancy is assessed by the IVF clinic, whose team of fertility specialists was reported as blinded to group assignment. Concealment of allocation is unclear (Domain 1), so some leakage is possible, but the report states blinding.

Both arms underwent the same IVF/ICSI cycle and the same ultrasound-based pregnancy ascertainment after embryo transfer; the lifestyle programme precedes the cycle and does not add detection opportunities for the outcome.
Clinical pregnancy is defined as ultrasound visualization of a gestational sac, a standard and sensitive method for this IVF outcome.

Both the per-cycle-attempt (12/21 vs 7/20, OR 2.47) and per-ET (12/18 vs 7/17, OR 2.85) analyses are reported in Table 3, so there is no sign a favourable subset of analyses was chosen; no adjusted-versus-unadjusted alternatives are suggested.

Clinical pregnancy is defined as ultrasound-visualized gestational sac and the registered primary outcome is the same domain. No evidence that multiple eligible measurements or time points were taken and only one reported; both per-patient and per-transfer results are shown.

No protocol or SAP is available. The registry record (NCT01952795) names 'Pregnancy rate' 14 days after embryo transfer as primary outcome but gives no analysis specification (population, per-cycle vs per-ET, effect measure). The paper reports both per-attempt and per-ET rates, so the analysis plan cannot be compared with what was reported.

Demographic, disease and clinical characteristics did not differ significantly; only lipid-lowering medication and SGLT-2 inhibitor use differed, compatible with chance across many comparisons in 14,752 patients. Group sizes 7356 vs 7396 match the intended 1:1 ratio.
An interactive voice-response system assigned patients: central remote allocation independent of enrolling site staff, matching the guidance example for Yes.

Allocation used computer-generated block randomization within site, stratified by CV disease history, in a large trial run jointly by Duke Clinical Research Institute and the Oxford Diabetes Trials Unit. The report does not say explicitly that order within blocks was random, but a computer-generated randomization sequence from experienced trial units makes a random component reasonable to assume.

The primary analysis was a Cox model in the intention-to-treat population, defined as all randomized patients (14,752), stratified by cardiovascular disease history; the per-protocol analysis was only a sensitivity analysis.

The trial is described as double-blind and placebo-controlled with matching placebo once-weekly injections, so participants were most likely unaware of assignment. Blinding is not verified by guess testing and the injection device could in principle reveal nothing about arm.
Double-blind design with matching placebo and central interactive voice-response allocation; only the DSMB had access to unblinded data, so site personnel were most likely unaware of assignment.

Figure S2 shows 7,093 exenatide and 7,094 placebo participants completed the study with vital status known. Non-completers without a primary endpoint (the participants whose outcome is effectively missing) were 286 (3.9%) exenatide and 255 (3.4%) placebo; vital status remained unknown for only 1.1% and 1.2%. Observed versus expected person-years of MACE follow-up were 95.1% and 94.5%. The observed events (839 and 905) are about three times the number of participants with missing data, and censoring rates are similar between arms, so any bias from missing data is necessarily small. Not strictly all participants, hence probably yes.
