All components were adjudicated by an independent clinical events classification committee whose members were unaware of trial-group assignments; the trial itself was double-blind with matching placebo, so site reporters were also most likely unaware.

Both arms followed the same visit schedule and the same event-reporting and adjudication process, with matching placebo injections once weekly, so no differential detection opportunities are expected. Events were adjudicated by one committee under the same definitions.

The primary outcome is prespecified, with CV death, nonfatal MI and nonfatal stroke defined in the protocol and the Clinical Event Definitions of the supplement and classified by an independent clinical events committee. This is an established, sensitive method for MACE.

The SAP specifies one primary analysis, a Cox proportional-hazards model in the ITT population stratified by prior CV event, with hazard ratio and 95% CI. The article reports exactly this analysis, with the same stratification and ITT population. The per-protocol result is reported as a sensitivity analysis alongside it and is not a substitute, so there is no sign of selection among multiple analyses.

The outcome is a single prespecified time-to-first-event composite of adjudicated CV death, nonfatal MI and nonfatal stroke over the whole follow-up. The registry lists it as the primary efficacy and safety outcome with one time frame. The report presents this same composite, so no alternative eligible measurement or time point appears to have been chosen from.

The registry entry was first submitted on 2010-06-10, before the start date of 2010-06-18. It names the primary composite of CV death, nonfatal MI or nonfatal stroke as time to first event, with superiority and non-inferiority tests. SAP edition 4 (23 February 2017) was dated before primary completion on 2017-04-21. It specifies the same ITT stratified Cox model for the composite. The report analyses the outcome as specified. The SAP date alone does not prove finalization before unblinding, so the answer is probably yes.

Table 1 shows one significant difference (hypertension 48% vs 26%, P=.029) among about 30 baseline comparisons, compatible with chance. Baseline 6MWT (458.5 vs 478 m, P=.3) and other key prognostic factors (age, ASA, stage, FEV1, procedure) are similar. Randomized group sizes (66 vs 58) are close to 1:1. The caveat is that Table 1 covers only the 95 analysed participants, not all 124 randomized.

The main report and the registry record describe the sequence generator but not how assignments were delivered or hidden from enrolling staff (no central service, envelopes or independent pharmacy). Single-centre trial with consecutive patients. Neither the registry nor the supplement describes concealment, and there is no protocol or SAP. Circumstances support neither a probable yes nor a probable no. The blinded assessor does not address concealment.
The report states participants were randomly assigned 1:1 by computer-generated random numbers, which is a random component.

Analysis was of the 95 randomized patients who underwent surgery with confirmed non-metastatic cancer (52 vs 43), with multiple imputation; exclusions (benign diagnosis, metastatic disease, no surgery) were post-randomization but plausibly eligibility-related and not driven by the intervention. Not a naive per-protocol analysis.

Compliance was monitored by weekly calls and a booklet, but the report gives no information on whether deviations from assigned intervention arose because of the trial context (e.g. REHAB participants starting exercise pre-operatively).

Home-based exercise/nutrition/relaxation program starting 4 weeks before surgery versus after surgery; participants necessarily know timing of their program. Only the outcome assessor is described as blinded.
Kinesiologist, dietitian and psychology-trained personnel delivered personalized prescriptions and weekly calls and so knew the assigned timing; blinding applied only to the assessor.

The rate of missing 6MWT data before multiple imputation was 35% pre-operatively, 43% at 4 weeks and 48% at 8 weeks (p5 lines 1-2), far beyond what could be 'nearly all' for a continuous outcome. Imputed data count as missing. Per-arm counts are not given.

Missing data were handled by multiple imputation by fully conditional specification from other observed data (p3 lines 25-31). No sensitivity analysis addressing a relationship between missingness and the true 6MWT value is reported. The per-protocol analysis (n=28 vs 19) restricts to compliers and does not address missingness. Imputation not shown to correct MNAR bias.

With 35-48% of 6MWT data missing, the report gives neither proportions missing by arm nor reasons for missing visits, and the analysis did not model missingness mechanisms beyond imputation. Reasons suggesting independence from the outcome are not documented, and information expected to be reported is absent, so likelihood of outcome-dependent missingness cannot be excluded.

Patients recovering from lung cancer surgery may skip 6MWT visits because of poor health, complications or poor functional status, so missingness could depend on the true walking distance. No documented reasons unrelated to the outcome are given.

The 6MWT is an observer-measured test and the article states 'The assessor, who was blinded to group assignment, used a standardized protocol and script'. Registry lists masking as none, but the article specifically reports a blinded assessor.
All outcomes were measured with the same method at the same scheduled time points (baseline, within 1 week of operation, 4 and 8 weeks) in both arms; active scheduled testing, not passive detection.
The 6MWT is an established, validated measure of functional capacity, administered per American Thoracic Society guidelines with a standardized protocol and script.

The Methods describe one main analysis (repeated-measures ANOVA on multiply imputed data, 10 datasets) plus a per-protocol analysis, and the article reports both. No sign of several adjusted or alternative models with only one shown. The null finding makes result-driven selection less plausible, though no SAP exists to confirm the intended analysis.

The 6MWT is the single primary outcome measure, in a registry entry that lists the 8-week time frame, and the article reports it at all measured time points (baseline, pre-operation, 4 and 8 weeks), including the 8-week row used for this Result. The Methods say all outcomes were measured at the same time points. The Result target spans all time points, so there is no sign of a subset being chosen for its results. The registered 8-week primary versus the multi-time-point report is not a result-dependent narrowing.

The only dated plan is the ClinicalTrials.gov record (NCT02938104), first submitted 2016-02-02 with start 2014-08; the article says enrolment began November 2014. The registration therefore post-dates the start of enrolment, when outcome data were already accruing, so it cannot show what was fixed beforehand. The record names the 6MWT at 8 weeks as primary but gives no analysis detail. No protocol or SAP was found among the Sources (registry document discovery listed no documents). Per guidance, this gives No information.

Table 1 shows baseline characteristics (HbA1c about 8.0-8.2%, BMI 32.2-32.9, metformin use 86-96%) similar across the six groups, and the text states baseline demographics were similar; no imbalance suggesting a randomization problem.

Eligible patients were randomized at Visit 3 and assigned to arms 'via IWRS'; allocation was central and remote, and investigators only enrolled participants. The study was double-blind with study drug supplied per IWRS assignment, so allocation could not be foreseen before assignment.

Participants were 'randomly allocated (1:1:1:1:1:1) to one of the six parallel treatment groups by use of an interactive web response system' with stratification by HbA1c, metformin use and BMI; the protocol says the 'randomization scheme will be performed using IWRS that will ensure balance between treatment arms'. A sponsor-run IWRS implies a computer-generated random sequence, though the generator is not described explicitly.

Safety data, including Table 3 adverse events, are reported in the safety population: 'all randomised participants who received at least one dose of study drug' (316 of 318; one untreated participant each in the 1 mg and 10 mg groups). Under RoB 2 guidance this is an exclusion based on receipt of intervention rather than missing outcome data, so it is not a full ITT analysis. It was prespecified in the protocol and SAP and applies to only two participants.

Protocol 7.3: 'This is a double-blind study. Although the patient and the investigator will know which dose group ... they will not know whether the patient is receiving LY3298176, dulaglutide 1.5 mg, or placebo.' Placebo and dulaglutide patients were distributed across the dose-volume cohorts to maintain the blind. Participants therefore did not know drug identity. GI side effects are shared by incretin agents and are not specific to one intervention; no report of blinding failure.

Investigators and site staff were likewise masked to whether a patient received tirzepatide, dulaglutide or placebo (protocol 7.3); allocation was by central IWRS and 'a minimum number of Lilly personnel will see the randomization table'. Only the dose-group level was known.

Only 2 of 318 randomized (0.6%) were excluded, both never treated, so no treatment-emergent AE could occur in them; one each from the 1 mg and 10 mg arms, so exclusions are not concentrated in one comparison arm. The exclusion is unlikely to materially change cholecystitis counts (2 events in total), although with such a rare outcome even small exclusions carry some uncertainty.

Safety data are reported for 316 of 318 randomised participants ("the mITT and safety population included 316 participants"); only the two never-treated participants (one each in the 1 mg and 10 mg groups) lack safety data. Although 283 (90%) completed the study, adverse events are routinely recorded up to withdrawal, so non-completers still contribute events up to dropout, and the SAP analyses safety on the safety population without imputation. Outcome data are therefore probably available for nearly all randomised participants; the 0.6% excluded as untreated is too few to matter.

The assessors are the site investigators who diagnosed and recorded the AE. The protocol states that "Although the investigator and patients will know dose group assignment ... they will not know whether they are actually receiving placebo, LY3298176, or dulaglutide". The paper reports a double-blind design with placebo and dulaglutide patients further randomised to the dose-level masks. Assessors were therefore unaware of the actual intervention. Unblinding through GI side effects is possible but does not by itself make assessors aware.

All six arms followed the same visit schedule and the same AE reporting process in a double-dummy design (each patient received the same number of injections of active or placebo). Methods and timing were comparable. A residual concern is that more GI symptoms in tirzepatide arms could prompt more abdominal work-up, but cholecystitis is a clinically evident, serious event that would be diagnosed regardless of arm, so differential detection is judged unlikely.

Cholecystitis was recorded as an investigator-reported adverse event under the protocol AE/SAE reporting system ("all AEs occurring after signing the ICF are recorded in the CRF"; serious events reported within 24 hours). Safety outcomes were prespecified in the paper. Cholecystitis is a clinically evident diagnosis, so the method is sensitive to plausible effects.

The numerical result comes from the single prespecified safety-population AE analysis. Nothing indicates multiple eligible analyses of cholecystitis were run and one selected. Differences between the registry serious AE counts and Table 3 for pancreatitis reflect seriousness and adjudication, not cholecystitis selection.

Cholecystitis is reported as a treatment-emergent AE count in Table 3 by arm, from the safety analysis the SAP describes. There is no indication of multiple eligible measurements or definitions of cholecystitis from which one was chosen.

The registry record was first submitted 2017-04-24, before the study start (2017-05-24), and SAP v3 was approved 26-Mar-2018, before database lock, with the study team blinded until database lock. The SAP specifies safety analyses of treatment-emergent adverse events, so the AE analysis was planned before unblinded outcome data were available. Cholecystitis is not individually prespecified, so this is probably yes rather than yes.

Table 1 shows balanced baseline characteristics across demographics, severity scores, reason for admission and prior oxygen device, with no sizeable p values. The only notable difference is in the stratification subgroups (p=0.06; PaO2/FiO2 >200 in 18% vs 27%), which the authors explain by small per-centre permuted blocks across 28 centres and stratification; this is compatible with chance/stratified blocking and does not suggest subversion. Group sizes (142 vs 171) reflect post-randomisation exclusions (147 vs 175 randomised, close to 1:1).

Assignment was made through a centralised web-based system (G-ERDC, Clinfile) after inclusion criteria were validated, with block size stated to be unknown to investigators; the protocol confirms central, password-protected internet randomisation effective only after eligibility verification. This is remote allocation independent of enrolling staff and the small fixed block size is not exposed to recruiters, so allocations were not predictable.
The report states randomisation was computer-generated in permuted blocks of four, stratified by centre and PaO2/FiO2 ratio; a computer-generated permuted-block sequence has a random component.

The primary outcome was analysed in the intention-to-treat population by randomised group (protocol: ITT, with failures of the assigned method retained in their group). 9 of 322 randomised were excluded: 5 with no recorded data, 2 withdrawn consent/legal protection, 1 not intubated and 1 cardiac arrest, as decided by a blind review board; these are mostly missing-data or ineligibility-type exclusions not driven by the assigned intervention, so the analysis is ITT/modified ITT in RoB 2 terms (missing data considered in Domain 3).

The report describes delivery of both interventions and a standardised intubation bundle; the only departures from assigned preoxygenation were stopping preoxygenation in 3 NIV and 6 HFO patients, mainly for severe hypoxaemia, which the protocol explicitly permits (investigator may switch method or intubate immediately, counted as failure of the assigned method and analysed by ITT). These are clinically driven changes consistent with the protocol rather than trial-context deviations, and nothing reported suggests non-protocol co-interventions arising from lack of equipoise.

The trial was described as non-blinded, open-label; NIV (face mask on ICU ventilator) and high-flow nasal cannula are visibly different devices, so patients (who were consenting or under emergency inclusion while awake) could not be unaware of their assignment.

Individual assignments could not be masked and the devices are physically distinct, so clinicians delivering preoxygenation and intubation knew the allocation. Only investigators/coordinating centre were blind to group outcomes and adjudicators were blind to group.

Of 322 randomised, 313 (97.2%) were analysed; the 9 not analysed were 5 with no recorded data, 2 withdrawn consent/legal protection, 1 not intubated and 1 cardiac arrest. Even if all 9 were counted as missing (at most 5 truly missing outcome data), the 80 observed events (33+47) greatly outnumber them, so the outcome, whatever it was in these participants, could not have made an important difference. The outcome was recorded continuously on a dedicated oximeter and adjudicated offline, with all analysed patients contributing.

Events were determined from stored oximetry curves extracted by an independent biostatistician unaware of allocation and reviewed by an adjudication committee unaware of study groups, not by the unblinded bedside clinicians; the outcome is an automated device reading rather than a clinical decision by the aware care team.

The same device, sensors, threshold (<80% for at least 5 s) and window (induction to 5 min after capnographic confirmation) applied to both arms, with all recordings stored and analysed offline by the same process; no differential detection opportunities are described.

Pulse oximetry below 80% for at least 5 s is a prespecified, objective, standard way to detect severe desaturation; recording was continuous at 1 Hz on a dedicated monitor with single-use sensors given to all centres, so it is sensitive to plausible effects.

The reported result is the prespecified unadjusted chi2 ITT comparison named in the protocol and the report's methods. The adjusted logistic regression is reported as a sensitivity analysis and prespecified subgroups are described; agreeing sensitivity analyses are evidence against selection. The headline result is the plan's primary analysis, not one picked among unreported alternatives.

The outcome is a single binary event (SpO2 <80% during the intubation procedure) measured by continuous oximetry. The registered definition, the protocol primary criterion and the reported outcome coincide, with a single registered time frame (through 5 minutes after preoxygenation). No alternative thresholds or time windows for the primary outcome are described in the plan, and the reported result is the prespecified primary one.

Protocol version 1 (16/07/2014) and the registry entry (first submitted 2016-01-19, start 2016-04, i.e. before enrolment) both name severe hypoxaemia/desaturation below 80% during intubation as the primary outcome. The protocol specifies a Chi2 comparison between groups on an ITT basis, later completed by logistic regression. The report uses an unadjusted chi2 test in the ITT population, with prespecified stratification subgroups and an adjusted logistic sensitivity analysis. Both dated plans precede unblinded outcome data. Only protocol version 1 is available, so later amendments cannot be excluded, hence probably_yes.

Table 1 shows similar age, sex and DSM-5 symptom counts across arms, and the authors report groups were similar for demographics and drug use at baseline at the final analysis. Group sizes (23, 12, 24, 23) are consistent with the staged allocation. Any baseline differences in cannabis use measures are compatible with chance in a small trial.

The code was held by an independent emergency unblinding service (Sealed Envelope) and the drug manufacturer, which labelled identical packages with anonymous participant numbers; only masked investigators enrolled participants, and capsules were identical. The small block size could in principle allow prediction, but participants and investigators were masked, so predicting assignments was not feasible.

The report states the sequence was generated by the trial statistician using block randomisation with the R command blockrand; blockrand creates randomly permuted blocks, so a random component is very likely, although the report does not state explicitly that order within blocks was random.

"All analyses were done on an intention-to-treat basis. Missing data were handled using Bayesian multiple imputation under the assumption of missing at random." The CONSORT flow shows all randomised participants (23 placebo, 24 400 mg, 23 800 mg) included in the final ITT analysis. The reported week 16 means are descriptive raw-data summaries, but the trial analysis population is ITT.

Double-blind placebo-controlled trial with identical-size capsules containing microcrystalline cellulose filler with or without cannabidiol; "All investigators and participants remained masked throughout the duration of the trial." Nothing reported suggests blinding failed through intervention-specific side effects.

Investigators who enrolled participants, assigned interventions, did assessments and entered data were masked; the allocation code was held by an independent unblinding service and the manufacturer, and unmasking occurred only after database lock.

Figure 1 shows all randomised participants (23 placebo, 24 400 mg, 23 800 mg) in the final ITT analysis, and 77 of 82 (94%) completed the 4-week treatment, but no report gives how many participants had an observed Cannabis Withdrawal Scale score at week 16 (a follow-up site visit). Table S5 gives raw means without denominators, and the report says missing data were handled by Bayesian multiple imputation, which counts as missing.

Missing data were handled by Bayesian multiple imputation assuming missing at random within a model with time, baseline score and participant random intercept; no sensitivity analysis to missing-not-at-random assumptions is reported, and such imputation is not assumed to correct bias.

None of the five reasons for a Yes is shown: the few reported dropouts during treatment (1 placebo, 1 in each other arm shown in Figure 1) had reasons such as lost to follow-up, missed visits or psychotropic medication, and no differences in proportions or reasons between arms are reported; "no participants dropped out because of treatment". Week 16 missingness is unreported, so this is a judgement.
Loss to follow-up in a cannabis cessation trial could relate to participants' withdrawal symptoms and cannabis use, so missingness could depend on the true score.

The outcome is participant-reported, so the participant is the assessor. "All investigators and participants remained masked throughout the duration of the trial", with identical capsules and masked investigators doing assessments, so both participant and data collector were blinded. Treatment-guess data are not reported.

All arms had the same weekly treatment-period site visits and the same follow-up schedule (weeks 6, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24) and identical scale administration; the intervention (identical capsules) involved no extra contacts in any arm.

The Cannabis Withdrawal Scale is a standard self-report instrument for cannabis withdrawal, used as a pre-specified secondary endpoint, and nothing in the report suggests poor validity or insensitivity to plausible effects.

The Result is a descriptive raw-data mean per group and time point, "Summary statistics stratified by treatment group and timepoint were obtained from raw data", so there is essentially one way to compute it, and the model-based contrasts (treatment weeks and all data) were also reported. No evidence suggests alternative analyses were run and withheld.

The scale was a single total score, and Table S5 reports the group means at every assessed time point from baseline through week 16 (weeks 20 and 24 not assessed), so no time point appears to have been picked from a larger set. The report states the total score was the one recorded.

The registry record (first submitted 2014-01-22, before the March 2014 start) lists only a single broad secondary outcome, "Psychological Wellbeing, Cognition and Endocannabinoids", and does not name the Cannabis Withdrawal Scale or week 16. The OSF protocol (https://osf.io/3cbef/) is cited but was not captured, so no dated source shows this scale and time point were fixed before unblinded data. The article describes the scale among planned secondary endpoints, but that is not a dated plan.

The report states both groups were well matched at baseline including baseline 6MWD (248 vs 250 m, p=0.962). Table 1 shows similar age, sex, BMI, CR-POSSUM and MUST; small differences (e.g. antithrombotic drugs 12 vs 20, M1 12 vs 7) are compatible with chance. 92 were randomised per arm, matching the intended ratio.

Allocation was performed by a study coordinator not involved in clinical management, while eligibility was evaluated separately by a chief surgeon, so assignment was delivered by someone other than the enrolling clinician. No explicit concealment mechanism (central service, opaque envelopes) is described, so this is a judgement rather than a firm Yes.
Methods state patients were randomly allocated using computerised random numbers, which is a random component.

After completion of the whole study, 23 patients who underwent TAMIS were excluded from the analysis because their outcomes differed dramatically, leaving 149 analysed 'on an intention to treat basis'. These patients met the eligibility criteria and were randomised, their outcomes could have been measured, and the exclusion was decided post hoc after outcomes were seen. This is exclusion of eligible randomised participants, not exclusion for missing outcome data or ineligibility confirmed after randomisation.

Participants were aware of allocation, so deviations arising from the trial context are possible, for example controls independently starting exercise or non-protocol co-interventions. The report describes a compliance calculation from the work diary and notes that some follow-up data were lost to non-attendance, but it does not report adherence results, control-group exercise or co-interventions, or whether any departures from protocol arose from the trial context.

The prehabilitation arm underwent a 3-6 week programme with an information booklet, a work diary, weekly supervised exercise sessions, nutrition and a psychologist session, whereas controls received standard ERAS care. An exercise-based programme cannot be hidden from the participants receiving it, and no placebo or sham is described.

Physiotherapists, a nutritionist and a psychologist delivered the prehabilitation components to the allocated group, so those delivering the intervention must have known who was in it. The report states that surgeons and clinicians performing the operation and follow-up were blinded, which concerns the clinical team rather than the prehabilitation providers.

The excluded patients were a low-risk surgical subgroup defined by operation type, a characteristic unlikely to depend on allocation, and the analysed groups remained well matched at baseline including baseline 6MWD. The exclusion was a sizeable proportion of randomised patients and post hoc, but the stated reason concerns hospital stay and morbidity rather than 6MWD, so a substantial effect on the between-group 6MWD result is judged unlikely, though not excluded.

The Figure 1 footnote states that non-attendance led to lost functional and quality-of-life data, and the flow diagram (read earlier) shows 16 prehabilitation and 18 control patients who did not attend follow-up, about a quarter of the 149 analysed. Table 2 gives the group sizes as n = 77 and 72 without separate observed counts for 6MWD at surgery. The report does not state how many had a 6MWD measured the day before surgery, so data were probably not available for nearly all randomised participants, well below the usual 95% for a continuous outcome.

The statistical analysis section describes t-tests, Mann-Whitney U tests, chi-squared tests and a Cox model in SPSS, with no imputation, weighting or sensitivity analysis for missing outcome data. No evidence is presented that the result is robust to plausible values for the missing measurements.

The numbers not attending were similar in the two arms (16 and 18 per the flow diagram), so there is no difference in proportions missing that suggests outcome-dependent missingness. No reasons are reported that would suggest dependence on the true value or differ between groups, and the circumstances are not ones where dependence is widely understood to be likely. Dependence is plausible, which is the 'could' of 3.3, but is not shown to be likely.

Patients awaiting colorectal cancer surgery who did not attend follow-up may have done so because of poorer health or fitness, which relates to walking distance. The report gives no reasons for non-attendance that exclude this.

The registry says outcome assessors were masked and that those delivering the programme were not involved in outcome assessment, and the report says clinicians not involved in final evaluation were blinded. However, the report does not say who ran the treadmill 6MWD or whether that person knew allocation, and patients cannot be blinded to a training programme. The registry also lists weekly 6MWD checks at the physiotherapy visits for the prehabilitation arm only.

Both arms had 6MWD measured by the same treadmill method at first visit, the day before surgery, and 4 and 8 weeks after surgery. The prehabilitation arm had extra weekly 6MWD checks during training, but the outcome compared here is the common day-before-surgery assessment.

The result is an objective walking distance on a treadmill, with little room for tester judgement. The registry describes masked assessors and the report describes blinded clinicians. There is no sign of strong tester preconceptions, though this is not established.
The 6MWD is effort-dependent and the treadmill speed was set to tire the patient, so an unblinded tester's verbal encouragement or speed choice could be influenced by knowledge of allocation.

6MWD on a treadmill is a standard, pre-registered functional capacity measure (registry primary outcomes 7 and 8) and is sensitive to plausible training effects. Nothing suggests poor validity or a ceiling or floor problem.

The analysis excluded 23 TAMIS patients after the whole study was completed, because outcomes in that group were 'dramatically different'. An analysis including them was therefore possible, but it is not reported. The stated reason concerns length of stay and morbidity rather than the 6MWD effect, so there is no clear evidence the choice was driven by the 6MWD result. Without a SAP, it cannot be judged whether the analysis was planned, or whether adjusted and unadjusted versions or other analyses were run.

6MWD was measured at baseline, the day before surgery, and at 4 and 8 weeks after surgery. The report presents the time-of-surgery, 4-week and 8-week results in Table 2, including the non-significant 4-week difference, and reports both percentage of baseline and absolute values. The registry's 6MWD primary outcomes (by operation, and at 8 weeks) are all reported. This does not look like selection of one favourable time point or scale.

The registry entry was first submitted 2018-11-27, after the stated start of 2018-11-01, and the article reports enrolment from October 2017 to February 2019, so outcome data were already accruing. No protocol or SAP is available (the registry capture lists no linked documents). The registry's primary outcomes name 6MWD change by operation and at 8 weeks, but no source dated before outcome data could be seen fixes this measurement and analysis. The article also reports excluding 23 TAMIS patients 'after completion of the whole study'.

Table 1 reports 223 participants per arm, matching the 1:1 ratio, and demographics, diabetes duration, metformin dose, TZD use, weight and BMI are similar between arms. Baseline HbA1c was 7.6% in both arms. The only visible difference is mean diabetes duration (8.7 vs 9.6 years), which is compatible with chance. Nothing suggests a randomization problem. Comparable baseline of the run-in groups also fits the stratification.

Allocation was central: kits were packaged according to a centrally generated kit-number list and treatment numbers were allocated via a centralized interactive voice response system, with investigators having no access to the randomization code. This is remote allocation independent of enrolment staff, meeting the minimal criteria for concealment.

The report describes central 1:1 randomization with a centrally generated randomized treatment kit number list, stratified by post-run-in HbA1c and TZD use. It does not say outright that a computer random generator was used, but this is a large (140 centres, 25 countries) sponsor-run phase III trial published in a journal with word limits, and a centrally generated randomization list is the standard random sequence.

The safety population is all randomized participants exposed to at least one dose (223 per arm, matching 446 randomized), analysed descriptively by assigned group. Exclusion of unexposed participants is minimal given that the counts equal the randomized totals. Events are counted in the on-treatment window (first dose to 3 days after last dose), a feature of AE ascertainment rather than exclusion of participants.

Reported changes from assigned treatment were discontinuations for adverse events (more on lixisenatide, mostly GI) and rescue therapy in one participant per group (p3 l14-26). Stopping a drug for toxicity and rescue therapy are consistent with the protocol and with what would occur outside a trial; there is no evidence that the trial context produced non-protocol interventions.

The trial is double-blind with volume-matched injectable placebo and centrally generated kit numbers, so participants were not told their assignment. However RoB 2 guidance says to answer Yes/Probably yes when participants experience side effects known to be specific to one intervention; lixisenatide has characteristic GI side effects, and GI-related discontinuations were 10 vs 0 (main article p3 l14-26), so some participants may have inferred their assignment. Answering conservatively only activates the trial-context question 2.3.

Allocation was central via IVRS with a kit-number list, so site personnel had no access to the code; double-blind placebo-controlled design. Investigators' knowledge of GI tolerability does not identify the arm with certainty.

446 participants were randomized and the safety population (the denominator for the serious AE table) is 223 per arm, i.e. every randomized participant (registry participant flow lines 1659-1672). Serious AEs were collected over a defined on-treatment window (first dose to 3 days after last dose) for the whole safety population, so an AE outcome status exists for all randomized participants. Treatment discontinuation (29 lixisenatide vs 12 placebo) shortens the exposure window for some participants but is not outcome-data loss; AE ascertainment is by design limited to that window, and median exposure was 169 days in both arms.

Assessors of these events are the site investigators who judge and report serious AEs from clinical records. The trial is double-blind with matching injectable placebo and central allocation by kit-number list, so investigators are blinded unless unblinded by side effects; the sources report no unblinding of investigators. Deducing the intervention from drug side effects does not itself establish awareness of assignment (guidance section 5.1.3).

Both arms followed the same double-blind schedule with identical injection regimen and visit structure, and SAEs were collected over the same window (first dose to 3 days after last dose) with the same coding. Placebo-controlled design means the intervention does not add extra contacts. A possible diagnostic-detection effect exists because lixisenatide causes more GI symptoms (nausea/vomiting) that could prompt more GI work-ups, but this would tend to increase detection in the lixisenatide arm, whereas reported events were in the placebo arm.

The outcomes are serious clinical events (acute cholecystitis, ischaemic colitis, upper GI haemorrhage) captured as serious TEAEs and coded in MedDRA 14.0 across the whole safety population, a standard regulatory AE reporting system. Such events are clinically overt and detectable by routine care. The registry labels AE assessment as 'non systematic', so there was no targeted ascertainment for these specific events, which is a mild limitation but not evidence of an insensitive method.

Safety was analysed descriptively by treatment group, so the reported result is a raw participant count per arm in the safety population. There is no model, adjustment, imputation or composite definition that could have produced alternative estimates, and the counts are consistent between registry and paper where overlapping. Lack of an SAP is noted, but descriptive counting leaves little room for analytic selection.

The requested outcome is the occurrence of specific serious GI events, a simple participant count over one on-treatment window (first dose to 3 days after last dose). The registry reports the complete serious AE table by MedDRA preferred term for both arms, so these events were not picked from a wider reported set; there is no scale or alternative time point to choose among. The three requested events and the pancreatitis statement come from the same ascertainment. Lack of a protocol means this rests on the nature of the outcome rather than documented intentions.

No captured Source specifies this outcome before outcome data could be seen. The registry record (first submitted 2009-09-10, before the 2009-10 start) lists only efficacy outcomes plus symptomatic hypoglycaemia as registered outcomes; it does not register GI serious adverse events as an outcome. The paper states only that safety was analysed descriptively in the safety population. No protocol or SAP is among the Sources, and the registry document discovery found no linked documents. Serious AEs are routine safety reporting, but under the guidance an outcome that no pre-specified source mentions is No information.

Table 1 baseline characteristics for the safety population (n=161/161/160) are reported as well matched; group sizes (161/161/160 plus 2 untreated placebo) match the 2:2:1:1 ratio, and differences such as age (55.4/54.6/58.2) and HbA1c (64.0/65.0/64.0) are compatible with chance.

Treatment was matching placebo, double-blind to participants and investigators (registry masking: participant, investigator), delivered via identical pen auto-injectors in a multicentre industry trial, which typically implies centrally allocated, numbered treatment kits. The mechanism is not described, so only 'probably yes'. Study drug volume was not blinded, but this is a titration-step volume difference that does not reveal the next allocation.

Report and registry state a randomized, double-blind, parallel-group multicentre trial with 2:2:1:1 allocation stratified by HbA1c and BMI; no sequence-generation method is described. A large (n=484, 75 centres, 15 countries) industry-sponsored phase 3 trial with stratified 2:2:1:1 allocation and an independent DMC most plausibly used a computer-generated random sequence, so 'probably yes' rather than 'no information'.

The AE results come from the safety population, defined as all randomized participants exposed to at least one dose; two randomized placebo participants who received no treatment were excluded. This is an exclusion based on intervention received rather than missing outcome data, so it is not a strict ITT or RoB 2 mITT, although the departure is minimal.

The trial was double-blind with matching placebo and identical pen auto-injectors; the registry lists participants and investigators as masked. Study drug volume was not blinded, but this relates to titration-step volume matching between regimens, not active vs placebo. GI adverse events were more frequent on lixisenatide, so partial unblinding by side effects is possible, but nothing reported indicates blinding failed.

Investigators were masked per the registry and the report says double-blind with matching placebo; the sponsor and an independent DMC oversaw the trial. Who exactly was blinded is not itemised beyond participant and investigator.

Only 2 of 484 randomized participants (about 0.4%, both placebo, neither treated) were excluded. Untreated participants would be expected to contribute little to adverse-event counts, so the exclusion is unlikely to materially change a 4/160 vs 15/322 comparison, even allowing for the rare events.

Registry participant flow shows 484 randomized (placebo 162, lixisenatide 322) and a safety population of 482 (placebo 160, lixisenatide 322); only the 2 placebo participants who never received study drug have no AE data. AEs were collected from first dose to 3 days after last dose, so participants who discontinued early still contribute AE data for their exposure period; treatment discontinuation (35/162 placebo, 70/322 lixisenatide not completed) is not missing outcome data for an on-treatment AE count. Observed gastritis events (4 and 15) are not outnumbered by the 2 missing participants in a way that matters; 2/484 (0.4%) missing is nearly all. Residual uncertainty: AE ascertainment after treatment stop is not captured by design.

The trial was double-blind with matching placebo (participants and investigators masked per registry design; only study drug volume was not blinded). AEs are reported by participants and judged by investigators who are therefore probably unaware of assignment. Deducing the arm from GI side effects does not by itself cause bias per guidance.

Both arms were followed with the same visit schedule and AE window (first dose to 3 days after last dose) and the same MedDRA coding. Lixisenatide causes frequent nausea/vomiting, which could prompt more clinical work-up and thus diagnostic detection of gastritis/cholecystitis, but no source describes differential testing.

Gastritis and cholecystitis were captured as MedDRA 13.1-coded adverse events (serious and other >=5%) in the registry results, a standard system for identifying harms; nothing suggests the method was insensitive or invalid for these events.

The result is a simple participant count per group in the safety population, tabulated descriptively. The paper states safety was analysed by descriptive comparison, and the registry gives the same counts. There are no adjusted or alternative models for this event that could have been chosen on the basis of results. The counts agree across the paper and the registry.

Gastritis is a count of participants with MedDRA-coded events over the whole double-blind period. The registry AE tables list all serious events and all non-serious events above the 5% threshold by preferred term, so reporting follows a systematic rule and not a choice among results. Gastritis is one of a standard list, not picked from alternative scales, definitions or time points. There is no evidence of several eligible definitions or time points for this event from which one was chosen.

The registry record was first submitted 2008-09-30 (start 2008-09), but its registered outcomes (HbA1c primary; FPG, weight, HbA1c targets, rescue therapy secondary; weight-loss and symptomatic hypoglycemia as other) do not include gastritis, cholecystitis or any GI adverse-event outcome. No protocol or SAP is linked (provenance capture: no_linked_documents_in_current_record) and the paper cites none. So no source dated before outcome data specifies this measurement or analysis. Gastritis appears only in the posted AE tables (safety population, descriptive, MedDRA 13.1, 'non-systematic assessment', 5% threshold for non-serious events), which were posted in 2016, after unblinding.

Table 1 shows groups of 312 and 306 with similar sex, age, BMI, Beighton score, eligibility criteria and graft details; the text states 'No statistical differences were found between groups for any patient characteristics'. Only meniscal repair (P<.05) and time to return to sport (P=.01, a post-randomization variable) differ, compatible with chance across ~30 comparisons.

After arthroscopy confirmed eligibility, 'the patient was then randomized in a 1:1 ratio, via telephone or a web-based software program (Empower Inc)'. This is remote/central allocation after eligibility confirmation, consistent with concealment. Small blocks (2 and 4) could allow predictability only if recruiters knew block boundaries; stratification by surgeon and varied block sizes with remote assignment make this unlikely, and nothing suggests foreknowledge.

Patients were randomized 1:1 by telephone or web-based software, 'stratified by surgeon, sex, and meniscal repair ... in permuted block sizes of 2 and 4'. Random permuted blocks with varied sizes implies a random component; the generation method (e.g., computer-generated) is not spelled out, so Probably yes rather than Yes.

The report states all patients were analysed in the group to which they were randomized (ITT). Exclusions from the primary analysis (298/312 and 291/306) were for missing outcome data (loss to follow-up or withdrawal), which counts as a modified ITT acceptable for this Domain.

No crossover, contamination or non-protocol co-intervention attributable to the trial context is reported. All patients had the same standardized ACLR and received identical standardized written and oral rehabilitation instructions. Rehabilitation compliance and return-to-sport timing were not standardized or monitored, but such variation would be consistent with usual care outside the trial and there is no indication it arose from the trial context.
Patients were not blinded: the Limitations state that "patients were not blinded to their treatment allocation. This was not possible due to the presence of the lateral incision".

Surgeons performed the LET only in the allocated arm and were not blinded; the report describes only the outcome assessor as blinded. The registry's DOUBLE masking entry conflicts with the article, but the article's description of the surgical procedure is more specific and the LET cannot be hidden from the surgeon.

Primary-outcome data were available for 298/312 (ACLR) and 291/306 (ACLR+LET) randomized patients, i.e. 589/618 (95.3%). 29 patients (about 5%: 18 lost to follow-up, 11 withdrawn) lacked data, split almost equally (14 vs 15; 4.5% vs 4.9%). Observed events (120+72=192) greatly outnumber the 29 missing participants, so even extreme outcomes in the missing patients could change the risk difference only modestly and could not plausibly reverse the 40% vs 25% contrast. The report also describes a MICE sensitivity analysis including all 312 and 306 randomized patients.

The primary outcome (pivot shift) was assessed at each visit by "an appropriately trained clinician who was not a member of the surgical team, blinded to group allocation", and a Tubigrip bandage covered the knee to hide the LET incision. The examiners are therefore probably unaware, though bandage concealment is not perfect and patients were unblinded; graft rupture confirmation by MRI or arthroscopy is a hard structural finding.

Both arms had the same scheduled visits (3, 6, 12 and 24 months), the same examination and the same definition and thresholds of failure; ascertainment was protocolised, not passive. LET does not obviously prompt extra visits or imaging by design.

The primary outcome is a pre-specified composite of IKDC-graded pivot shift and graft rupture confirmed by MRI or arthroscopy. The report notes the pivot shift is "the most specific of all clinical ACL tests" and that a positive pivot shift after ACLR is "a well-accepted definition of a failed ACLR". Low sensitivity would act equally in both arms (non-differential), and the trial acknowledges the test is subjective, but the method is not unsuitable for detecting plausible effects.

The report analyses the primary outcome with the method the registry specified (Mantel-Haenszel with random effect of surgeon, RRR, RD, NNT), by intention to treat, and adds a multiple-imputation sensitivity analysis, which agrees with the main analysis. Reporting a pre-specified primary analysis plus agreeing sensitivity analysis is evidence against selection. No suggestion that adjusted or alternative models were run and withheld.

The primary outcome is a single registered 24-month clinical failure composite. The article reports one primary result at 24 months, with a separate graft rupture result analysed the same way, which is a component of the composite and not a substitute. Visits occurred at 3, 6, 12 and 24 months, but the registered primary time frame is 24 months only, which the report uses. No evidence of other eligible definitions or time points being measured and withheld.

The ClinicalTrials.gov record was first submitted 2013-12-02, before enrolment began (start 2014-01; enrolment Jan 2014 to Mar 2017). It lists the primary outcome (graft failure: symptomatic instability requiring revision, or positive/asymmetric pivot shift) at 24 months, with a pre-planned Mantel-Haenszel test with random effect of surgeon, RR/RD with 95% CI and NNT. The report analyses the primary outcome exactly this way ("Mantel-Haenszel test (random effect of surgeon)", RRR, RD, NNT). No protocol or SAP is available, and the current record cannot show earlier versions, so this is a probable rather than definite answer. The article's composite adds a persistence requirement for grade 1 pivot shift and graft rupture by MRI or arthroscopy, which the registry does not spell out.

Table 1 shows similar groups (38 vs 39; baseline 6MWT 421 vs 425 m, adjusted P = 1.000; similar age, ASA, stage, comorbidities). Differences such as sex (55% vs 69% male) and BMI are compatible with chance. Allocation ratio 1:1 is approximately kept. Table 1 covers analysed participants only, but the text says the 12 excluded randomized patients were similar.

Allocation was concealed with sequentially numbered sealed envelopes, assigned after baseline assessment was complete. Envelope opacity, tamper-proofing, who held them and opening only after irreversible assignment are not described, so Yes is not warranted; no sign of foreknowledge of allocation. Surgery scheduling was not affected by group. The registry captured nothing further.
The Methods state patients were randomly assigned 1:1 by computer-generated random numbers, which is a random component.

77 of 89 randomized were analysed. Exclusions were no resection, emergency surgery, operated elsewhere (reasons not plausibly influenced by assignment, as randomization preceded surgery scheduling which was unaffected by group), plus withdrawal/loss to follow-up (missing outcome data, handled in Domain 3). Analysis was by randomized group with all analysed completing the 6MWT; this is akin to a modified ITT excluding missing data and ineligible participants.

The report describes delivery, weekly adherence contact and compliance by period. Compliance differences (Table 3) reflect ordinary non-adherence that could occur outside a trial. The rehabilitation arm was promised the program after surgery, which reduces the incentive to seek it elsewhere, and the authors report most of that arm did not increase physical activity before surgery. No non-protocol co-interventions attributed to the trial context are reported.

A home-based exercise, nutrition and relaxation program started 4 weeks before surgery versus after surgery cannot be hidden; the authors state patients could not be blinded and no sham was used. Single-blind refers to the outcome assessor only.

The kinesiologist, dietitian and psychologist delivering the program consulted each patient at the baseline visit (prehab) or pre-surgery visit (rehab), so they necessarily knew the timing and thus the assignment. Only the outcome measurer is reported as blinded.

Fig. 1 (CONSORT) shows 89 randomized (45 prehab, 44 rehab) and 77 analysed (38, 39). Of the 12 not analysed, 4 were excluded for reasons unrelated to outcome measurement (emergency surgery, no resection, 2 operated elsewhere) and 8 had missing outcome data (prehab: 1 withdrew consent plus 4 lost to follow-up = 5; rehab: 3 lost to follow-up). So 8/89 (9%) had missing 6MWT data, up to 12/89 (13.5%) if all exclusions are counted against the randomized denominator. This exceeds the ~5% usually tolerated for a continuous outcome, and the intended population is all randomized.

Multiple imputation was applied only to secondary outcomes with missing items; the primary 6MWT analysis was a complete-case analysis of 77 participants, with no sensitivity analysis or assumptions about the excluded or lost participants. The authors only note that the characteristics of excluded patients were similar to those analysed, which is not a sensitivity analysis of the outcome.

Missing outcome proportions are similar (prehab 5/45, 11%; rehab 3/44, 7%), a difference of two participants. The reported reasons do not indicate outcome-dependent attrition and are not described as differing in kind between arms. The remaining exclusions (emergency surgery, no resection, other hospital) are unrelated to outcome. Dependence is plausible (3.3) but no specific reason makes it likely, so Some concerns rather than High.

Withdrawal of consent and unexplained loss to follow-up (8 of 89) could plausibly relate to recovery or functional status after surgery, which would relate to 6MWT distance. Not all missingness is for documented outcome-unrelated reasons.

The 6MWT was conducted by an assessor blinded to group assignment, and the abstract describes the trial as single-blind. The 6MWT is a performance test whose recorded distance is measured by the assessor, who gave only standardized motivational messages.

Both groups were tested with the same 6MWT protocol (15 m hallway, 6 min, standard ATS motivational messages) at the same scheduled time points (baseline, before surgery, 4 and 8 weeks after surgery). The 8-week outcome is a scheduled, active measurement rather than passive event detection. The interventions are identical in content and differ only in timing, so there is no differential opportunity for detection.

The 6MWT is described as validated in the colorectal surgical population, correlated with maximal oxygen consumption, and a 20 m change was prespecified as clinically meaningful. It is sensitive to the plausible effect size (mean differences of tens of metres).

The Methods state that the primary outcome was analysed as the mean difference compared with baseline at 8 weeks, and that changes over time were also analysed with a random-coefficients model; both analyses are reported (overall time-by-group P = 0.032 and the 8-week mean difference). Reporting a primary analysis alongside a longitudinal model that agrees is evidence against selection. There is no sign of unreported adjusted or alternative analyses, although no SAP was available to confirm the intended analyses.

The registry names a single primary outcome, the 6MWT, at baseline, preop, 4 and 8 weeks. The report presents the 6MWT at the same time points (preoperative, 4 and 8 weeks, Table 2) and designates 8 weeks as primary, matching the title and abstract, so reported results correspond to the intended measurements. The 6MWT is a single standardised test with one distance metric, leaving little room to choose among scales or definitions. Registry text gives a 20 m hallway while the paper used 15 m, a procedural detail with no direction.

The ClinicalTrials.gov entry was first submitted 2011-05-17, before the 2011-07 start date and so before outcome data could accrue, and names the 6-minute walk test as the primary outcome with time frame baseline, preop, 4 weeks, 8 weeks postop. The report analyses the 6MWT at 8 weeks as its primary outcome, as its Methods describe (mean difference compared with baseline), at the registered time point. The entry gives no analysis detail and no protocol or SAP was captured, so this is an inference from a dated registry plan, which the guidance treats as Probably yes. The current record cannot show earlier versions.

Arms were equal at 9 per group as intended. Table I shows differences in sex ratio (7:1 vs 4:4 women:men) and mean time suffering (36.5 vs 23.25 months) in 8 per arm, but such differences are compatible with chance in so small a sample, and no P values or large excess of differences are shown. The 8-week pre-op knee extension medians are similar (33.6 vs 37.1 lbs). Table I appears to describe only analysed participants, so the check is not complete, and the analysis adjusted for baseline values.

Nothing describes who held the sequence or how assignment was delivered. Blinding of the assessor and surgeon after assignment is not concealment of the sequence. The circumstances (small student pilot, no sample size calculation, blocks possibly predictable by the unblinded intervention physiotherapist) support neither a probable yes nor a probable no.

The report states randomization was 'via random permutated blocks', i.e. random permuted blocks, which contain a random component. The generation mechanism (software, table) is not described, so Probably yes rather than Yes.

All 18 completed; 16 were analysed in their randomized groups. Two (one per arm) were excluded after surgery because grade 4 OA, an exclusion criterion (grades 3-4 OA), was found at surgery and had not been seen on pre-surgery imaging. Eligibility was therefore confirmed only after randomization and could not plausibly have been influenced by assignment, which RoB 2 treats as appropriate. The 2 exclusions are balanced across arms, 11%, so Probably yes rather than Yes.

The report describes delivery at all five visits: both groups got the same post-operative rehabilitation guide, hydrotherapy, massage and surgeon, and the study visits were scripted. No non-protocol co-interventions, crossover, or trial-context-driven changes are described, and the report gives no sign of any. Adherence to the home programme was monitored by diaries but adherence data are not reported. Ordinary non-adherence would not count here.
The report states it 'was not possible to blind the physiotherapist carrying out the intervention or the participants'; exercise instruction versus massage cannot be hidden.
The intervention physiotherapist delivered the exercise instruction or massage and was not blinded, per the same passage.

All 18 randomized participants completed the study with no drop-outs, so 12-week outcome assessments were presumably obtained for all. The 2 participants left out of the analysis were excluded for grade 4 OA found at surgery (eligibility), not because outcome data were missing; that exclusion is handled under Domain 2 (2.6).

The chartered physiotherapist who performed the HHD testing is explicitly stated to have been blinded to group, separate from the unblinded physiotherapist who delivered the intervention. The outcome is observer-recorded from a device reading, so the participant is not the assessor.

The test procedure was the same for every test and individual, with the same couch, a practice trial then four trials per movement, and the highest value recorded, in both arms at the same visits. The intervention was home exercise, which gave no extra opportunities for outcome ascertainment.

Hand-held dynamometry with a calibrated MicroFet2 is described as a reliable, validated method of testing isometric strength, and knee extension was tested in a standardized seated position. Nothing suggests insensitivity to plausible effects.

The methods describe one analysis strategy (mixed ANCOVA on logged variables, adjusted for baseline) applied uniformly to every outcome variable, and the results report that analysis for all of them. There is no suggestion of several analyses with only one reported. Table III medians are descriptive and do not conflict with the adjusted analysis.

The methods list the muscle groups tested (hip abductors, adductors, flexors, external rotators and knee extensors) and all visits, and the results tables present the knee extension values at each time point (Table III) and the adjusted comparison (Table II) rather than a chosen subset. The results text also notes that not all values were significant, so non-significant results were reported. No sign of selection from multiple measurements is apparent.

The article describes a mixed ANCOVA on logged outcome variables but nothing dated before outcome data were available shows this analysis was pre-specified. The trial reports no sample size calculation and designates no primary outcome.

Baseline characteristics were similar overall. Some imbalances (PaO2/FiO2 318 vs 375, P = 0.009; more difficult intubation history and acute respiratory failure in HFNC) are modest and compatible with chance given many comparisons. Baseline data cover the 184 analysed patients, not all 192 randomized.

Allocation was via a secure computer-generated online remote system run by an independent research promotion unit with no role in recruitment; the protocol describes web-based randomization with login and automatic assignment at inclusion. Allocation could not be foreseen by recruiters despite open-label design and fixed block size.

The allocation list was computer-generated by the study statistician, with fixed blocks of six stratified by center; the protocol says the list is created by the Research Department statistician. Within-block order is not stated to be random, but computer generation by an experienced unit makes a random sequence probable.

An intent-to-treat analysis by randomized group was prespecified in the protocol and reported (184 patients; the 183-patient per-protocol analysis was secondary). Eight randomized patients were left out: 2 found to be under legal guardianship (ineligible, discovered after randomization), 3 who improved and were not intubated (no longer eligible, not influenced by assignment) and 3 who withdrew consent. These are ineligibility or missing-data exclusions that assignment could not plausibly have influenced, so the analysis is close to ITT. No patient was analysed in the wrong group.

Preoxygenation and intubation are a single brief procedure delivered per protocol in both groups. The only reported deviation was one HFNC patient who did not receive HFNC because no device was available, which is a logistic failure not caused by the trial context. Hypnotic and blocker doses did not differ between groups (eTable 1). The report describes delivery and adherence and mentions no non-protocol co-interventions or cross-over.

The trial is open-label (HFNC nasal prongs versus a face mask with bag) and the devices cannot be hidden from the patient; registry lists Masking: NONE. Many patients were sedated or comatose at inclusion, but awareness during the preoxygenation procedure is still probable. Answered yes because the device is obvious.
Clinicians delivering preoxygenation and intubation necessarily applied the allocated device and knew the assignment; the authors note the unblinded device as a limitation.

192 were randomized and 184 were analysed (ITT: HFNC 95, SMO 89). The 8 excluded patients were 3 who withdrew consent, 2 under guardianship and 3 who improved and were not intubated. The report states no patient was lost to follow-up, and eTable 2 lists 0 missing values for mortality at day 28 in both groups. The 4% not analysed is small relative to the 50 observed deaths, and the exclusion reasons were not tied to the outcome. I answer probably yes rather than yes because the 8 excluded patients have no reported day-28 status and the ascertainment method is not described.

The trial is open-label: the registry lists 'Masking: NONE', and the report describes no blinding of participants, clinicians or outcome assessors. The sources do not say who recorded day-28 vital status. Preoxygenation with HFNC versus a bag-valve mask is visibly different, so staff recording the outcome were probably aware of the assignment.

Both arms received the same single preoxygenation episode before ICU intubation and were followed for the same 28-day window. Mortality was analysed identically (Mantel-Haenszel, stratified by center) in both arms, and the report says no patient was lost to follow-up. The intervention involves no extra contacts or tests after intubation that would create more chances to detect death in one arm. The protocol plans the same models for all secondary criteria in both groups. A bounded lexical search for vital-status wording found no hits, which is not evidence of absence. I answer probably no rather than no because the ascertainment procedure is not described.

All-cause mortality is an observer-reported outcome that involves no judgement, so knowing the assignment is unlikely to influence its assessment, even for unblinded assessors. The outcome is death at day 28, not a cause-specific or adjudicated event.

Day-28 all-cause mortality is a prespecified secondary endpoint named in the Methods ('mortality rate on day 28'). Death is a binary event that any reasonable ascertainment method can detect, so the method is sensitive to plausible effects. I found no report of poor validity. How vital status was ascertained is not described, so I answer probably no rather than no.

The Methods describe one analysis plan for all binary secondary outcomes: Mantel-Haenszel chi-square tests with a center-adjusted Mantel-Haenszel relative risk, and no imputation. Table 3 reports the day-28 mortality result in that form. The report gives no sign that unadjusted, adjusted or other models were run for this outcome and only some reported. The protocol lists several possible model families, but I found no evidence that alternatives were estimated for mortality.

The outcome is all-cause death by day 28, which has a single way of being measured at the planned follow-up. The protocol names it once as a secondary criterion, and the report gives one corresponding result (Table 3, 26 (27) vs 24 (27)). The separate ICU 'Death, n (%)' row (25 vs 23) is a different measure that is also reported, so nothing suggests a favourable one was picked from several.

Protocol version 2 is dated 22/07/2015, before the first patient was enrolled in April 2016, and the registry entry was first submitted on 2016-02-02, before the 2016-04-28 start. The protocol lists 'Death of the patient within the 28 days following intubation or discharge from the ICU (if discharge before D28)' as a secondary judgement criterion, and states that all analyses will be intention-to-treat. The report names mortality on day 28 as a secondary endpoint and analyses it in the ITT population. The protocol plans generalized linear mixed or survival models accounting for center. The report uses Mantel-Haenszel tests and a Mantel-Haenszel relative risk stratified by center. Both account for center. The difference in method is generic and not visibly tied to the results. I answer probably yes rather than yes because I did not find a separately dated analysis plan finalized before unblinding.

Table 1 shows near-identical baseline characteristics (gestational age 26.1 in both arms, PDA size, respiratory support, inotropes, postnatal age, birth weight, sex). The authors say baseline characteristics appeared well balanced. Group sizes were 326 vs 327 for the intended 1:1 ratio. Table 1 shows the analysed participants (324/322, after 7 consent withdrawals), but the balance on minimization factors is compatible with chance, and with minimization.

Allocation was by a secure web-based system hosted by the independent NPEU CTU with 24/7 telephone backup, 'ensuring concealment of the group assignments'. Participants were enrolled by delegated site clinicians. The protocol says trial drug packs were allocated by the central randomisation system, with identical cartons for ibuprofen and placebo, so assignment was delivered centrally and irreversibly.

Dynamic randomization used a probabilistic minimization algorithm at 1:1 run by the NPEU Clinical Trials Unit. Minimization is generated with a random element, which RoB 2 guidance treats as a random sequence.

Analysis followed the ITT principle with infants excluded only for missing data (7 consent withdrawals and 10 with missing primary-outcome data); this mITT is considered appropriate for this domain, and open-label treatment did not lead to exclusion or regrouping.
Matched placebo (0.9% saline) in identical coded cartons allocated by the central system; parents, clinicians and assessors were masked. Blinding of parents/infants is not obviously compromised.
Clinicians and nurses were masked via identical cartons and concealed central allocation; unmasking only for emergencies. Ibuprofen has no obvious bedside signature that would reveal allocation.

Primary-outcome data were available for 318/326 ibuprofen (97.5%) and 318/327 placebo (97.2%) randomized infants; 17 of 653 (2.6%) were missing (7 consent withdrawals plus 10 with missing primary data). The observed events (220 and 202) vastly outnumber the 8 and 9 infants missing per arm, so even extreme outcomes in missing infants could not change the estimate materially, and proportions are balanced between arms. Death status is largely ascertainable.

Outcome assessors were explicitly masked to allocation, and the matched placebo preserved masking of clinicians and families who record routine data. Death is objective and BPD grading uses a standardised physiological test.

Same outcome definition, timing (36 weeks PMA) and routine clinical or trial-related data sources applied in both arms; the oxygen reduction test was missed at similar rates (13/86 vs 13/94). The intervention adds no extra contacts that would increase detection.

Death or moderate/severe BPD at 36 weeks PMA is a prespecified, standard neonatal outcome assessed with a recognised physiological oxygen-reduction challenge and routine clinical data; nothing suggests the method is insensitive or invalid.

The SAP and protocol prespecify a single primary analysis: covariate-adjusted risk ratio under the ITT principle, with crude estimates also presented and primary inference on the adjusted estimate. The reported 1.09 (0.98 to 1.20) is that analysis. Reported sensitivity analyses (excluding open-label treatment outside criteria) are additional and do not suggest selection. Adjusted and crude estimates both being planned limits selective choice.

The primary outcome is a single prespecified composite (death or moderate/severe BPD) at one time point (36 weeks PMA), assessed by a defined physiological challenge, identical in the protocol and the report. The report presents the components as secondary outcomes alongside it; no alternative time points or definitions of the primary outcome were evidently measured and withheld.

The SAP document history (versions 0.1 to 1.0, 2015 to 8 Feb 2021) records every version, including final v1.0, as 'Not yet unblinded'. The SAP and protocol specify adjusted risk ratios for binary outcomes (log-binomial, Poisson with robust variance if non-convergent), adjustment for minimisation factors with centre as a random effect and multiple births nested, and the primary composite at 36 weeks PMA. The report states the same primary outcome and analysis. The only reported departure in method (Poisson fallback) is the prespecified contingency.

Group sizes of 54 and 53 match the 1:1 intent. The baseline characteristics (age, sex, injury-to-surgery interval, meniscal injury) and the preoperative pivot shift, KT-1000, Lysholm and IKDC values in Tables 2-4 look similar, with no flagged significant differences. Table 1 describes only the 102 analysed participants (95% of those randomized), which limits the check slightly.

The report says only that a coin was flipped 'behind closed doors prior to the surgical appointments'. It does not say who flipped it, whether the enrolling surgeon could know or influence the allocation, or whether assignment was irreversible before enrolment. Per-patient coin flips leave no pre-existing list to foresee, but there is no independent allocation or safeguard, and no protocol or registry record is available. I found nothing to support either probable answer.
Patients were randomized by simple randomization (flipping a coin), which is a random component under RoB 2 guidance.

The flow chart shows 107 randomized and allocated to intervention, with 2 (A) and 3 (B) lost to follow-up and 52/50 analysed. The only exclusions are participants without follow-up data, i.e. a modified ITT excluding participants with missing outcome data, which is appropriate here; the missingness is assessed in Domain 3. Participants appear analysed by randomized group.

The report describes the interventions and follow-up and gives no crossover, contamination, non-protocol co-intervention or protocol departure. All surgeries were done by the same fellowship-trained surgeon, and all 107 randomized participants are shown as receiving the allocated intervention. The 5 lost to follow-up are a missing-data matter (Domain 3). Absence of reported deviations in a report that describes delivery supports probably no, although the report does not explicitly discuss deviations or the postoperative rehabilitation protocol.

Surgical comparison of isolated ACLR versus ACLR plus ALL reconstruction. The authors state blinding of patients was not possible without unnecessary incisions in the isolated ACLR group, so participants knew their assigned procedure.
One surgeon performed all operations and necessarily knew which reconstruction was done; the authors state surgeons could not be blinded.

107 were randomized and 102 (95.3%) were analysed (52/54 in A, 50/53 in B); 5 (4.6-4.7%) were lost to follow-up, 2 versus 3, i.e. similar proportions per arm. For the dichotomous pivot-shift result, a plausible worst case for the 5 missing (all abnormal in A, all normal in B, or the reverse) would give roughly 45/54 (83%) vs 48/53 (91%) or 43/54 (80%) vs 50/53 (94%), so the direction and a clear between-arm gap persist. The 5 missing therefore probably could not make an important difference. Reasons for loss are not reported beyond 'did not complete follow-up'.

The pivot shift was examined by a surgeon who did not take part in the surgeries, but blinding of this examiner to allocation is not reported. Patients were not blinded, and the combined procedure leaves an extra lateral incision. IKDC includes patient-reported components. Following guidance, absent blinding information the assessors are assumed aware.
All participants were assessed with the same protocolled examinations (pivot shift, KT-1000, IKDC) at the same postoperative follow-up, so measurement did not differ by arm.

Assessors were not the operating surgeons and had no evident stake in either procedure, and the direction of effect agrees across the device-based KT-1000 measure and the examiner-based pivot shift. Influence is possible but there is no specific reason to believe it occurred.

The pivot shift is a clinical examination graded by judgment, which the authors themselves describe as subjective and examiner dependent. The IKDC also contains patient-reported elements. Knowledge of allocation could influence both.

Pivot-shift grading, KT-1000 arthrometry and IKDC are standard, validated measures of ACL-reconstruction outcome and can detect the plausible between-group difference; nothing in the report suggests the methods were unsuitable.

Pivot shift is analysed as a simple proportion normal versus abnormal across the grades, with the full grade distribution shown in Table 2. No adjusted or alternative analyses are suggested, so selection among analyses is unlikely.

The Methods name pivot shift, KT-1000 laxity, Lysholm, Tegner and IKDC at one common follow-up, and the Results report every one of them, including non-significant Lysholm, Tegner and Lachman findings. This pattern argues against outcome-based selection of a single measurement, so the answer is a judgement made without a protocol.

No protocol, SAP or registry record is among the Sources, and the article cites none. No document dated before outcome data were available specifies this measurement or analysis, so prespecification cannot be confirmed.

Table 1 reports baseline data only for the 305 completers (145/160), not all 548 randomised (272/276 per Figure 1), so imbalance in the randomised sample cannot be assessed. Among completers only age differs (29.1 vs 27.4 years, P=0.008, text says 27.9) and baseline WC is balanced (P=0.640); this alone is compatible with chance but may also reflect differential attrition.

Randomisation lists with ID numbers and randomisation codes were distributed to each of the five clinics and the enrolling study nurse took the lowest available ID from the list. This is a site-held list used by enrolling staff with no described safeguard such as central/remote allocation, opaque sealed envelopes or independent allocator. With a fixed block size of six, later allocations in a block could be predicted if assignments were known. Intervention requires CHP contact, so assignments become known after enrolment. Preparation of the lists by IHSR and blinding of the authors to codes do not show concealment from enrolling nurses.

The report states women were randomised 1:1 using computer-generated random allocation sequences with block size six, prepared by the IHSR. Computer generation is a random component; the registry confirms randomised parallel allocation.

Table 2 analyses 305 women (145 vs 160) in their randomised groups; the 243 of 548 randomised women absent were lost mainly through pregnancy or attrition, i.e. missing endpoint data. Excluding participants with missing outcome data is acceptable in this domain (modified ITT); the missing data are assessed in Domain 3.

The report describes intervention components and control care but I found no description of adherence, contamination, co-interventions or non-protocol interventions arising from the trial context, so this cannot be judged either way.

The intervention was six contact points with community health promoters plus a mobile app; controls received standard care with no CHP contact or app. Participants could not be unaware of such an intervention, and no blinding is described (registry masking: None).
CHPs delivering the behaviour change communication necessarily knew which women were in the intervention arm; allocation used site-held lists applied by the enrolling nurse. Registry masking is None.
Of 548 randomised women, 305 (145 intervention, 160 control) had endpoint WC and were analysed, so 243 (44.4%) have no outcome data. This is far from 'nearly all' (95%) for a continuous outcome.

The analysis is a complete-case comparison (t-test, chi-square, bootstrapping controlling for age group). No imputation, weighting or sensitivity analysis for missing endpoint data is described; age-group adjustment does not show robustness to outcome-dependent missingness.

Missingness was very large (44%) and differed between arms (127/272 = 46.7% intervention vs 116/276 = 42.0% control). Pregnancy, the main reason, directly alters WC (true value), and in an unblinded lifestyle trial engagement-related dropout plausibly differs by arm and relates to WC change. Baseline age differed between completers (29.1 vs 27.4, P=0.008), suggesting differential retention; no analysis accounted for this beyond age-group.

Main reason for missing data was pregnancy (which itself changes waist circumference) plus other attrition from a lifestyle trial; loss to follow-up could relate to weight/WC trajectory and engagement.

Data collectors were nurses separate from the BCC-trained nurses, but no blinding of data collectors to allocation is reported (registry masking: None), and the participants, who take part in the measurement interaction, were aware of their arm. Under the guidance, assessors are treated as aware unless there is convincing evidence otherwise.
