Both arms had WC measured at the baseline and endpoint visits by the same nurse data collectors using the same WHO STEPS procedure; control participants were phoned to remind them of the endpoint visit. Intervention contacts were with separate CHPs, not the measuring nurses.

Assessors were independent of the intervention team and followed standardised procedures; the outcome is physical and not self-reported; no strong prior belief of effect on WC is described, and the observed WC change was similar between arms.
Tape-measure WC involves some observer judgement (landmark location, tension), so knowledge of allocation could influence the measurement, though it is a largely objective anthropometric measure.
WC was measured by trained study nurses following standardised WHO STEPS procedures, a valid and sensitive method for a pre-specified primary outcome.

The methods name a single primary hypothesis for change in WC, and the article reports both endpoint WC and change in WC (Table 2) with consistent null findings (P=0.547 and 0.811), plus a subgroup analysis. Nothing suggests multiple adjusted or unadjusted analyses were run and only a favourable one reported. The result is null, which argues against selection. The details of the bootstrapping (age-group) are thinly described.

WC is the single registered and reported primary outcome, measured once at baseline and once at endpoint by nurses using WHO STEPS procedures. There is one registered time frame and no evidence of multiple WC scales, assessors or time points from which to select. The reported result matches the registered primary outcome.

The ClinicalTrials.gov record was first submitted 2015-11-18, before the start date of 2015-11-23, and lists 'Difference in waist circumference' (Months 0-8) as the primary outcome. The article reports the primary outcome as change in WC from baseline to ~33 weeks (8 months), and analyses it as its methods describe (null hypothesis of no difference in WC change). Per the guidance, a pre-enrolment registry entry naming this outcome and time point is a dated plan, so Probably yes even without analysis detail. No separate SAP or protocol was captured, and the registry shows only the current version, so 'probably' rather than 'yes'.
Table 1 shows near-identical baseline characteristics across 4731 vs 4732 patients, matching the 1:1 ratio; differences are compatible with chance.
Sequence was sequestered and investigators obtained treatment assignment through a central interactive voice or web response system, with matched placebo devices; this is remote central allocation.
Methods state allocation followed a sequestered, fixed, computer-generated randomisation code using balanced permuted blocks, which is a random component.

The primary time-to-event analysis was in the intention-to-treat population, including all randomised patients whether or not treatment was taken, until study closure or last vital-status date. Table 2 denominators (4731 and 4732) cover all randomised patients.

Placebo matched for device, diluent and injected volume, and the report states all investigators and patients were masked to treatment group. Nothing in the inspected passages suggests blinding failed.

All investigators were masked, allocation was sequestered and assignment obtained through an interactive voice/web response system, and placebo matched the active device and volume, so carers and deliverers were probably unaware.

All 9463 randomised patients were analysed in the time-to-event ITT analysis. Follow-up time attained for cardiovascular outcomes was 98.5% (albiglutide) and 97.9% (placebo), and vital status follow-up was 99.8%. Incomplete cardiovascular event assessment at study end affected 112 albiglutide and 155 placebo patients (267 total, about 2.8% of those randomised), and vital status was unknown for 61 (0.6%). The 766 observed first events (338 + 428) outnumber the participants with incomplete assessment roughly threefold, and some of those 267 may have had an event before follow-up ended. Missing outcome information is therefore small enough to make no important difference to the hazard ratio.

The committee that assessed all primary-composite components and death was explicitly unaware of group assignment, and all investigators and patients were masked with a matched placebo, so earlier clinical decisions by site investigators were also made blinded. No report of broken blinding was found in the inspected passages.

Both groups received weekly injections of identical-appearing active/placebo with the same visit schedule and the same committee, definitions and outcome (first occurrence) applied to all participants. No intervention-specific extra contacts or passive-detection mechanism is described, so differential ascertainment is probably not present.

The primary outcome (CV death, MI, stroke) is prespecified and was assessed by an independent clinical events classification committee against defined clinical event definitions. Nothing in the inspected passages suggests the method is insensitive or poorly validated.

The SAP and registry specify an unadjusted Cox model with treatment as the only covariate and a non-inferiority (margin 1.3) then superiority test; the report presents exactly this analysis in the ITT population, with the same Cox treatment-only model stated in the Table 2 footnote. The SAP also lists supplemental analyses, which the report is not shown to have chosen between on the basis of results.

The registered, SAP-specified and reported primary outcome is the same single time-to-first-event composite of CEC-adjudicated CV death, MI or stroke over the whole study; there are no alternative scales or time points for it. Its components and the four-component composite are reported separately as secondary outcomes, but they are different outcomes, not alternative measurements of this one.

The registry record, first submitted 2015-06-04 (before the 2015-07-01 start), names the CEC-adjudicated CV death/MI/stroke time-to-first-event primary outcome analysed by Cox regression with treatment as the only covariate in the ITT population. The Reporting and Analysis Plan (effective 30-NOV-2017, approved 14-Nov-2017) specifies the same primary analysis and the non-inferiority-then-superiority testing at the end of the study, and states that final analyses follow database lock and unblinding of randomisation codes. The report (Cox, treatment only, ITT) follows this. Protocol amendments seen only reworded the Cox model description or adjusted the follow-up/event target on blinded aggregate data.

Baseline characteristics were balanced between groups (409 vs 408 randomized, matching the 1:1 ratio; Table 1 key prognostic factors MRC grade, HIV status, age nearly identical). Only four characteristics differed at P<=0.05 (plasma sodium, previous TB, CSF white-cell count, CSF lymphocyte percentage), out of a long list in Table S3. This is a small number consistent with chance, and none is a strong prognostic imbalance at the P<0.001 level.

The study pharmacist prepared visually matched, identical, sequentially numbered treatment packs per the randomization list, dispensed in sequence as patients were recruited. The protocol states that only two central pharmacists held the master list and that bottles were coded, sealed and prepared centrally, with variable block sizes limiting prediction. This matches the guidance's criteria for sequentially numbered, identical drug containers.

Allocation followed a computer-generated randomization list with variable block sizes of 4 and 6, stratified by site, HIV status and MRC grade; the protocol confirms block randomization with variable block size within strata.

The primary analysis population was the intention-to-treat population of all randomized patients; Table 3 uses denominators of 409 and 408, equal to the number randomized. The per-protocol analysis was a separate repeat for the primary outcome only.

The trial was placebo-controlled with visually matched placebos of rifampicin and levofloxacin in coded, sealed packs prepared centrally; the report states participants, enrolling physicians and investigators remained unaware of assignment until the last patient completed follow-up. Only 9 patients (6 standard, 3 intensified) had assignment revealed.

Attending physicians enrolled patients and gave study drug from numbered packs but were unaware of assignment; allocation was concealed centrally by pharmacists holding the master list, accessed only for authorized emergency unblinding. Only 9 patients had assignment revealed.

Table 3 reports denominators equal to all randomized patients (409 and 408). Follow-up losses were small and balanced: 22 vs 21 lost to follow-up, 5 vs 2 withdrew, 1 went home to die (standard), 1 vs 2 withdrew/died before treatment, i.e. roughly 6% overall (about 29 vs 25). Adverse events were recorded by daily inpatient review and monthly visits, so most events (which occur early during intensive treatment) were captured before any loss. The 469 patients with at least one event greatly outnumber the patients with any follow-up loss, so missing data could have made no important difference.

Treatment was given as identically packed, centrally coded placebo-matched drugs, and enrolling physicians and investigators remained unaware of assignment until the last patient completed follow-up, with unblinding only in emergencies. The investigators who reviewed patients daily recorded the AEs, and laboratory grading is rule-based. Awareness through deduction of side effects does not by itself count as assessor awareness here.

Both arms were followed with the same schedule of daily inpatient review, monthly visits and laboratory monitoring, and the same grading rules. The intervention was oral drugs added for 8 weeks with matched placebo, with no extra visits attributable to assignment. Higher counts of some events (seizures, vision impairment) in the intensified arm may reflect real toxicity rather than detection differences.

AEs were captured by daily clinical review in hospital and monthly visits with laboratory monitoring to 9 months, recorded on dedicated CLINEVE/NEREVE forms, with a grading table for laboratory abnormalities and a defined 'new abnormality' rule. Only grade 3/4 events were systematically collected, and missing grade was designated 3/4, a conservative rule. The method is a defined system, so it is unlikely to be insensitive to plausible effects.

The SAP prespecified the patient-count comparison by Fisher's exact test, with no adjusted alternatives for AEs. The report uses this test for the 'Any event' result and Table S8, and shows the total-episode comparison by Wilcoxon rank-sum, which the SAP said would be summarized only. The SAP called the many comparisons descriptive because of multiplicity. No evidence was found of other analyses being run and left unreported.

The protocol and SAP define a single approach for this outcome: the number of patients with any grade 3/4 clinical AE, and with a new grade 3/4 laboratory abnormality as defined. The report presents these (Table 3, Table S8) along with total event counts, which the SAP says would be summarized. The 9-month window is the whole follow-up, so there is no alternative time point to choose from. Nothing suggests a result-based choice among alternative definitions or time points.

Protocol v11.0 (24 Feb 2011) prespecified comparing the proportion of patients with at least one grade 3/4 AE, overall and by event type. The SAP v2.0 (5 April 2015) is labelled 'final version prior to unblinding' and prespecifies the same summary for grade 3/4 AEs and for laboratory abnormalities, with the new-abnormality definition. The one departure (Fisher's exact test instead of stratified CMH) is stated in the SAP before unblinding with result-independent reasons (reproducibility, sparse events). The report follows the SAP. The 'final version prior to unblinding' label is self-declared rather than independently dated.

Table 1 reports baseline characteristics for all 18 randomized participants. All 12 comparisons have p values of 0.15 or higher, including baseline cannabis use and THC/creatinine ratio. Group sizes of 10 and 8 are compatible with chance. The age difference (24.4 vs 28.9) is not statistically significant.

Medication was dispensed by the McLean pharmacy as blister packs of identical capsules containing nabilone or placebo (plus riboflavin), so enrolling staff and participants appear not to have known the next allocation. The sequential numbering and independence of the pharmacy are not described, so only Probably yes.

Article and protocol say participants were randomized, with stratification by daily vs non-daily use, but neither (nor the registry) states how the allocation sequence was generated or that it had a random component. Protocol pages 2, 3 (l41-54), 5 and 11 were read for this and contain no sequence details.

The report states an intent-to-treat approach including all randomized participants, with all available data from those lost to follow-up or missing visits included. Adverse events were reported by arm for the randomized sample (10 nabilone and 8 placebo). The analysis population for the adverse event counts is not stated explicitly, so Probably yes.

The registry lists quadruple masking including participants, and the protocol describes a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial. The pharmacy prepared identical capsules (nabilone or placebo plus riboflavin) in blister packs. The article itself does not describe blinding or test its success. Reported adverse events (nausea, sedation) occurred in both arms, so there is no clear evidence that side effects unblinded participants. A nabilone-specific sedative effect could still partly unblind.

The registry lists care provider and investigator masking and the protocol states double-blind. Study medication was prepared and dispensed by the pharmacy as identical blister packs, so study staff plausibly did not know assignments. Allocation concealment was judged probably adequate in Domain 1.

Eighteen participants were randomized and only 12 (6 per arm) completed the 10-week treatment, so 6 of 18 (33%) left early: 4 of 10 on nabilone and 2 of 8 on placebo. Adverse events were assessed at each visit, so early leavers contributed events only up to withdrawal; no source reports adverse event data after withdrawal.
The only missing-data handling described is inclusion of all available data in an ITT analysis. No sensitivity analysis is described for adverse events.

Documented reasons (time constraints, moving, missed visits, pregnancy) are not clearly outcome-related, and missing proportions differ modestly (4/10 vs 2/8). No source shows adverse events drove dropout.

Withdrawal reasons were mostly not health-related, but the safety text says no other participants discontinued medication due to adverse events, implying at least one did. Participants who leave cannot report later adverse events, so missingness could depend on the true value.

Adverse events were elicited through a clinician interview, so both the participant and the physician are involved. The registry lists quadruple masking (participant, care provider, investigator, outcomes assessor) and the protocol says double-blind, with identical pharmacy-prepared capsules. Both parties are therefore probably unaware of assignment. The article does not describe blinding or whether it was maintained.

Both arms had the same weekly visits with the same physician, the same Medical Management sessions and the same open-ended method. Collection was active at every visit rather than passive. Nothing suggests the active drug led to extra visits or tests.

A clinician assessed adverse events at each study visit with an open-ended interview and a comprehensive review of clinical measurements, and the study physician monitored side effects weekly. The protocol also uses a standard Adverse Events Checklist. This is a conventional, sensitive method for mild-to-moderate adverse events. Adverse events were not a registered outcome and no formal definition is given, which is a weakness but not evidence of an unsuitable method.

The result is a simple count of events and participants per arm with no effect estimate, so there is little room to choose among models, transformations or covariate sets. The article describes a single ITT approach and no alternative analyses of adverse events are mentioned.

The protocol planned two side-effect instruments, a standard Adverse Events Checklist and the Frequency and Intensity of Side Effects Rating, while the article reports only clinician-ascertained event counts. The side-effect data could therefore have been summarised in more than one way, and the intentions are too vague to show whether the reported counts correspond to all planned measures.

The registry entry was first submitted on 2011-04-26, after the study start (2010-06; article says enrollment began September 2010), and none of its registered outcomes is adverse events. The protocol is undated in the pages read, and its statistical analysis section (8.9) covers cannabis-use outcomes, not adverse event counts. The article states a primary hypothesis of no difference in adverse events, but no source dated before outcome data were available specifies how this result would be analysed.

Group sizes were 2710 vs 2728, close to the 1:1 ratio. The report states 'the two groups were well balanced for demographic, clinical, and procedural characteristics, and non-trial-related medications' and Table 1 (all randomised patients) shows near-identical values for age, sex, diabetes, indication, extent of CAD and prior DAPT. Nothing suggests imbalance beyond chance or excessive similarity.

Allocation was by a web-based interactive response system run by the MRCC (Seoul), which the protocol describes as 'independently conducted online' after eligibility was confirmed and consent obtained. This is a central, remote allocation service independent of enrolling site staff, which meets the guidance criterion for 'Yes'. Open-label status affects blinding after assignment, not concealment before it.

Patients were 'randomly assigned' by a web-based IWRS developed by an independent academic coordinating centre (MRCC), 1:1, in a large multicentre trial. The protocol says randomization was 'balanced, stratified by the center, and independently conducted online via Interactive Web Response Service'. Neither source names the random-number generation method, but a computerised central system in a large trial run by an experienced trials centre and published in the Lancet makes a random sequence reasonable to assume.

'All patients randomly assigned were included in the primary intention-to-treat analysis.' The ITT population included all randomised patients (2710 vs 2728), with incomplete follow-up censored. The primary Result reported here (HR 0.73, 0.59-0.90) is the ITT result; a per-protocol analysis was reported separately.

The report describes delivery and adherence. Only 35 (0.6%) patients used a different antiplatelet regimen from the allocated one, and discontinuation for under 3 months was similar between groups (281 [5.1%] vs 272 [4.9%]). Nothing reported suggests that recruitment effects or investigators' beliefs led to non-protocol interventions. These small, balanced departures look like ordinary non-adherence that could occur outside a trial. The protocol allowed additional visits at physicians' discretion, and the report does not discuss why departures occurred.

The trial was open-label: 'Participants and study investigators were not masked to the assigned group.' The protocol also describes a 'prospective, randomized, open-labeled' design. Participants therefore knew whether they took clopidogrel or aspirin.
'Participants and study investigators were not masked to the assigned group.' No placebo was used, so investigators and carers delivering follow-up care knew the assignment.

Of 5438 randomised patients, ascertainment of the primary endpoint was complete in 5338 (98.2%), so about 100 (1.8%) lacked complete ascertainment. This matches the flow: 9 withdrew consent (8 clopidogrel, 1 aspirin) and 91 were lost to follow-up (41 clopidogrel, 50 aspirin), which is about 1.8% in each arm (49/2710 vs 51/2728). Vital status was cross-checked in all randomised patients through national registries. The 35 patients who used a different regimen stayed in follow-up and ITT analysis, so they are not missing. The 359 observed primary events are about 3.6 times the roughly 100 patients with missing data, and some of those 100 had an event before dropout. The protocol also required phone, letter or direct contact for patients who refused visits.
Final outcome assessment was done by an independent clinical events committee that was unaware of treatment assignment, despite open-label treatment.

Follow-up visits, surveillance and event definitions were identical in both arms, and a clinical events committee masked to treatment assignment adjudicated outcomes, so measurement or ascertainment was unlikely to differ by arm despite open-label design.

The composite comprises all-cause death, MI, stroke, ACS readmission and BARC >=3 bleeding, measured with prespecified standardised definitions and adjudicated by an independent clinical events committee, with vital-status cross-checks and source verification. This is an appropriate method for these outcomes.

The protocol prespecified an unadjusted analysis of the primary outcome on ITT and per-protocol bases at 2 years, and the report presents the ITT Cox model with the per-protocol analysis also done, with no other factors in the model. No evidence of multiple adjusted or alternative analyses with selective reporting.

The primary composite, its components and the 24-month time point were specified in the registry and protocol; the report presents that composite at that time point. The outcome is time to first event with standardised definitions, leaving little room for alternative measurements; the thrombotic composite and any-bleeding composite are labelled secondary/post hoc and the primary is not replaced.

The registry entry was first submitted 21 Jan 2014, before enrolment began (26 Mar 2014), and names this composite primary outcome (MACE plus BARC>=3 bleeding) with a 2-year time frame; the protocol in the supplement specifies a non-covariate-adjusted ITT and per-protocol analysis at 2 years. The report analyses the same composite at 24 months with ITT Cox model, as planned. Current registry record cannot show earlier versions, hence probably rather than definitely.

Baseline characteristics of the mothers and infants were similar. The only noted difference was HELLP syndrome (7 [5.1%] vs 1 [0.7%]) among many compared variables, which is compatible with chance and not a key prognostic imbalance large enough to bias the result. Group sizes 136 vs 137 match the 1:1 ratio.

Randomization was coordinated centrally with a web-based system, and the protocol states the trial was protected from selection bias by concealed, stratified, blocked randomization with varying block sizes (4-8), limiting predictability. Consent preceded randomization. Central web allocation is independent of the enrolling staff.

Infants were randomly assigned using a central web-based system, stratified by center and gestational age, with randomly varying block sizes of 4-8 (main report and protocol). The sequence-generation algorithm (e.g., computer random numbers) is not spelled out, but this is a multicenter, investigator-independent central randomization with variable blocks, which makes a random component reasonable to assume.

The primary result is the intention-to-treat analysis including all 273 randomized infants in their assigned groups (136 vs 137); the per-protocol analysis is reported separately and is not the selected Result.

Deviations were few and consistent with protocol: 135/136 in expectant management received no COXi (1 got open-label treatment under prespecified criteria); in the ibuprofen group 2 did not receive the first course due to contraindications that emerged after randomization (pulmonary hemorrhage, IVH). Rescue and later courses followed prespecified criteria (Table S1) and contraindication-driven omissions are protocol-consistent. Cointerventions (Table 3) differed modestly (paracetamol 25.0% vs 38.0%, diuretics 50.0% vs 41.6%, glucocorticoids 38.2% vs 46.0%) but there is no evidence these arose from trial context rather than clinical need or ordinary practice.
Expectant management versus early ibuprofen cannot be masked; the report states blinding was not possible and the trial was open-label, with no placebo.
Clinicians delivering care knew the allocation (no placebo; blinding not possible per the protocol), so carers were aware of assignment.

The report states that at 36 weeks' postmenstrual age data on the composite primary outcome were available for all 273 randomized infants (136 vs 137), and all were in the ITT analysis. Death is counted as an event within the composite, so the lower BPD denominators (117 vs 112) reflect deaths rather than missing data. The six infants lacking the oxygen reduction test had BPD severity classified by a committee, so their outcomes were still determined.
The trial was unblinded, so the clinicians who diagnosed NEC and BPD knew the assignment. Only 6 BPD severity classifications were made by a blinded committee.
Both groups followed the same protocolized echo and clinical schedule and the same outcome definitions; the composite was available for all 273 infants.

The criteria are explicit and objective (Bell stage, timed oxygen reduction test, death), the comparison is between two active strategies, and the most influential components (death and test-based BPD) leave little room for judgement. The authors also judged bias unlikely.
NEC staging and BPD classification are observer-reported and involve some clinical judgement, which knowledge of assignment could influence. Death is objective.
NEC (Bell stage IIa or higher), BPD (Bancalari definition with the Walsh oxygen reduction test) and death are standard, prespecified outcomes assessed at 36 weeks PMA; the methods are appropriate.

The SAP prespecifies the crude absolute risk difference and risk ratio, with a one-sided 95% CI for noninferiority, in ITT with a per-protocol analysis. The article reports both ITT and per-protocol results (concordant: -17.2 vs -17.8). Sensitivity analyses were prespecified. No evidence of unreported alternative analyses.

The composite of NEC (Bell IIa or higher), moderate-to-severe BPD, or death at 36 weeks PMA is the single prespecified primary outcome. The reported composite matches the protocol definition. Components are also reported, not selected. The BPD sensitivity classification is auxiliary and prespecified.

The original protocol (v1.71, Aug 2016) predates recruitment (started Dec 2016). The protocol and the SAP were published (BMC Pediatr 2018; Trials 2021) while follow-up was still ongoing. The SAP states that analyses start only after database lock and SAP submission for publication. It prespecifies the composite primary outcome and the crude absolute risk difference with a one-sided 95% CI, in the ITT population. The report follows this and the Table 2 footnote calls it the prespecified primary analysis. The registry record was not retrievable, so this rests on the protocol and SAP.

Group sizes were 56 vs 54 (close to 1:1). Preoperative pivot shift (P=.761), KT-1000 (P=.364), Lysholm (P=.871), Tegner (P=.485) and IKDC (P>.999) were all similar between groups, so there is no imbalance beyond chance. Baseline data are given only for the 103 analysed participants, which limits the check slightly.

Because assignment followed a fixed rule based on birth date, anyone enrolling patients could know the forthcoming allocation in advance. No central allocation, envelopes or other concealment safeguard is described anywhere in the single main report, and the guidance says concealment is usually impossible for such systematic methods.

Allocation was by birth date parity (odd-numbered day to group A, even-numbered day to group B). This is a deterministic, systematic rule with no random component; the RoB 2 guidance lists date of birth as a quasi-random, inadequate method despite the authors calling the trial randomized.

Of 110 randomized, 103 were analysed in their assigned groups; the 7 excluded (3 in A, 4 in B) left the country and lacked follow-up outcome data. This is a modified ITT excluding only participants with missing outcome data, which is appropriate here; the missing data are handled in Domain 3.

The report describes the surgical technique and rehabilitation but does not report adherence, crossover, contamination or non-protocol co-interventions, nor whether any arose from the trial context. With participants and surgeons unblinded and a non-concealed allocation, this cannot be judged either way.
The authors state they could not blind participants to their treatment group; the interventions (surgery with or without ALL reconstruction) are also not concealable.
Surgeons delivering the interventions knew which procedure they performed, and allocation by birth-date parity was not concealed, so carers were aware of assignment.

110 patients were randomized (56 vs 54) and 103 were analysed (53 vs 50), so KT-1000 data were available for 93.6% of randomized participants. The 7 missing (3 in group A, 4 in group B) left the country, a reason unrelated to knee laxity, and the numbers are balanced. The KT-1000 effect is large relative to its spread (medians 1.3 vs 1.8 mm, narrow IQRs, P<.001), so 7 missing continuous values are unlikely to have made an important difference. This is slightly under the ~95% rule of thumb, hence probably yes rather than yes.

Pre- and postoperative assessments were done by a different experienced sports surgeon, not the operating surgeon. The operated knees were covered by a white stocking to ensure blinding of the examiner, which was applied to KT-1000, pivot shift, and clinical examination. Blinding may not have been perfect, for example because of scars or patient comments, and no check on blinding success is reported, so probably no rather than no.

The same assessor, the same KT-1000 protocol and the same preoperative and postoperative schedule were applied in both groups. The measurement was scheduled per protocol rather than passively collected, and nothing suggests the intervention created different opportunities to detect the outcome.

Postoperative laxity was measured with the KT-1000 arthrometer at 20 lb, a standard instrument for anterior knee laxity, with a stated testing position (30° flexion, 15-25° external rotation). It can detect the plausible between-group difference (medians 1.3 vs 1.8 mm).

The report describes one analytic approach: non-parametric comparison of medians with the Mann-Whitney U test for continuous variables and Fisher exact test for categorical ones. It shows both continuous and categorized KT-1000 results (Table 3), and no adjusted or alternative analyses are mentioned. There is no sign of several analyses with only one reported.

The methods list the assessments performed: KT-1000 at 20 lb, anterior drawer, Lachman, pivot shift, Lysholm, Tegner and IKDC. The results report all of these at the same final follow-up (Tables 2-4), including the null ones, and the abstract states that only KT-1000 differed. The KT-1000 result was a single measurement at 20 lb with pre- and postoperative values both shown. Nothing suggests that other eligible measurements were omitted on the basis of results.

The only Source is the main article. It describes the analysis methods (SPSS 17, Fisher exact, Mann-Whitney U, P<.05) but cites no protocol, statistical analysis plan or trial registration, and no dated source shows the measurement and analysis were fixed before outcome data were available. Also, no power analysis or sample-size calculation was done (p8 l12-17).
Baseline characteristics were reported as similar between groups in age, severity, organ failures and diagnosis; no imbalance suggesting a randomisation problem.
Allocation used opaque sealed envelopes; the sequence generator was independent of eligibility determination. Sequential numbering and opening only after irreversible enrolment are not stated.
A computer-generated 1:1 randomisation was generated by a statistician not involved in eligibility or outcome assessment.

The analysis is a modified ITT that excludes patients who withdrew consent, were ineligible or improved before intubation, and additionally one reference patient whose SpO2 could not be recorded (49 of 50 enrolled). The SpO2 exclusion concerns the primary outcome, yet vital status at day 28 would still be measurable, so excluding an eligible randomised patient is not a missing-outcome exclusion for this Result. Exclusion of those who improved before intubation is also post-randomisation and based on course.

The intervention is a single brief preoxygenation (4 min) before intubation with a fixed protocol; intubation succeeded in 100% of patients in both groups. No co-intervention, crossover or protocol deviation arising from the trial context is reported, and a short pre-procedure intervention leaves little scope for trial-context deviations affecting day-28 mortality.

NIV was performed and a nasal cannula positioned in both groups to allow blinding; the reference group had a sham HFNC with matching noise, and the flow meter was hidden. Patients were hypoxaemic and about to be intubated. Participant blinding is not stated explicitly.
The authors state that the operator performing intubation could be aware of the group and could not be blinded given the HFNC flow; blinding applied to the outcome observer only.

Only about 1 of 50 enrolled patients (2%) was excluded for a reason (SpO2 not recorded) unrelated to prognosis, with 17+15 survivors among 49 analysed; baseline groups were similar. Substantial impact on day-28 mortality is unlikely, though the number excluded for improving before intubation is unclear.

The flow chart shows 50 randomised, with 49 analysed (25 and 24) and one excluded for SpO2 not recorded. Table 2 gives day-28 vital status for all 49 analysed (32 alive, 17 dead), and no loss to follow-up or missing vital status is reported. At most one randomised patient lacks a reported day-28 outcome, far fewer than the 17 observed deaths, so the result could not be materially changed. The report has no explicit statement about follow-up completeness.

The paper states that the study was blinded to the observer collecting the data, and that the assessor was an independent observer who did not know the group of inclusion; the supplement says data were collected by trained coordinators or residents blinded to the intervention. The operator could not be blinded, and the registry lists masking as NONE, but for day-28 vital status the collector is most plausibly blinded.

Mortality at day 28 was a prespecified outcome in a short ICU-based follow-up with the same data-collection procedure (case report forms) for both arms; the interventions do not involve differing numbers of encounters that would change ascertainment of death.
Vital status at day 28 is a pre-specified secondary outcome and an objective, standard measure; nothing suggests the method is insensitive or invalid.

Mortality is a binary outcome with a single pre-described comparison (chi-square or Fisher test); one result is reported in Table 2 and described as not differing between groups, with no sign of multiple adjusted or alternative analyses. A per-protocol analysis is also reported and showed no difference in mortality, which argues against selection.

Day-28 all-cause mortality has essentially one way of being measured, and the registry description and Methods name the same outcome and time point (mortality at 28 days). The abstract and Results call it ICU mortality but no separate ICU mortality is reported, so no alternative eligible measurement is apparent.

The registry record describes mortality at 28 days as a secondary outcome and states chi-square/Fisher tests for qualitative variables, matching the report. But it was first submitted on 2015-08-07, after the 2015-06-23 start and after enrolment began in July 2015, so it cannot date a plan before outcome data accrued. No linked protocol or SAP is in the dossier (the registry capture lists no documents). The article says the analysis plan was previously published (ref 25, BMJ Open), but that document is not available here and its date relative to unblinded data is unknown. Mortality is also not among the formally registered outcome fields (only lowest SpO2 and complications), only in the description text.

Table 2 shows balanced groups of 100 each in sex, age, weight, baseline ALT, haemoglobin, creatinine clearance and hepatitis status; the authors say baseline characteristics were similar. Differences are small and compatible with chance, and group sizes match the 1:1:1 ratio.

Sealed, serially numbered, opaque envelopes were supplied to centres and the schedule was prepared by an independent person, which matches the minimal criteria for envelope concealment. Not reported: that envelopes were opened sequentially only after irreversible assignment, or tamper-proof sealing. Fixed blocks of nine could in principle allow prediction of last allocations in an open-label trial, but the block size is not stated to be known to recruiters and there is no sign of manipulation.

A schedule was created by an independent person and allocation was 1:1:1 in blocks of nine, with envelopes carrying the allocated regimen. The report does not name the random mechanism (e.g. computer random numbers) or state that order within blocks was random. A random sequence is nonetheless a reasonable assumption for a multicentre trial run by an academic trials group with independent schedule generation and an ethics-approved protocol.
Safety analysis was of patients receiving at least one dose, but denominators equal the 100 per arm randomised, so no randomised participants appear excluded and analysis was by assigned group.

No protocol-inconsistent changes arising from the trial context are reported. Doses were directly observed by staff or DTMs, and the one treatment interruption (toxicity) is a protocol-consistent response. Regimens differ only in rifampicin dose, so there is little scope for contamination or co-intervention.
Open-label trial without placebo; no attempt to conceal regimen from patients after randomisation.
Researchers and health care staff were explicitly not blinded; only laboratory staff and an independent SAE clinician were blinded.

The Result is analysed on 100 patients per arm, equal to the number randomised. Missingness is reported only at the level of individual scheduled ALT tests (81 of 1800, 4.5%), with about six tests per patient plus symptom-driven visits, so a patient would lack outcome data only if every test were missing, which is implausible. A grade 3 rise could still be hidden if it occurred only at a missed test, but with grade 3 events persisting across nearby visits that is unlikely to change counts materially.

The Result counts grade 3 ALT rises, an automated laboratory value assessed by laboratory staff who were stated to be blinded to regimen. The authors also state bias was minimised because outcomes were laboratory based and the clinician deciding on treatment modification was blinded.

ALT was measured on the same schedule (2, 4, 8, 12, 16 weeks) and graded the same way in all arms. Arms differ only in rifampicin dose and had the same contact schedule, so there is no extra detection opportunity in one arm.
Pre-specified outcome measured with serial serum ALT graded by the standard DAIDS scale against each laboratory's normal range; an appropriate and sensitive method for hepatotoxicity.
The result is a simple count per arm with a trend test, in the safety population the methods describe. There is no sign of multiple analyses or of an analysis selected on results.

Hepatotoxicity was measured by serial ALT graded with the DAIDS system, and Table 3 reports ALT grades across all arms. The grade 3 ALT counts are part of the stated primary outcome, with no sign that a measurement was chosen from several based on results.

The only Source is the published article. No protocol, statistical analysis plan or registry record dated before outcome data is available, so the pre-specified analysis intentions for this measurement cannot be verified.

Group sizes were 73 and 72 under 1:1 allocation, and Table 1 shows groups generally well balanced with no significant between-group differences. The diabetes (10% vs 18%) and bicuspid valve (54% vs 67%) differences are modest and compatible with chance in 145 patients.

Patients were randomized through a Web-based interactive response system after informed consent, a remote central method, and block sizes varied, limiting predictability of the last allocation in a block. Allocation concealment is therefore judged adequate even though the trial is open-label after assignment.

The main report and protocol both state the allocation sequence was computer-generated, stratified by centre, using a permuted-block sequence with variable block size, which includes a random component.

The report and protocol specify intention-to-treat analysis of all 145 randomized patients in their assigned groups regardless of treatment received or crossover; the per-protocol analysis is a separate supplementary analysis.

Intervention delivery is well described. All early-surgery patients who did not cross over had surgery within 2 months (median 23 days). Surgery in the conservative group (74%) followed protocol-specified referral triggers (symptoms, LVEF <50%, velocity rise), which are protocol-consistent changes. Only 2 conservative-to-surgery and 4 surgery-to-conservative crossovers (5% and 3%) were inconsistent with the protocol; they are of the kind that occur outside trials (patient/clinician choice), and nothing reported suggests the trial context drove them.
The trial compared early aortic-valve replacement surgery with conservative care and is described as open-label; surgery cannot be concealed from participants.
Clinicians delivering surgery or follow-up care knew the assignment; the limitations section states the open-label design and clinicians' knowledge of assignment.

Death status was available for all randomized participants: 'No patients were lost to follow-up'; all 145 (73 early surgery, 72 conservative care) were analysed by ITT with median follow-up 6.2 and 6.1 years. Vital status is an event-based outcome, with 20 deaths observed and none missing.

The protocol states that deaths and other clinical events were reviewed and adjudicated by a Clinical Events Committee of non-participating cardiologists who were blinded to treatment assignment. Care providers were aware of assignment, but death is not an intervention-provider decision and is classified by the blinded committee.

Both groups followed the same visit schedule (4 weeks to 1 year, then every 3 to 6 months until close-out) with coordinators calling patients who missed visits, and no patient was lost to follow-up in either group. Death is a fixed event that is not subject to diagnostic detection differences, so ascertainment should not differ by group.

All-cause death is a prespecified secondary end point ascertained over a median of about 6 years with no patient lost to follow-up; vital status is an objective, valid and sensitive measure of mortality.

The Methods describe one analysis for the end points: ITT with stratified Cox proportional-hazards regression with Firth correction, because randomization was stratified by centre. The protocol specifies ITT analysis of all end points and says any additional analyses will be descriptive only. The article reports no alternative models for all-cause death, and the only other analysis reported is a per-protocol analysis of the primary end point.

All-cause death over the entire follow-up has one way of being measured, so there are no alternative scales or definitions to choose from. The registry, protocol and article all name the same end point and the article reports it as a prespecified secondary end point.

The registry entry, first submitted 12 July 2010 with a start date of 2010-07, lists all-cause death as a registered secondary outcome over the entire follow-up. The protocol states that all primary and secondary end points will be analysed on an intention-to-treat basis, and the report analyses all-cause death by ITT as its Methods describe. Outcome data on a time-to-death end point with a minimum 10-year registered follow-up could not have been seen by the investigators at registration. The protocol and any SAP are undated in the captured pages, so this is a judgement and not a dated confirmation.

Table S2 for all 9340 randomized participants shows near-identical groups (4668 vs 4672, matching 1:1) on age, sex, diabetes duration, HbA1c, BMI, blood pressure, prior CVD and renal function; the appendix reports no statistically significant differences in baseline characteristics. The only noted difference was beta-blocker use (p=0.008), compatible with chance among many comparisons. Groups are not suspiciously similar.

Allocation was made through a trial-specific interactive voice/web response system accessed by internet or telephone, with access restricted to authorised persons. Study drug is visually identical placebo and active product, packed and labelled by the sponsor in non-subject-specific boxes, with the IV/WRS assigning a dispensing unit number at each dispensing visit. This is central, remote allocation with identical drug dispensed only after assignment.

The report and protocol state that participants were randomly assigned 1:1 through a randomisation session in a central IV/WRS. No passage describes how the sequence itself was generated (a search of the protocol for sequence-generation wording found nothing). This is a large multinational sponsor-run trial (410 sites, 9340 participants) with system-based central allocation, so a random sequence is reasonable to assume.

The primary analysis was a Cox model including all patients who underwent randomization (4668 vs 4672), analysed as randomized; the protocol's FAS primary analysis is by randomized group, with as-treated and per-protocol only as sensitivity analyses. Those who discontinued treatment were followed and retained.

The trial was double-blind and placebo-controlled; the protocol states placebo and active drug are visually identical and randomisation/dispensing is via IV/WRS. Liraglutide has GI side effects that could partly reveal allocation, but nothing reported suggests blinding failed in a way that changed participant behaviour.

Double-blind design with visually identical placebo, drug packed by the sponsor in non-subject-specific boxes, and allocation concealed via central IV/WRS (Domain 1). Code breaking is restricted to medical emergencies via IV/WRS. Carers and investigators were therefore probably unaware of assignments.

All 9340 randomized patients were analysed. Vital status was known in 99.7%, and 96.8% completed a final visit, died or had a primary outcome, so at most about 3% lacked complete follow-up. Primary outcome events (1302) far outnumber that number of participants (about 300), so even extreme outcomes in them would be unlikely to change the HR materially. Per-arm censoring counts are not reported in the text I read, hence 'probably'.

Events were adjudicated by an external, independent event-adjudication committee in a blinded fashion, and the trial was double-blind with identical placebo. The main report states the blinded adjudication of the cardiovascular outcomes; the sentence in the Outcomes paragraph groups the exploratory outcomes with it. Components are CV death, MI and stroke, all classified by that committee.

Events were collected through the same trial procedures in both arms, with identical visit schedules under a double-blind design, and adjudicated against the same definitions. The intervention involved no additional contacts compared with placebo, so there is no evident differential detection.

The outcome is a prespecified composite of CV death, MI (including silent) and stroke, ascertained by an external committee against predefined event definitions listed in the appendix. This is a standard, sensitive method for these events.

The primary Cox model with treatment as covariate on all randomized patients was the prespecified primary analysis; the SAP lists adjusted, site-random-effect, stratified and censoring sensitivity analyses as sensitivity analyses, and the report states the sensitivity analyses showed a similar magnitude. Reporting a primary analysis alongside concordant sensitivity analyses is evidence against selection.

The outcome is a single prespecified time-to-first-event composite with a defined event set and a single analysis horizon (event-driven, whole follow-up); the reported result corresponds to the primary endpoint defined in the protocol, and the report states the same definition. There is no sign of alternative measurements or time points from which it was chosen.

The protocol (including the version at p77 and the May 2014 version at p191) specifies the primary endpoint as time to first CV death, nonfatal MI or nonfatal stroke, and says blinding is maintained until database release and that the SAP is finalised before database release, with no unmasked between-group analyses beforehand. The final SAP v3.0 is dated 04 Dec 2014, before the planned closeout of follow-up (Aug 2014 to Dec 2015), and specifies the Cox primary analysis on the full analysis set with sensitivity analyses. The report follows this plan. No registry record was captured, and an explicit unblinding date is not given, hence 'probably'.

Table 1 for all 156 randomized participants shows group sizes 79 vs 77 and similar baseline characteristics, including baseline marijuana use (median 7 days of use in last 7 days, 30 in last 30 days in both arms); the authors note no significant differences except MCQ Emotion at P=.05, which is compatible with chance.

Randomization was conducted by a research pharmacist independent of the research team, and the pharmacy prepared identical-looking matching capsules dispensed in individual vials, so enrolling staff are unlikely to have known upcoming assignments. The fixed block size of 4 could in principle allow prediction, but allocations were not revealed to enrolling staff because of double blinding.

Double-blind trial described as randomized, with stratified fixed-block allocation run by an independent research pharmacist at an experienced academic centre. The report does not state that order within blocks was random, so a definite Yes is not warranted, but a random sequence is reasonable to assume.

All analyses were stated to be on the intent-to-treat population, with the primary outcome tabulated for all randomized (14/79 DRO, 12/77 PBO) and participants with missing weeks 7-8 data scored as using cannabis rather than excluded. Medication adherence was high and similar in both arms, and psychotherapy was given to all.

Double-blind design with identical-looking matching gelatin capsules prepared by the pharmacy; riboflavin added to all capsules. Dronabinol is psychoactive and some dose reductions were for feeling intoxicated (3 DRO, 1 PBO), so partial unblinding is possible, but nothing reports blinding failure.

Double-blind trial; the randomization was done by an independent research pharmacist and capsules were identical, so clinicians and therapists delivering care were most likely unaware of assignment. Allocation concealment was judged probably adequate in Domain 1.

Weeks 7-8 data are missing for dropouts and were scored as cannabis use (imputed, which counts as missing). Retention to week 8 was 61% PBO (47/77) and 77% DRO (61/79), so roughly 30 PBO (39%) and 18 DRO (23%) participants lacked real outcome data, far more than the 26 observed events.

The authors state their assumption (missing weeks 7-8 data scored as use) and ran a sensitivity analysis showing the null result would only become significant if missing DRO participants were at least 10 times more likely to be abstinent than observed ones and missing PBO participants at least 5 times less likely, which are implausible extremes. A last-two-weeks-of-participation analysis gave similar low, non-different rates (DRO 21.3%, PBO 19%). This addresses the plausible range of outcomes for missing participants.

Outcome is participant-reported, so the assessor is the participant. The trial was double-blind with identical-appearing matching placebo capsules, and no unblinding is reported. Interviewers were likewise blinded.
Both arms attended the same twice-weekly visits and had the same TLFB interview at the same time points; the intervention did not add contacts or detection opportunities.

Outcome was self-reported cannabis use by timeline followback, a standard method adapted for quantity, collected at twice-weekly visits. Urine screens were rejected as the outcome because oral dronabinol causes THC-positive results. In the placebo arm self-report correlated with urine screens (P=.003), supporting validity.

A single analysis is described in the Methods (mixed-effect logistic model with treatment and baseline dollars spent, ITT), and the observed counts (14/79 vs 12/77) are also reported. The authors reported a sensitivity analysis and a last-two-weeks analysis that agree with the primary result, which argues against selection. No evidence suggests other models were run and withheld.

The paper and registry both designate one primary outcome (abstinence in weeks 7 and 8 by TLFB) with identical definition and time frame. The paper reports it in the stated form, with the last-two-weeks abstinence analysis as a robustness check, and no sign of other abstinence definitions or time points being measured and withheld. Secondary outcomes are reported separately and labelled as such.

The registry entry names this exact primary outcome (TLFB abstinence, weeks 7 and 8), but it was first submitted 2005-09-16, after the 2005-03 study start and with recruitment running 3/05-8/09, so outcome data were already accruing. No protocol or SAP is available (the capture lists no linked documents). No source dated before outcome data could be seen therefore fixes the plan or analysis, and no statement says it was finalized before unblinding.

Table 1 shows baseline characteristics of all 122 randomized participants (61 per arm, exactly the 1:1 ratio); age, sex, race, education, withdrawal, craving, depression and cannabis-use patterns (days of use, amount per day) are similar between arms, with differences compatible with chance. No baseline test p-values suggesting excess imbalance are reported.

"A Ph.D. statistician at Columbia University independent of the research team conducted the randomization and maintained the allocation sequence"; study drug was "prepared by the un-blinded pharmacy" in matching capsules, and "Participants, investigators and study staff were blind to allocation". Allocation was held by an independent party and delivered as identical capsules, and random block sizes of 4/6/8 limit predictability. The exact mechanism by which assignments were transmitted to the pharmacy is not described, hence Probably yes rather than Yes.

Report states participants were randomized "using computer generated random blocks of sizes 4, 6, and 8, with a 1:1 allocation ratio stratified by joints used per week"; a computer-generated random sequence with randomly varied block sizes is a random component.

'All analyses were conducted on the intent-to-treat sample'; all 122 randomized participants (61 per arm) were analysed in their assigned groups. Adherence was similar between arms (median about 95% of pills in both).

Randomized, double-blind trial with matched placebo capsules (lactose filler, riboflavin) prepared by an unblinded pharmacy; 'Participants, investigators and study staff were blind to allocation'. Active-arm adverse effects (Table 3: dry mouth 44.3% vs 9.8%, intoxication 21.3% vs 3.3%, hypotension 16.4% vs 1.6%) could hint at allocation, but they are not clearly specific enough to establish awareness.

Allocation sequence was held by an independent statistician and medication was prepared by an unblinded pharmacy in identical capsules; investigators and study staff were reported blind. No evidence that clinicians knew allocation.

All 122 randomized participants were analysed (ITT), but 43 (35%) 'dropped out prior to maintenance phase completion' and the paper states 'the abstinence status of dropouts at this study point is not known' (assumed to continue using). Dropouts who had not already achieved 21 consecutive days contribute no observed outcome and are effectively counted as failures (imputed). Observed events (35) do not greatly outnumber participants lacking complete follow-up (43), so outcomes of the missing could materially change the estimate.

The authors analysed everyone as randomized with dropouts treated as non-abstinent, and note only that it is a 'reasonable assumption that most dropouts continue to use cannabis'. No sensitivity analysis or bias-correcting method addressing plausible outcomes of dropouts was reported.

Dropout was similar across arms (completion of titration and maintenance 37/61 vs 42/61, p = .24; 61 analysed per arm; flow diagram showed lost to follow-up 18 vs 21, side effects 5 vs 1). Reasons are mostly loss to follow-up and lack of interest in both arms, with no clear pattern suggesting outcome-dependent differential withdrawal. Dropouts are counted as non-abstinent, a conservative assumption that treats them similarly in both arms. Plausible dependence is the 'could' of 3.3 rather than a likely, differential mechanism.

Dropout from an outpatient cannabis treatment trial (loss to follow-up, lack of interest, side effects) could plausibly be related to continued use or to the ability to achieve abstinence, i.e. to the true outcome.

The assessor is the participant (self-reported TLFB), interviewed by study staff. Participants, investigators and study staff were reported blind with a matching placebo, and nothing reports that blinding was broken; per the guidance, a blinded participant in a placebo-controlled trial is treated as unaware.

TLFB was administered at the same two weekly visits in both arms using the same method and thresholds; the design had identical visit schedules for medication and placebo. The authors state under-reporting was likely similar in both arms.

The pre-specified outcome (at least 21 consecutive days of abstinence) was derived from daily TLFB self-report, a standard, validated method that the authors say is considered valid. The authors acknowledge the outcome 'was based solely on self-report rather than urine toxicological results' with possible under-reporting, but this is a limitation of non-differential misclassification, and dronabinol itself produces THC-positive urines, so urine could not confirm abstinence.

The Methods state the primary aim was to compare odds of consecutive abstinence between arms with all analyses done on the intention-to-treat sample, and the Results report the observed proportions with the primary test (chi-square p = .68). The reported null result is consistent with the pre-registered outcome, and there is no indication that multiple adjusted or unadjusted analyses were run with only one reported.

The registered primary outcome and the reported primary outcome are the same single measure (TLFB-based 21 consecutive abstinent days). The article reports it as the primary outcome with both arms' counts (17/61 vs 18/61), and the registry lists only this one primary outcome. The requested outcome (any 21 days of consecutive self-reported abstinence) is specific, so there is little room to select among alternative definitions or time points for it.

The registry entry was first submitted 2009-11-24, before the 2010-01 start date, and names the primary outcome as '21 Days of Consecutive Abstinence as Measured by the Time-line Followback' over the 12-week study. The report analyses exactly this outcome ('at least 21 consecutive days of abstinence based on TLFB self-report post randomization during titration and maintenance phase') as its primary aim. Per the guidance, a pre-enrolment registry entry naming this measurement and time point is a dated plan for it, so Probably yes even though no analysis detail or SAP is available.

Group sizes are 14/16/14 against an intended 1:1:1 ratio, and the authors state baseline characteristics were similar. Differences in weight, sex and baseline proteinuria/eGFR in Table 1 are plausible by chance with n=44 and no extreme P values or excess similarity are apparent.

Patients were centrally randomized by an algorithm used by all centers, which indicates central allocation independent of enrolling personnel, and all study personnel and participants were blinded. The sponsor supplied drugs and placebo, and randomization was run by an external company, supporting concealment.

Randomization used a centrally generated minimization algorithm with 1:1:1 allocation stratified by proteinuria. Per the guidance, minimization is generally implemented with a random element and is considered random.

The full analysis set was used, with all patients analysed according to randomized group regardless of adherence or protocol violations. Missing data (two placebo patients) were handled by LOCF, so no eligible participant was excluded based on intervention received.
Double-blind, placebo-controlled trial; all study personnel and participants were blinded. The placebo was supplied by the sponsor alongside the active drug, and nothing suggests blinding failed.
All study personnel were blinded during the trial, and the registry lists masking of care provider and investigator. Allocation was central.

44 participants were randomized and 42 (95.45%) completed; the only two discontinuations were placebo participants (COVID-19 outbreaks). Supplementary Table 1 shows week-24 missing data for 2 of 14 placebo, 0/16 telitacicept 160 mg and 0/14 telitacicept 240 mg, so outcome data were available for about 95% of randomized participants. The missing proportion is small, though somewhat higher in the placebo arm (about 14%) and the remainder were imputed by LOCF rather than observed.

The outcome is an automated laboratory value. The article states that all study personnel and participants were blinded, and the registry lists quadruple masking including outcomes assessor, in a double-blind placebo-controlled trial. Assessors were therefore probably unaware of assignment.

Pre-specified outcome measured by the same method every 4 weeks in all arms under the same schedule; the intervention is a weekly injection with identical visit schedule across arms, so no extra detection opportunity is evident.

The primary end point is 24-hour urinary protein excretion, a standard, objective laboratory measure of proteinuria in IgA nephropathy, pre-specified and determined at regular visits. Nothing suggests it is insensitive to plausible effects or poorly validated.

The report describes a single primary analysis (ANCOVA adjusted for baseline, full analysis set, LOCF) and reports a sensitivity analysis excluding patients with diabetes that did not change the results; there is no suggestion that multiple analyses were run and only a favourable one reported.

The registered primary outcome (24-hour urine protein, week 24) corresponds to the reported primary result; the measurement is a single 24-hour urine collection with one pre-specified time point, so there is little opportunity to select among measurements.

The registry record was first submitted on 2020-02-27 and posted 2020-03-02, before the 2020-04-13 start, and names the primary outcome as change from baseline in 24-hour urine protein excretion at week 24 based on 24-hour urine collection. The report analyses exactly this (mean change in 24-hour proteinuria, ANCOVA with baseline covariate) and states that no change in trial outcomes occurred after the trial commenced. No SAP is among the Sources, so the analysis details are inferred from the registry entry plus the methods.

334 vs 334 were randomized (exact 1:1). The report states baseline characteristics were well balanced, and Table 1 shows near-identical age, ECOG, disease-free interval, metastatic sites and prior therapy, with no significant differences noted. Differences are compatible with chance.

Allocation was via central IRT: investigators called or logged on to the IRT after confirming eligibility, the IRT assigned the randomization number and medication number, and the randomization number was not communicated to the caller. Randomization data were confidential and study drug and matching placebo were identical in packaging and appearance, with medication numbers assigned by IRT. This matches central remote allocation independent of enrolment staff.

Protocol 6.5.2 states the randomization list was produced by the IRT provider using a validated system that automates random assignment of patient numbers to randomization numbers, with 1:1 ratio stratified by liver/lung metastases. This is a random component.

Efficacy analyses were performed in the intention-to-treat population; all 668 randomized patients (334 vs 334) were analysed by stratified log-rank test and Cox model. Safety analyses used a different (treated) population, which does not apply to this Result.

The trial was double-blind and placebo-controlled; the protocol states patients were blinded until database lock and ribociclib and matching placebo are identical in packaging, labeling and appearance. Ribociclib-specific adverse events (e.g. neutropenia) could hint at assignment for some, but that is a lab finding and does not by itself show blinding failed.

Investigators and site staff were blinded per protocol; allocation was concealed via central IRT, identical placebo, and unblinding limited to emergencies (with arm not communicated to Novartis trial staff). Allocation concealment was adequate, so carers were probably unaware.

All 668 randomized patients (334 vs 334) were included in the ITT efficacy analysis. At the 29 Jan 2016 cutoff 243 had progressed or died, 349 were still on treatment (195 vs 154), and the protocol required continued 8- to 12-weekly tumor assessments after treatment discontinuation for reasons other than progression until progression, death, consent withdrawal, loss to follow-up or new antineoplastic therapy. Discontinuations for non-progression reasons were modest and similar (patient/physician decision 22 vs 26; adverse events 25 vs 7). Most censoring is therefore expected to be administrative at the data cutoff. The report gives no explicit numbers of patients lost to follow-up or withdrawing consent before progression, so nearly-all availability is a judgement rather than a documented count.

Double-blind placebo-controlled design with identical labeled medication and IRT-managed blinding; unblinding only in emergencies, so investigators assessing progression were presumed unaware of assignment. Blinded independent review of all imaging gave a concordant result (HR 0.59).
Same RECIST 1.1 imaging schedule and criteria in both arms of a double-blind trial; no report of arm-specific assessment methods or timing.

PFS was assessed by local radiologists/investigators using RECIST 1.1 imaging every 8 then 12 weeks, a standard and appropriate method for progression; an independent committee also reviewed all imaging.

The reported stratified log-rank and Cox HR is the pre-specified primary analysis in the ITT/FAS population; the protocol lists unstratified and per-protocol analyses only as sensitivity analyses, and the reported result matches the primary plan.

PFS per RECIST 1.1 by local assessment was the single pre-specified primary endpoint; the independent-review PFS was a labelled supportive analysis and was also reported (HR 0.59), so reported results correspond to intended measurements and there is no sign of choosing among time points or definitions.

The original protocol (Version 00) already specified PFS by local radiology assessment per RECIST 1.1 as the primary endpoint, analysed with a stratified log-rank test and stratified Cox model at interim and final looks, with BIRC PFS as supportive. The report follows this plan. The efficacy interim was a DMC-reviewed group-sequential look. Exact dates of Version 00 relative to enrolment and unblinding were not seen, so answer is probably rather than definitely yes.

Group sizes 484 vs 242 match the intended 2:1 ratio; Table 1 shows balanced demographics and prognostic factors (lung/liver 50.0% vs 50.0%, bone-only 21.3 vs 21.1, ECOG, prior therapy); the report states characteristics were well balanced. Minor differences (e.g., 4+ metastatic sites 7.9% vs 14.0%) are compatible with chance.

Randomization was via central IRT after eligibility confirmation; the randomization number is not communicated to the caller; study drug is identical-appearing ribociclib/placebo with medication numbers assigned by the system; randomization data kept confidential from study staff.

Protocol 6.3.2: a patient randomization list is produced by the IRT provider using a validated system that automates random assignment of patient numbers to randomization numbers; stratified 2:1. The main report confirms random 2:1 stratified assignment.

All efficacy analyses were in the full analysis set of all 726 randomized patients, by randomized arm; CONSORT shows ITT population equal to numbers randomized (484 and 242). SAP uses an ITT approach with no censoring for treatment discontinuation or new therapy. Crossover was not permitted at the primary analysis.

Double-blind, placebo-controlled design with identical packaging and appearance; unblinding only for emergencies until database lock. Ribociclib-specific toxicity (e.g. neutropenia) could hint at allocation for some patients, but no report of blinding failure.
Randomization via IRT with concealed allocation; investigators, site staff and local radiologists blinded until final database lock; identical placebo. Allocation concealment was adequate (Domain 1).

All 726 randomized patients (484 and 242) were in the full analysis set, with 361 PFS events (210 vs 151) at cutoff. Patients who discontinued treatment for any reason continued tumor assessments per protocol until progression, death, consent withdrawal or loss to follow-up, so treatment discontinuation (patient decision 21 vs 5; adverse events 41 vs 10) does not itself create missing data. Counts censored for withdrawal of consent or loss to follow-up are not reported at the 2017 cutoff, but with 361 events and SAP-prespecified censoring rules the number is expected to be small relative to events.

The trial was double-blind and placebo-controlled, and the protocol states that local radiologists remained blinded until final database lock, with identical packaging and emergency-only unblinding. Investigators who assess progression were therefore unlikely to know the assignment. Possible inference from adverse events such as neutropenia cannot be excluded, but no source reports blinding being broken.

Both arms used the same RECIST 1.1 method and schedule (every 8 weeks for 18 months, then every 12 weeks), and assessments continued per protocol after treatment discontinuation. Nothing suggests differing detection opportunities.
PFS was assessed per RECIST 1.1 on scheduled imaging, a standard validated method for progression in advanced breast cancer; a BIRC re-read of about 40% of patients supported the local result.

The protocol, SAP and registry prespecify the stratified log-rank test, Kaplan-Meier medians and a stratified Cox HR in the full analysis set under ITT, with default censoring rules. The report uses exactly these. The prespecified sensitivity and unstratified analyses are not alternative primary results, and no sign of selection from multiple analyses is seen.

The outcome is the single registered primary measurement: local-investigator PFS per RECIST 1.1 from randomization to progression or death. The reported result matches it. BIRC PFS was a separate registered secondary outcome, reported as supporting analysis (HR 0.492), and not substituted for the primary.

The registry entry was first submitted on 2015-04-01, before the study start on 2015-06-09. It names PFS per investigator assessment (local RECIST 1.1) as the primary outcome, analysed by stratified log-rank test with a stratified Cox HR. The protocol states the same primary endpoint and analysis, and the report follows them. Version 04 of the protocol and the SAP are dated after the 2017 cutoff, and the registry shown is the current record, so earlier versions cannot be compared. The core design and analysis are consistent across the registry, protocol, SAP and report, and the trial was double-blind, so a result-driven change is unlikely.

Group sizes 335 vs 337 for 1:1; Table 1 shows well-balanced demographic and prognostic characteristics (e.g. visceral disease 58% vs 56%, ECOG 0 73% vs 76%, bone-only 24% vs 23%, prior chemo for advanced disease 14% vs 14%). Differences are compatible with chance.

Allocation was by central IRT after eligibility confirmation; the randomisation number is not communicated to the caller; matching placebo of identical packaging/appearance and medication numbers assigned by IRT. Randomisation data kept confidential to prevent bias in recruitment/allocation.

Main report states permuted-block randomisation through IRT, stratified; protocol states the randomisation list is produced by the IRT provider using a validated system that automates random assignment of patient numbers to randomisation numbers.

All efficacy analyses were done in the full analysis set comprising all randomised patients per ITT; Figure 1 shows 335 and 337 patients included in efficacy analyses, equal to the number randomised in each arm. Primary test was a log-rank test stratified by randomisation factors.

Patients were masked to assignment using matching placebo with identical packaging, labelling, schedule and appearance. Ribociclib toxicity (e.g. neutropenia, QT prolongation) is mostly detected by laboratory/ECG monitoring rather than being patient-perceptible, and unblinding/crossover occurred only after the primary analysis, so nothing indicates blinding failed during the period relevant to this Result.

Investigators administering treatment, assessing outcomes and analysing data were masked; allocation was concealed through central IRT with identical placebo, and the sponsor remained masked until database lock (Oct 18, 2017) after the Aug 20, 2017 cutoff.

All 672 randomised patients (335 vs 337) were in the efficacy analysis, with 318 PFS events (131 vs 187).
