Baseline characteristics were largely balanced and a 1:1 ratio was achieved (2920 vs 2913). The proton pump inhibitor difference (92.5% vs 83.1%) is a discharge medication downstream of assignment, not a prognostic factor that could have influenced enrolment.
Registration and randomization were done through a central web-based EDC system after the decision to perform PCI, so enrolling staff could not know forthcoming assignments.
Allocation used stochastic minimization via the central EDC system, which contains a random element and is considered a random sequence under the official guidance.

The analysis is an ITT analysis by assigned group, but it is a 30-day landmark analysis that excludes participants who died or were lost by 30 days (129), those withdrawn or wrongly assigned (40, acceptable), and those who already had the endpoint before 30 days (about 106 for this endpoint). Excluding eligible randomized participants on the basis of early post-randomization events, which occur during differing 0-30 day regimens, is conditioning on a post-randomization variable. The authors state "Strictly speaking, this trial was not a randomized comparison between aspirin and clopidogrel used as monotherapy after 1 month."

The report describes delivery and adherence: 88.6% vs 87.8% on the assigned monotherapy at 60 days and 87.5% vs 87.2% at 1 year. The protocol allows dose reduction or P2Y12 switch for bleeding or intolerance and mandates site checks of the 1-month switch. Observed non-adherence looks like ordinary discontinuation that could happen outside a trial and is balanced; no evidence of trial-context-driven co-interventions or crossover.
The trial is described as "open-label, adjudicator-blinded"; aspirin-free prasugrel then clopidogrel vs DAPT then aspirin cannot be masked from participants.

Open-label design with drugs prescribed at the participating centres per protocol; site physicians and coordinators necessarily knew the assigned regimen (CRC checks the prescription complies with the assigned regimen at the 1-month visit).

Excluded participants are about 4-5% of those randomized, and the authors report that events within 1 month did not differ significantly between groups, baseline balance was maintained, and the overall 1-year ITT analysis (HR .95, .79-1.14), PP analyses and the 60-day landmark analysis were fully consistent. Substantial impact on this null result is therefore unlikely, although some risk from immortal-time/selection bias remains.

For the 30-day landmark analysis the report states "follow-up was completed in 99.3% both in the aspirin and clopidogrel groups", so only about 0.7% (roughly 40 of 5833) lack complete follow-up, equal across arms. At-risk counts for the cardiovascular composite are 2871 and 2856 with 114 and 113 observed events, so observed events (227) greatly outnumber participants with unobserved follow-up. Deaths before 30 days are events or exclusions by design of the landmark, not missing data; the 129 'dead by 30 days or lost to follow-up at 30 days' are not split by reason in the text, and the 40 post-randomization exclusions (withdrawn consent, no suitable lesion) have no outcome data excluded for outcome-related reasons and are addressed under Domain 2. The Figure 1 flow diagram numbers lost per arm were not available in the text, so this is probably rather than definitely yes.

The trial is open-label but "adjudicator-blinded"; "The clinical events related to the co-primary endpoints were centrally adjudicated with three or more event adjudicators blinded to the assigned group based on the site reports in the electronic data capturing system." The protocol states the CEC carries out the definitive rating of all clinical endpoints. The composite's classification is therefore done by blinded assessors. Site investigators who report events are unblinded, but the final classification is by the committee, so Probably no.

Both arms followed the same schedule with data collected at discharge, 1, 2 and 12 months in the same EDC, and the same endpoint definitions applied to both groups. Both groups switch to a single oral monotherapy at 30-59 days, so neither arm has extra contacts; ascertainment is active and protocol-driven rather than passive. The same blinded adjudicators and criteria apply in both arms.

The components (cardiovascular death, MI by ARC criteria, definite stent thrombosis by ARC criteria, ischaemic stroke with persistent symptoms >24 h) are standard, pre-specified clinical endpoints with defined criteria: "Myocardial infarction and stent thrombosis were adjudicated with the criteria of the Academic Research Consortium". Nothing suggests the method is insensitive to plausible effects or poorly validated.

The Methods name the 30-day landmark ITT analysis as the main analysis. Alternative analyses (overall 1-year, per-protocol, 60-day landmark, no staged PCI) are also reported, and they are consistent with the main result. This reporting of concordant alternatives argues against selection of a favourable estimate. The HR is null, and the report gives no sign of unreported analyses.

The outcome is a fixed adjudicated composite with a defined time window (30 days to 1 year, in line with the protocol's 1-12-month landmark). The report gives it under the same definition as the co-primary endpoint, with no alternative scales, assessors or time points from which to choose.

The protocol (version file dated 2023-06-01, before 1-year outcome data were analysed) states that aspirin vs clopidogrel beyond 1 month for cardiovascular and bleeding events 'is evaluated by the landmark analysis between 1 month and 12 months (exploratory analysis)'. The report presents the 30-day landmark analysis as its main analysis of the co-primary composites. The registry lists the composite only at 1 month, and the protocol carries no detailed SAP or date stamp for this analysis, so the plan is probable rather than certain. The report calls it a secondary analysis with no pre-specified power calculation.

Table 1 shows similar groups on GA, birth weight, Apgar, antenatal steroids, multiple births, PDA size, respiratory support and NT-proBNP. The only flagged difference is male sex (57% vs 40%, P = .04), compatible with chance among many comparisons. Allocation of 146 randomized (72 vs 74) is near 1:1. Table 1 covers the 142 analysed infants only.

The trial was double-blind and placebo-controlled with identical-volume saline; parents, staff and clinicians were blinded to allocation, and the code table was held by unblinded personnel (pharmacist/representative and nurse) who administered study drug and were excluded from endpoint reporting and analysis. This implies enrolling investigators lacked access to forthcoming assignments, though the exact mechanism is not described.

The report and protocol state a stratified (by GA) blocked 1:1 randomization with a randomization code table generated using SAS, i.e. a computer-generated sequence. Neither source states explicitly that order within blocks was random or whether block size varied, but a SAS-generated code table implies a random component.

The authors state that they performed a per-protocol analysis instead of intention-to-treat, including only infants who completed all 3 doses. 4 ibuprofen-arm infants (2 with NEC stage IIb or higher, 2 parental decline or discontinuation) were excluded after randomization and none from the nonintervention arm. Exclusion for toxicity or non-completion is not an appropriate post-randomization exclusion for the effect of assignment, and no ITT analysis is reported.

Double-blind, placebo-controlled design: the comparator received same-volume normal saline on the same schedule, and the report describes the trial as double-blind. Participants (neonates and their parents) were unlikely to know the allocation.

Care staff were blinded; an unblinded administrator who is not involved in care prepared and gave the study drug and was excluded from endpoint reporting and analysis. Regurgitation of the dose was prohibited, and concomitant and rescue treatment was at the neonatologist's discretion under blinded conditions.

4 of 74 ibuprofen-arm infants (about 5%) were excluded, all from one arm, and 2 were excluded for NEC, a serious intervention-related event plausibly linked to BPD or death. The exclusions are one-sided and related to prognosis, and the CI (-0.11 to 0.22) lies close to the noninferiority margin of -0.2, so a few events could change the conclusion.

The CONSORT flow and Table 2 show BPD-or-death status for 142 of 146 randomized infants (nonintervention 72 of 72; ibuprofen 70 of 74). The only infants without outcome data in the analysis are the 4 ibuprofen-arm post-randomization exclusions (about 2.7% of those randomized); no loss to follow-up of analysed infants is reported, and death is itself an event in the composite. The 67 observed events greatly outnumber the 4 infants without data, so missing data alone could make no important difference. Whether these 4 infants had outcome data collected is not reported; their exclusion from the analysis is addressed under Domain 2, not here.

The trial is described as double-blind with a matching saline placebo, and the protocol states that the unblinded pharmacist or nurse who prepared and gave the drug was excluded from endpoint reporting and analysis. The registry lists masking of participant, care provider, investigator and outcomes assessor. No source reports that blinding was broken. Death is an objective observer-recorded component and BPD is based on an oxygen or ventilation requirement recorded by blinded care staff.

Both arms received the same-schedule 3-dose regimen (ibuprofen or saline placebo), were hospitalised neonates assessed on the same protocol schedule, and the same endpoint definition and 36-week threshold applied to both. There is no passive collection and no extra contact in one arm that would create more opportunities to detect BPD or death.

Pre-specified primary endpoint. BPD is defined as need for supplemental oxygen and/or positive pressure to keep saturation above 90% at 36 weeks, and death up to 36 weeks; both are standard neonatal outcomes that can detect plausible effects. The protocol defines the endpoint the same way.

The reported primary result is the prespecified unadjusted per-protocol comparison against the prespecified noninferiority margin. No evidence of other analyses of this outcome having been run and withheld; the adjusted models in Table 3 are additional, not substituted.

The primary outcome is a single BPD-or-death determination at 36 weeks GA; the registry, protocol and report agree on the measure and time point, leaving no evident room for choosing among multiple eligible measurements.

The registry entry (submitted before the July 2014 start) names BPD or mortality at 36 weeks PMA as the primary outcome, and the protocol prespecifies the composite endpoint, per-protocol analysis and noninferiority margin. The report analyses the primary outcome as planned. Caveat: the registry record is a current capture, not a historical version, and the SAP was not seen.
Baseline characteristics in Table 1 were well balanced between groups; only duration of type 2 diabetes differed marginally (P=0.048), consistent with chance.

Allocation was performed through a central IV/WRS accessed at randomisation, with drug supply controlled by the IV/WRS and identical-looking placebo and active pens, so allocation was concealed until participants were assigned.

Participants were randomised 1:1:1:1 through a central interactive voice/web response system (IV/WRS) with stratification by CV disease, insulin treatment and eGFR. Central IV/WRS randomisation in a large sponsor-run multinational trial implies a computer-generated random sequence, though the generation method is not stated explicitly.

The primary outcome was analysed by intention to treat in the full analysis set of all randomized patients according to planned treatment (1648 vs 1649 patients), using a Cox model stratified by randomization strata; the SAP states follow-up irrespective of adherence.

The trial was double-blind and placebo-controlled with volume-matched placebo; the protocol states placebo and active drug are identical in appearance, taste and smell, and supply was IV/WRS-controlled.
Double-blind design with identical-looking placebo pens and central IV/WRS allocation and supply, so investigators and carers delivering the interventions were blinded to assignment.

Of 3297 randomized patients, 3232 (98.0%) attended the last follow-up visit, were contacted by telephone, or died, and vital status was known for 99.6%. The SAP required follow-up of all randomized subjects regardless of adherence to treatment. Roughly 65 patients (2.0%) lack final contact, far fewer than the 254 primary events (108 + 146), so their outcomes could not materially change the hazard ratio. Treatment discontinuation (about 20%) did not end outcome follow-up under the ITT design.

The article states that each outcome except peripheral revascularization (not part of the primary composite) was adjudicated in a blinded fashion by an external, independent event-adjudication committee. In a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial the committee did not know the assignment. The committee classifies the events, which makes the assessors unaware.

Events were prespecified and ascertained through the same quarterly site-visit schedule and the same adjudication process in both arms. The placebo was identical and volume-matched, and the intervention involved no extra contacts. It is a double-blind trial, so there is no reason to expect different ascertainment or thresholds between arms.

The primary composite (CV death, nonfatal MI including silent, nonfatal stroke) was prespecified and used standard clinical events with definitions listed in the appendix (Table S4). Each component was adjudicated by an external, independent committee. Nothing suggests the method was insensitive or invalid.

The primary analysis matches the prespecified stratified Cox proportional-hazards model on the full analysis set. The article and the SAP also report prespecified sensitivity analyses (dose-level analysis, on-treatment and other censoring strategies), which agree in direction. This is evidence against selection. The SAP names no alternative primary analysis, and the only addition it lists, the on-treatment sensitivity analysis, was added as a sensitivity analysis and not as a replacement.

The primary outcome is a single prespecified time-to-first-event composite with one registered time frame, up to week 109. The registry, the methods and Table 2 define it identically (CV death, nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke). The article does not choose between scales or time points. The secondary composites are reported alongside it and labelled as secondary.

The registry record was first submitted 2012-10-29, before the start date of 2013-02-21. It registers the primary outcome as time from randomisation to first MACE (CV death, nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke) up to week 109, which is the reported composite. The article reports the prespecified Cox model, stratified by the randomisation factors with pooled treatment, and the protocol and SAP describe the same analysis. The final SAP is dated 16 March 2016, one day after primary completion, but the registry entry (and protocol) pre-date enrolment, and the SAP states that its only changes to the protocol were clarifications (observation periods, censoring, definitions). It does not mention any change driven by results.

Table 1 baseline characteristics for all randomized participants (257 vs 246, close to the intended 1:1 ratio) are similar between groups, with no imbalance beyond chance in key prognostic factors such as eGFR and proteinuria. Minimization on those variables is expected to produce similar groups.

Allocation used a central, web-based randomisation system run by Data Management at The George Institute (24/7 password-protected encrypted interface), with the Master Randomisation List held by Data Management and accessible only to authorised senior staff. This is remote allocation by a unit independent of site enrolment staff. Participants were assigned a number via the system and randomised only after all baseline data were collected; the trial was placebo-controlled with matching placebo, masked to patients, investigators and site staff.

Main report: "Randomization was performed using a minimization algorithm based on the 4 stratification variables; the algorithm was centrally generated and used by all centers." Protocol v8.0 section 6.6: 1:1 allocation using a web-based randomisation system with a minimisation algorithm, schedule generated by the randomisation code administrator at The George Institute. Minimization generally includes a random element and is treated as random under the guidance.

Main report: "All analyses were conducted by analyzing all patients according to the group they were randomized to, regardless of treatment adherence or protocol violations." The SAP section 4.1 prespecifies ITT with "All randomized participants ... analysed in the group to which they were assigned regardless of protocol violations." Figure 1 shows 257 and 246 as included in the analysis, and participants who stopped treatment (including the 23 stopped on safety advice) continued follow-up and were included. Table 2 gives n = 257 vs 246. The only people missing from the eGFR slope are those lacking eGFR data (assessed in Domain 3).

The published trial was "randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled" with "matching placebo"; "Patients, investigators, site staff, and sponsors were masked to treatment assignment." Protocol v5.0 section 6.7: "Both the patient and study personnel at each site will be blinded to treatment assignment." Nothing reports blinding failure. Glucocorticoid adverse effects could hint at assignment for some participants, but they are not specific enough to indicate that most participants knew their group.

Investigators and site staff were masked with matching placebo. Protocol v5.0 section 6.7 blinds study personnel at each site and the End Point Adjudication Committee. Allocation was concealed by central web-based minimization, with the randomisation list held by Data Management and not accessible to site staff. Unblinding was permitted only when management required it, with a documented reason and with follow-up maintained.

The report states almost all participants were followed to the end of the trial with negligible missing data. Figure 1 shows 257 methylprednisolone and 246 placebo participants in the analysis, and 493/503 (98%) had vital status at completion, with only 10 (3 withdrew consent, 7 lost to follow-up; 7 vs 3 by arm) lacking follow-up. The SAP slope is computed per participant from all eGFR values with no imputation, so participants lacking follow-up are about 2% of those randomized, too few to change a continuous-outcome mean difference of 2.46 materially. Probably yes rather than Yes because the number contributing at least two eGFR values to the slope is not reported.

The outcome is an automated laboratory value (serum creatinine converted to eGFR by formula), so the assessor is the laboratory process. Patients, investigators, site staff and sponsors were masked to treatment assignment with matching placebo, and no report indicates unblinding. Assessors are therefore probably unaware.

Both arms followed the same visit schedule (monthly for 3 months, every 3 months to month 12, then annually) with the same creatinine measurement and eGFR equation. Participants and staff were masked, and the intervention involved no additional contacts compared with placebo. The result relies on scheduled measurements, not passive detection.

eGFR was calculated with the CKD-EPI equation from serum creatinine, measured with IDMS-traceable calibration (enzymatic method in a single central laboratory in China, local laboratories elsewhere), and the slope was a prespecified secondary end point computed from all eGFR values (SAP 3.10.2.2). This is a standard, valid method for kidney function decline.

The SAP pre-specifies the slope analysis and two sensitivity analyses; Table 2 reports all three (all visits, excluding high-exposure values, excluding treatment values) with consistent effects. The mixed-model trajectory analysis is a separate prespecified analysis of trajectory, not the slope result. No evidence that analyses were run and selectively withheld.

eGFR is a single creatinine-derived measure (CKD-EPI, central lab) taken on a fixed visit schedule, and the SAP defines the slope from all available eGFR values per patient. The registry lists one annual eGFR decline outcome. The report presents that slope using all visits plus the two pre-specified exclusion variants, so no eligible alternative measurement appears omitted.

The registry record, first submitted 2012-03-15 before the 2012-05-05 start, lists secondary outcome 4 'Annual eGFR decline rate' (1-6 years). The SAP (v1.0, 4 March 2016, and the final v1.0 of 21JUL2021, which states 'Changes in Planned Analysis: Not applicable') pre-specifies the per-patient slope of all eGFR values compared by t-test, with sensitivity analyses excluding high-dose exposure values. The report names the same outcome and the same three variants, analysed by randomized group. No interim efficacy analysis was done, although high-dose cohort interim results were unblinded and published in 2017.

Equal group sizes (60/60/60) match the 1:1:1 ratio. Table 1 shows similar age, sex, weight, BMI, cavitation, HIV, and baseline bacillary load; the noted differences (smear grade 3+ 60% vs 47-48%, small weight differences) are compatible with chance.

The sequence resided in the EDC system; only pharmacy staff received the arm assignment from the EDC and prepared study-drug kits, while all other staff were blinded. Varying block sizes limit predictability. This supports concealment from enrolling personnel, though the exact release mechanism is not detailed.

Participants were 'randomly allocated (1:1:1) in blocks of varying size'; the sequence was generated by the study statistician and programmed into the EDC system. Varying block sizes and a statistician-generated programmed sequence make a random component reasonable to assume, although the method and random order within blocks are not explicitly stated in the main report.

All 180 randomized participants (60 per arm) were included in the safety analysis, which covers the SAE counts in Table 5 with a denominator of 60 per arm. Analysis was by randomized arm (trend test across assigned doses). The sensitivity analysis excluding halt periods is secondary.

The registry describes a double-blinded trial in which subjects, clinicians and laboratory staff were blinded, with matched placebo capsules making up the additional rifampin capsules so every patient in a weight band received the same number of tablets. Nothing in the report suggests blinding failed.

The allocation sequence was held in the EDC system; only pharmacy staff, who prepared the kits, received arm assignments, and all other staff were blinded. Pharmacy staff did not supervise treatment or grade outcomes. Registry masking lists participant, care provider and outcomes assessor.

All 180 randomized participants (60 per arm) were included in the safety analysis, and Table 5 uses n = 60 per arm as denominators. SAEs were captured at every study contact (daily DOT in the intensive phase) and reported for the entire study. Registry flow shows 48/48/47 completed, so about 9 withdrawals/losses overall, but the safety analysis still counted all randomized participants; SAEs occurring before dropout are captured, and the extent of SAE ascertainment after dropout is not fully documented.

Randomization was programmed in the EDC and only pharmacy staff saw assignments. The site PI had no access to the randomization code except in emergencies. The registry lists masking of participant, care provider and outcomes assessor, with a placebo matched to the additional rifampin capsules. Assessors of SAEs were therefore probably unaware of assignment.

All three arms followed the same schedule with the same visits, daily DOT contacts in the intensive phase, and the same SAE definitions and reporting rules. The arms differed only in rifampin dose, so no arm had extra visits or passive detection. The main report states SAEs were analyzed identically in all arms.

SAEs were assessed with a protocol-defined system: standard DMID serious criteria, AEs triaged at every contact, SAEs reported to the sponsor within 24 hours, and followed to resolution (protocol p93). Table E7 lists each SAE by category. Nothing suggests the method was insensitive or invalid.

The analysis is a simple count of participants with SAEs with a pre-specified one-sided Cochran-Armitage trend test, used identically across all safety outcomes. The report adds a time-to-event log-rank approach and a halt-exclusion sensitivity analysis, but no evidence suggests analyses were run and selectively reported. Reporting sensitivity analyses argues against selection.

An SAE is a defined event with one measurement (participant had at least one SAE), and Table 5 reports both the entire-study and safety-period windows, with Table E7 listing every SAE. No alternative scales or definitions exist from which one could have been chosen, and all windows are reported.

Protocol v7.0 (25 Sept 2014, during blinded enrolment, which began 2013-09) states a safety analysis plan including secondary analyses of all SAEs, ITT analysis, and a full SAP completed before any analyses. The report follows this: Methods say SAEs got similar tests (Cochran-Armitage for proportions) as the main AE endpoint, and Table 5 reports SAEs for the entire study and the safety period. The trial was double-blind, so outcome data were not unblinded to investigators before the plan was fixed. The exact SAP and its date are not in the Sources.
